preamble: An Act to consolidate and amend the law relating to Criminal Procedure.

glossary.audio-video electronic means: Real-time transmission technology (video-conferencing or similar) permitted under the Sanhita for taking evidence, conducting examinations, or ensuring a party's presence/participation without requiring physical attendance at the same location.
glossary.bail: Release of a person accused or suspected of an offence from custody, on conditions imposed by an officer or Court, on execution of a bond or bail bond.
glossary.bailable offence: An offence shown as bailable in the First Schedule, or made bailable by any other law in force.
glossary.non-bailable offence: Any offence that is not a bailable offence.
glossary.bail bond: A written undertaking executed by an accused person (and, where required, sureties) to secure their release from custody, promising appearance before the court as directed.
glossary.bond: A written undertaking, with or without sureties, by which a person binds themselves to appear before a court or officer when required, or to perform some other stated obligation.
glossary.charge: The formal, written accusation framed by a Court stating the specific offence (and the law/section under which it is punishable) that an accused must answer at trial — the document that fixes the boundaries of what the prosecution must prove and what the accused must defend against.
glossary.cognizable offence: An offence for which a police officer may arrest without a warrant and start an investigation without prior permission of a Magistrate — typically the more serious category of offence, as classified in the First Schedule to this Sanhita.
glossary.cognizable case: A case involving a cognizable offence.
glossary.complaint: An oral or written allegation to a Magistrate that a person has committed an offence, with a view to the Magistrate taking action, but not including a police report.
glossary.electronic communication: Communication of written, verbal, pictorial, or video content transmitted between persons or devices by means of an electronic device such as a phone, computer, or camera.
glossary.high court: The High Court for a State, or the corresponding High Court/highest criminal appellate court for a Union territory.
glossary.inquiry: Every inquiry, other than a trial, conducted under the Sanhita by a Magistrate or Court.
glossary.investigation: All proceedings under the Sanhita for the collection of evidence, conducted by a police officer or a person authorised by a Magistrate.
glossary.judicial proceeding: Any proceeding in the course of which evidence is or may legally be taken on oath.
glossary.local jurisdiction: The geographical area over which a particular court has authority to inquire into and try offences, ordinarily the district or region assigned to it.
glossary.non-cognizable offence: An offence for which a police officer has no authority to arrest without a warrant and cannot investigate without the order of a Magistrate — typically a less serious category of offence, as classified in the First Schedule to this Sanhita.
glossary.non-cognizable case: A case involving a non-cognizable offence.
glossary.notification: A notification published in the Official Gazette.
glossary.offence: Any act or omission made punishable by any law in force, including certain acts under the Cattle Trespass Act, 1871.
glossary.officer in charge of a police station: Includes, when the regular officer in charge is absent or unable to act, the next-in-rank officer present above the rank of constable, or another officer so directed by the State Government.
glossary.place: Includes a house, building, tent, vehicle and vessel.
glossary.police report: A report forwarded by a police officer to a Magistrate under sub-section (3) of section 193.
glossary.police station: Any post or place declared by the State Government to be a police station, including any local area so specified.
glossary.public prosecutor: The government-appointed law officer conducting prosecutions on behalf of the State; for the specially protected category of defamation complaints under section 222(2), only the Public Prosecutor (not a private complainant) may set the case in motion before a Court of Session, and only with prior government sanction. Within the appeals framework (Chapter XXXI), the Public Prosecutor is entitled to notice and hearing on the State's behalf (sections 426, 427) and is the officer directed to actually present a State/Central Government appeal against an inadequate sentence (section 418) or an acquittal (section 419).
glossary.sub-division: A territorial sub-unit of a district, created by the State Government after consultation with the High Court.
glossary.summons-case: A case relating to an offence not punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for a term exceeding two years -- the counterpart to a 'warrant-case'. Summons-cases follow a simpler, less formal trial procedure (Chapter XXI) since a formal charge need not be framed.
glossary.victim: A person who has suffered loss or injury caused by, or as a result of, the act or omission for which the accused has been charged, and includes the person's guardian or legal heir in appropriate cases.
glossary.warrant-case: A case relating to an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for a term exceeding two years -- as opposed to a 'summons-case', which covers offences not punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding two years. Warrant-cases follow a more elaborate trial procedure (Chapter XX) reflecting the greater stakes involved.
glossary.construction of references: The interpretive rule for how references to undefined terms in other laws are to be read under this Sanhita.
glossary.judicial magistrate: A Magistrate exercising judicial functions, such as appreciating evidence or making decisions exposing a person to punishment, detention, or trial.
glossary.executive magistrate: A Magistrate exercising executive (as opposed to judicial) functions under the Sanhita, such as initiating preventive security proceedings for keeping the peace or good behaviour.
glossary.bharatiya nyaya sanhita: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — India's substantive criminal (penal) code, replacing the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
glossary.saving clause: A statutory provision preserving the operation of other laws or rights that would otherwise be affected by the new enactment.
glossary.special law: A law applicable to a particular subject matter, as distinct from a general law.
glossary.local law: A law applicable only to a particular part of the country.
glossary.criminal courts: The classes of courts constituted under the Sanhita for criminal trials: Courts of Session, Judicial Magistrates (first and second class), and Executive Magistrates.
glossary.court of session: The principal criminal trial court of a sessions division, presided over by a Sessions Judge appointed by the High Court.
glossary.sessions division: An administrative territorial unit into which a State is divided for the organisation of Courts of Session, distinct from ordinary district boundaries.
glossary.district: A territorial sub-unit of a sessions division, for the purposes of the Sanhita.
glossary.sessions judge: The presiding judicial officer of a Court of Session, appointed by the High Court.
glossary.additional sessions judge: A judge appointed to assist a Sessions Judge in a sessions division, empowered to try cases specifically made over by the Sessions Judge or directed by the High Court.
glossary.chief judicial magistrate: The senior-most Judicial Magistrate in a district, responsible for administrative control over subordinate Magistrates, including empowering, assigning, and transferring cases among them.
glossary.additional chief judicial magistrate: A Judicial Magistrate of the first class appointed to exercise some or all powers of the Chief Judicial Magistrate.
glossary.sub-divisional judicial magistrate: A Judicial Magistrate of the first class designated to supervise Judicial Magistrates within a sub-division.
glossary.special judicial magistrate: A government post-holder conferred Judicial Magistrate powers by the High Court for particular cases or areas, for a term not exceeding one year at a time.
glossary.special court: A Court of Judicial Magistrates established for a particular case or class of cases, with exclusive jurisdiction over that category in its local area.
glossary.district magistrate: The senior Executive Magistrate in charge of a district, vested with specific powers under the Sanhita including release and supervision functions relating to security proceedings.
glossary.additional district magistrate: An Executive Magistrate appointed to exercise some or all powers of the District Magistrate.
glossary.sub-divisional magistrate: An Executive Magistrate exercising authority over a sub-division of a district, who may receive warrantless-arrest reports under Section 59 if the District Magistrate so directs.
glossary.special executive magistrate: An Executive Magistrate or senior police officer (Superintendent of Police rank or above) appointed for particular areas or functions, for a fixed term.
glossary.commissioner of police: A senior police officer who may, under other laws, be conferred some or all powers of an Executive Magistrate.
glossary.additional public prosecutor: A law officer appointed to assist or act alongside the Public Prosecutor.
glossary.special public prosecutor: An advocate of at least ten years' practice appointed by the Central or State Government to conduct a particular case or class of cases.
glossary.assistant public prosecutor: A law officer appointed to conduct prosecutions in the Courts of Magistrates.
glossary.panel of names: A list of persons considered fit for appointment as Public Prosecutor or Additional Public Prosecutor, prepared by the District Magistrate in consultation with the Sessions Judge.
glossary.cadre of prosecuting officers: A regular service cadre in a State that includes the post of Public Prosecutor and provides for promotion of Assistant Public Prosecutors to that post.
glossary.directorate of prosecution: A State-level body headed by the Director of Prosecution, functioning under the Home Department, overseeing and monitoring prosecution of criminal cases.
glossary.director of prosecution: The head of the State's Directorate of Prosecution, responsible for monitoring the most serious criminal cases.
glossary.deputy director of prosecution: An officer of the Directorate of Prosecution responsible for scrutinising police reports and monitoring mid-severity criminal cases.
glossary.assistant director of prosecution: An officer of the District Directorate of Prosecution responsible for monitoring less serious criminal cases.
glossary.first schedule: The Schedule to the Sanhita classifying offences by their triable court, cognizability, and bailability.
glossary.community service: Unremunerated work ordered by a Court as a form of punishment that benefits the community, available as a sentencing option to Magistrates.
glossary.default imprisonment: Imprisonment imposed in lieu of payment of a fine, subject to statutory caps under Section 24.
glossary.consecutive sentences: Sentences for multiple offences at one trial that run one after another, subject to statutory caps on the aggregate term.
glossary.concurrent sentences: Sentences for multiple offences at one trial that run simultaneously.
glossary.successor-in-office: The person who succeeds a Judge or Magistrate in an office, and who may exercise the powers and duties of that office in ongoing proceedings.
glossary.superior officers of police: Police officers ranked above the officer in charge of a police station, holding equivalent powers across their appointed local area.
glossary.breach of the peace: Conduct that disturbs public order or tranquillity, or is likely to provoke violence or disorder.
glossary.proclaimed offender: A person formally declared as such by a Court under Section 84(4), after failing to appear pursuant to a proclamation, where the underlying offence is punishable with 10+ years' imprisonment, life imprisonment, or death.
glossary.village headman: The senior officer or functionary responsible for administration of a village, included within the meaning of an officer employed in connection with the affairs of a village.
glossary.panchayat: The local self-government body of a village.
glossary.reasons in writing: A police officer's documented justification, required under Section 35, for making or not making an arrest in specified circumstances.
glossary.notice of appearance: A written direction issued by a police officer under Section 35(3) requiring a person to appear before him instead of being arrested.
glossary.memorandum of arrest: A written record of an arrest, prepared by the arresting officer, attested by a witness and countersigned by the person arrested.
glossary.designated police officer: A police officer, appointed under Section 37, responsible for maintaining and prominently displaying up-to-date information about arrested persons and the police officers who arrested/hold them, and for receiving arrest-notification information under Section 48.
glossary.police control room: A facility established by the State Government at the district and State level to coordinate and record policing information, including arrests.
glossary.citizen's arrest: The power of a private person to arrest another who commits a non-bailable and cognizable offence in his presence, or who is a proclaimed offender.
glossary.surety: A person who undertakes responsibility for ensuring another person's compliance with bail or bond conditions.
glossary.armed forces of the union: The military forces of India (Army, Navy, Air Force, and other forces raised and maintained by the Union) as distinguished from state police and other civil armed forces.
glossary.submission to custody: An arrested person's acknowledgment of arrest by word or conduct, which may substitute for actual physical touch or confinement.
glossary.free ingress: Unobstructed entry into a place, which an occupier must afford to an arresting officer or warrant-holder on demand.
glossary.registered medical practitioner: A medical practitioner who holds a recognised medical qualification and is enrolled on a State or National Medical Register — as defined in section 51, and required to conduct the medical examination of a rape victim under section 184.
glossary.medical officer: A doctor in the service of the Central Government or a State Government, the primary examiner responsible for checking every arrested person's physical condition soon after arrest under Section 53.
glossary.dna profiling: A forensic technique for identifying an individual from biological material (such as blood, hair, or bodily fluids) by analysing distinctive patterns in their DNA — routinely used in sexual offence investigations, including the medical examination under section 184.
glossary.twenty-four hours: The maximum period, exclusive of journey time to the Magistrate's Court, that a person arrested without warrant may be held in police custody without a Magistrate's special order under Section 187 (Section 58).
glossary.special order: A specific judicial order by a Magistrate under Section 187 authorising continued police custody of an arrested person beyond the ordinary 24-hour limit.
glossary.lawful custody: Custody that is legally authorised — for example, custody following a valid arrest or under a court order — as distinguished from unlawful detention.
glossary.presiding officer: The judge or Magistrate in charge of a Court, whose signature (or that of an officer the High Court authorises) is required on a summons or warrant issued by that Court.
glossary.digital signature: An electronic form of signature recognised as equivalent to a physical signature for authenticating an encrypted or electronic summons or warrant under the Sanhita.
glossary.due diligence: Genuine, reasonable effort — as opposed to a token or perfunctory attempt — required before a Court or officer may resort to a substituted mode of service (family-member service or affixation) instead of personal service.
glossary.conspicuous part: A visible, noticeable location on a house or homestead (such as a main door) where a summons duplicate is affixed as a last-resort mode of service under Section 67.
glossary.affidavit: A written statement of facts, sworn or affirmed to be true before an authorised officer (a Judge, Magistrate, Commissioner of Oaths, or notary), which may be used as evidence in place of the deponent's oral testimony, subject to the Court's power to summon the deponent for cross-examination.
glossary.escaped convict: A person who has broken out of lawful custody after conviction, against whom a Chief Judicial Magistrate or first-class Magistrate may direct a warrant to any person under Section 75.
glossary.thirty kilometres: The proximity threshold under Section 82 within which a person arrested outside the issuing Court's district may be produced directly before that Court instead of the local Executive Magistrate/DSP/Commissioner.
glossary.removal in custody: The process of transferring an arrested person, under police escort, from the place/authority of arrest to the Court that issued the warrant against them.
glossary.proclamation: A public notice issued by a Court under Section 84, requiring a person against whom a warrant cannot be executed (because they have absconded or are concealing themselves) to appear at a specified place and time, not less than 30 days from publication.
glossary.conclusive evidence: Evidence that is treated as legally decisive and not open to rebuttal, as with a Court's written statement of due publication of a proclamation under Section 84(3).
glossary.attachment: A legal process by which property is taken into the custody of the law (a Court or Magistrate) so that it cannot be transferred, damaged, or dealt with, pending resolution of a dispute over it or to secure recovery of a sum due.
glossary.receiver: A person appointed by a Court (or, under section 165, by a Magistrate) to take custody of and manage disputed property pending the resolution of a dispute over who is entitled to possess it, protecting the property from waste or loss in the meantime.
glossary.collector: The senior revenue officer of a district, through whom attachment of revenue-paying land is carried out under Section 85(4).
glossary.contracting state: A foreign State with which India has reciprocal arrangements for legal assistance in criminal matters, as governed by Chapter VIII, relevant to cross-border identification and forfeiture of a proclaimed person's property under Section 86.
glossary.net proceeds: The amount realised from the sale of attached property after deducting all costs incurred as a consequence of the attachment, as restored to a person under Section 88(3).
glossary.digital evidence: Evidence in electronic form, including data stored on or transmitted by communication devices, expressly covered by the production-summons power under Section 94.
glossary.search-warrant: A written order issued by a court or magistrate authorising a named person to search a specified place for specified items and, if found, to seize them.
glossary.proceeds of crime: Property derived or obtained, directly or indirectly, as a result of criminal activity or the commission of an offence, liable to attachment, forfeiture, or victim-restitution under Section 107.
glossary.show cause: A formal notice requiring a person to explain, within a specified period (14 days under Section 107), why an adverse order (such as attachment) should not be made against them.
glossary.ex parte order: An order made by a Court after hearing only one side, typically because the other party failed to appear or respond despite being given the opportunity.
glossary.rateably distribute: To divide proceeds of crime proportionately among all persons affected by the crime, as directed by the District Magistrate under Section 107(6)-(7).
glossary.forfeited to government: The legal consequence, under Sections 98 and 107, by which ownership of specified property (unlawful publications, or unclaimed/surplus proceeds of crime) vests in the Government.
glossary.impound: To take and retain official custody of a document or thing, as a Court may do under Section 109 in respect of anything produced before it.
glossary.letter of request: A formal request issued by a Court or competent authority to a Court or authority in another country (or received from one), asking for assistance such as examining a witness, recording a statement, or producing documents/things relevant to a criminal investigation.
glossary.administrator: The District Magistrate (or an officer nominated by them) appointed by the Court to receive, manage, and eventually dispose of property that has been seized, attached, or forfeited under Chapter VIII.
glossary.tracing: Determining the nature, source, disposition, movement, title, or ownership of property — the investigative process of following an asset's history and trail.
glossary.identifying: Establishing proof that property was derived from, or used in, the commission of an offence.
glossary.person affected: The person against whom a notice of forfeiture under section 119 is issued — i.e., the owner (or apparent owner) of property alleged to be proceeds of crime.
glossary.market value: The price the property would fetch if sold in the open market, used as the basis for calculating a fine in lieu of forfeiture under section 121.
glossary.null and void: Legally without effect from the outset, as if it never happened — used here to strip legal effect from property transfers made to defeat an attachment or forfeiture proceeding.
glossary.public tranquillity: The state of calm and order in society that the criminal law seeks to protect and preserve.
glossary.habitual offender: A person who, by pattern of repeated conduct (not a single isolated act), commits or is involved in specified categories of offences such as theft, receiving stolen property, or breach of the peace.
glossary.sureties: Persons who undertake, by executing a bond, to be answerable for another person's compliance with the terms of that bond (such as keeping the peace or maintaining good behaviour), and who may be held liable if the bond is breached.
glossary.general repute: A person's reputation in the community, admissible as evidence to prove a fact such as habitual criminal conduct, without requiring proof of specific individual acts.
glossary.sufficient means: The financial capacity of a person to provide maintenance to a dependant, a threshold that must be proved before a maintenance order can be made under section 144.
glossary.just ground: A legally sufficient reason recognised by the Magistrate for a wife's refusal to resume living with her husband, such as his having contracted another marriage or keeping a mistress.
glossary.interim maintenance: A monthly allowance and proceeding expenses ordered by the Magistrate to a dependant while a maintenance application under section 144 is still pending, meant to provide urgent relief before the case is finally decided.
glossary.wilfully avoiding service: Deliberately evading being served with legal process, a ground on which a Magistrate may proceed to hear and decide a maintenance case ex parte.
glossary.unlawful assembly: An assembly of five or more persons with a common object that falls within the categories made unlawful under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (e.g., to overawe by criminal force, commit mischief, or use criminal force to achieve an unlawful common object). Section 148 also extends dispersal powers to any assembly of five or more persons merely likely to disturb the public peace, even before it becomes technically 'unlawful.'
glossary.public nuisance: An act, omission, or state of affairs that causes injury, danger, or annoyance to the public or to people generally who dwell or occupy property in the vicinity, or that obstructs the public's lawful use of a way, river, channel, or public place. Chapter XI Part B (sections 152-162) gives Magistrates summary powers to order removal or regulation of public nuisances.
glossary.sanction: Formal prior authorisation or approval required from a specified higher authority before a particular action (such as prosecution or a particular procedural step) may be taken.
glossary.conditional order: An order made under section 152 that is not yet final — it directs the person concerned either to perform a specified act (such as removing an obstruction) within a fixed time, or to appear and show cause why the order should not be made absolute.
glossary.absolute order: The final, binding form that a conditional order under section 152 takes once the person against whom it is made either defaults entirely (triggering section 155) or appears, shows cause, and fails to satisfy the Magistrate that the order is unreasonable (section 157).
glossary.easement: A legal right to use land or water belonging to someone else in a specific limited way — for example, a right of way, a right to draw water, or a right of passage — without owning it.
glossary.ex parte: A proceeding, order, or hearing conducted for the benefit of, or on the application of, one party only, without requiring the presence or participation of the other side — typically used for urgent situations where advance notice is impracticable or would defeat the purpose of the order.
glossary.affray: A disturbance caused by two or more persons fighting in a public place in a manner that alarms the public; one of the harms sections 162 and 163 empower a Magistrate to prevent.
glossary.local inquiry: A fact-finding inquiry conducted at or near the site of a dispute or matter in issue, typically deputed by a Magistrate to a subordinate officer or Magistrate, whose report may then be read as evidence in the case.
glossary.first information report: Commonly abbreviated FIR — the written record an officer in charge of a police station makes under section 173 of information about a cognizable offence, whether given orally or by electronic communication, which sets the investigation machinery in motion.
glossary.prima facie case: A case that, on the face of the material available, appears to disclose sufficient grounds to proceed further — not a final finding of guilt, but enough to justify continuing an inquiry, preliminary enquiry, or investigation.
glossary.public servant: A person holding a public office or performing public duties, as defined for criminal-law purposes in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — includes government officials, and receives special procedural protections, such as the sanction requirement before prosecution and the safeguards in section 175(4) before a Magistrate can order investigation of a complaint against one arising from official duties.
glossary.forensic expert: A trained specialist in scientific crime-scene examination (e.g., fingerprints, DNA, ballistics, trace evidence) whose visit to the crime scene is now mandatory under section 176(3) for offences punishable with seven years' imprisonment or more, to collect and preserve forensic evidence, videographed as part of the process.
glossary.confession: A statement made by an accused person admitting guilt or acknowledging incriminating facts about an offence, which — if recorded voluntarily before a Magistrate under section 183, with the required warnings and safeguards — may be used as evidence against the maker at trial.
glossary.self-incrimination: The constitutional and evidentiary protection (reflected in section 180(2) and Article 20(3) of the Constitution) that a person questioned during investigation cannot be compelled to answer questions whose answers would expose them to a criminal charge, penalty, or forfeiture.
glossary.examination-in-chief: The first stage of questioning a witness at trial, conducted by the party who called that witness, before the witness is cross-examined by the opposing side. Under section 183(6)(b), a disabled victim's pre-recorded statement can substitute for a live examination-in-chief.
glossary.case-diary: The day-to-day record a police officer is required to maintain of the proceedings in an investigation, including grounds of belief, steps taken, and reasoning.
glossary.remand: A Magistrate's order authorising the continued custody (police or judicial) of a person already arrested, pending further investigation or trial.
glossary.case diary: The day-by-day official record a police officer must maintain during an investigation, recording the time information was received, steps taken, places visited, and circumstances ascertained; distinct from a witness statement, and not itself evidence.
glossary.inquest: A preliminary police or magisterial inquiry into the apparent cause of an unnatural or suspicious death, aimed at establishing how the death occurred before any formal offence investigation begins.
glossary.civil surgeon: A government-appointed medical officer, typically heading district-level medical services, designated to conduct post-mortem and other medico-legal examinations under criminal procedure law.
glossary.further investigation: Additional investigation conducted by police into an offence after a final report has already been forwarded to the Magistrate, upon discovery of fresh oral or documentary evidence.
glossary.chargesheet: The common name for the police report filed under section 193 (the erstwhile 'charge-sheet') at the conclusion of investigation, stating whether an offence appears to have been committed and by whom, forming the basis for the Magistrate to take cognizance.
glossary.continuing offence: An offence that is not complete in a single act but continues to be committed over time and potentially across more than one place, such as ongoing unlawful confinement or continuing nuisance.
glossary.dacoity: Robbery committed jointly by five or more persons, a specifically defined and aggravated form of robbery under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
glossary.criminal breach of trust: An offence where a person entrusted with property, or with dominion over property, dishonestly misappropriates or converts it to their own use in violation of that trust.
glossary.venue: The particular court or place, among those otherwise having jurisdiction, where a case is actually inquired into or tried.
glossary.cognizance: The formal application of judicial mind by a Magistrate or court to the facts of a case for the purpose of proceeding further, marking the point at which a court becomes seized of a matter.
glossary.extraterritorial jurisdiction: The power of a country's courts to inquire into and try offences committed outside its own territory, typically limited to offences by its own citizens or on its registered ships/aircraft.
glossary.deposition: The written record of a witness's evidence, taken down during an examination (including examination on commission), which can be read or received as evidence under specified conditions.
glossary.commission (for taking evidence): A court's formal authorisation to a designated person to record evidence at a place the court itself cannot conveniently visit, with the recorded evidence then read into the trial record.
glossary.committal: The formal procedure by which a Magistrate, after a preliminary inquiry, sends a case triable exclusively by a Court of Session to that Court, since a Court of Session generally cannot take original cognizance on its own.
glossary.criminal conspiracy: An agreement between two or more persons to commit an illegal act, or a legal act by illegal means, itself treated as a distinct offence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita even if the planned act is never carried out.
glossary.contempt of lawful authority: A category of offences (BNS Chapter X-type provisions) punishing disobedience to, or obstruction of, the lawful orders and processes of public servants and courts.
glossary.proclamation under article 356: The Constitutional mechanism (President's Rule) by which the President of India assumes the functions of a State Government when satisfied that the State's governance cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution.
glossary.preliminary investigation: A limited, sanction-preceding police inquiry ordered by government before deciding whether to accord sanction or consent to prosecute, distinct from a full investigation under Chapter XIII.
glossary.aggrieved person: The person directly harmed by an offence, whose complaint (or, in specified circumstances, a permitted relative's or representative's complaint) is legally required before certain offences can be prosecuted.
glossary.prima facie: On the face of it; a standard requiring enough apparent evidence to make out a case at first glance, without yet weighing it against a defence — used here as the threshold a Magistrate/Court must find before taking cognizance in specified sensitive offences.
glossary.commanding officer: The officer in charge of a member of the Armed Forces of the Union, whose certification and countersignature are required for that member's spouse to authorise someone else to file a complaint on their behalf when the member cannot obtain leave.
glossary.examination on oath: The Magistrate's recording of sworn statements from a complainant and any witnesses present, taken to establish a preliminary basis before the case proceeds, distinct from the fuller trial-stage examination.
glossary.process (issue of): A court's formal act of compelling an accused person's appearance or the production of evidence, typically by summons or warrant, marking the start of active proceedings against the accused.
glossary.sufficient ground for proceeding: The threshold finding a Magistrate must reach — based on the complainant's sworn statement, witness statements, and any inquiry or investigation — before issuing process against an accused; absence of this ground requires dismissal of the complaint.
glossary.petty offence: An offence punishable only with a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees, excluding Motor Vehicles Act offences and other offences whose law already allows conviction in absentia on a guilty plea — eligible for the simplified special-summons procedure.
glossary.process-fees: Statutory fees payable for the issuance of court process (such as summons or warrants); non-payment within a reasonable time can lead to dismissal of the complaint.
glossary.compounding (of offence): The legally permitted settlement of certain offences between the complainant/victim and the accused, which brings the criminal proceeding to an end without a full trial, available only for offences the Sanhita specifically designates as compoundable.
glossary.complaint case: A criminal proceeding instituted otherwise than on a police report — that is, begun directly on a private or authorised complaint, or on the Magistrate's own information/knowledge — as distinguished from a police-report (chargesheet) case.
glossary.illustration: A short hypothetical example appended to a statutory provision to show how the rule applies in practice — illustrations are not independent law but aids to interpreting the section they accompany.
glossary.joinder of charges: The rule-set governing when multiple distinct offences (or multiple accused persons) may lawfully be combined into a single charge and tried together in one trial, rather than requiring a separate charge and separate trial for each offence.
glossary.same transaction: A series of acts so connected in purpose, time, and continuity that they form one continuous course of criminal conduct — the legal test that allows multiple offences arising from that connected conduct to be charged and tried together instead of separately.
glossary.acquittal: A formal finding or legal outcome that the accused is not held guilty of the charge — either by the Court's decision after trial, or, as under section 247, by operation of law when a remaining charge is withdrawn or its trial stayed after conviction on another charge from the same charge-sheet.
glossary.conviction: The Court's formal finding, after trial, that the accused is guilty of the offence charged.
glossary.discharge: An order releasing an accused person from a case before trial proper begins, made when the Judge finds insufficient ground to proceed against him — distinct from an acquittal, which follows a full trial on the merits.
glossary.plea: The accused's formal response to a charge once it has been read and explained to him — typically either pleading guilty (admitting the offence) or claiming to be tried (denying it and requiring the prosecution to prove its case).
glossary.cross-examination: The questioning of a witness by the opposing party (typically the defence, for a prosecution witness) after that witness's initial examination, aimed at testing or challenging the witness's testimony.
glossary.in camera: A trial or hearing conducted privately, with the general public excluded from the courtroom — as opposed to an open, public hearing.
glossary.compensation: A sum of money ordered to be paid, under section 260, by a person whose unfounded accusation led to a discharge or acquittal, to the wrongly accused person -- distinct from a fine, though recovered in the same manner as one.
glossary.summons: A written order issued by a Court or Magistrate directing a person to appear before it, or to produce a document or other thing, on a specified date.
glossary.cross-examine: To question a witness called by the opposing party, typically to test, challenge, or undermine the witness's earlier testimony given in examination-in-chief.
glossary.re-examination: The further questioning of a witness by the party who originally called them, conducted after cross-examination, generally limited to clarifying matters raised during cross-examination.
glossary.complainant: The person who sets criminal proceedings in motion by lodging a complaint before a Magistrate, alleging that an offence has been committed.
glossary.compound: To settle or resolve a criminal case by private agreement between the complainant/victim and the accused, permitted only for certain offences specified by law, resulting in acquittal of the accused.
glossary.summary trial: An abbreviated trial procedure (Chapter XXII) for certain minor offences, in which the Magistrate follows summons-case procedure but with a simplified, condensed record and judgment, and a maximum sentence of three months' imprisonment.
glossary.plea bargaining: A pre-trial process (Chapter XXIII) in which an accused, having applied voluntarily, negotiates with the prosecution/complainant and victim to work out a mutually satisfactory disposition of the case -- typically involving compensation to the victim and a reduced sentence -- in exchange for the accused's cooperation, without a full contested trial.
glossary.probation: A method of dealing with certain offenders, particularly first-time or less serious offenders, by releasing them under supervision or on a bond of good conduct instead of, or after, imposing an ordinary sentence of imprisonment.
glossary.special leave petition: A discretionary petition filed directly before the Supreme Court of India under Article 136 of the Constitution, seeking permission to appeal against any judgment, decree, determination, sentence, or order passed by any court or tribunal in the country.
glossary.writ petition: A petition filed before the High Court (under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution) or the Supreme Court, invoking the court's constitutional power to issue directions, orders, or writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights or for any other purpose, or to exercise superintendence over subordinate courts and tribunals.
glossary.set off: The process of crediting, or deducting, a period the accused has already spent in detention (e.g., as an undertrial) against the total term of imprisonment ultimately imposed as a sentence, so the accused does not serve that period twice.
glossary.non obstante clause: A statutory clause (typically beginning "notwithstanding") that gives the provision it introduces overriding effect over anything inconsistent in other provisions of the same or another law.
glossary.preventive detention: Detention of a person by state authority not as punishment for a proven offence, but to prevent them from committing a future act prejudicial to public order, security, or similar specified interests, typically under a special preventive detention law.
glossary.subsidiary jail: A place declared by the State Government, by general or special order, to function as a jail for the purposes of this Chapter, even though it may not be a full-fledged central or district prison.
glossary.borstal institution: A specialised institution for the reform and rehabilitation of young offenders, emphasising education and vocational training over ordinary imprisonment.
glossary.commission (examination on): A procedure under which a Court authorises a designated person (a commissioner) to record the evidence of a witness who cannot conveniently attend court in person, with the recorded evidence then read as evidence in the case.
glossary.countersign: A second, confirming signature (here, of the Chief Judicial Magistrate) required to validate certain orders made by a Magistrate of the second class before they can be acted upon by a prison official.
glossary.language of the court: The language which the State Government has determined, under section 307, to be the official language used for recording proceedings in a particular Court (other than the High Court) within that State.
glossary.memorandum (of evidence): A written note capturing the substance of a witness's evidence, made by the Magistrate as the examination proceeds, used in place of a full verbatim record in summons-cases and certain inquiries.
glossary.narrative form: A method of recording evidence as a continuous, connected written account in the witness's own words (as opposed to a strict question-and-answer transcript), which is the ordinary default method the Magistrate or Judge may depart from in appropriate cases.
glossary.demeanour: The manner, conduct, and bearing of a witness while giving evidence and under examination -- for example, hesitation, confidence, nervousness, or evasiveness -- which a Judge or Magistrate may note as relevant to assessing credibility.
glossary.interpreter: A person appointed by a Criminal Court to translate evidence or statements from one language into another so that the Court, the accused, or another participant can understand proceedings conducted in an unfamiliar language.
glossary.examination of accused: The formal questioning of the accused by the Court (distinct from witness examination), during which the accused is given an opportunity to explain circumstances appearing in the evidence against him; recorded in full under section 316.
glossary.interrogatories: A formal written list of questions submitted by a party to a proceeding, to be put to a witness being examined on commission, on matters the Court or Magistrate directing the commission considers relevant to the case.
glossary.adjournment: The postponement of a hearing, trial, or proceeding to a later date or time, here specifically to allow sufficient time for a commission to be executed and returned to the Court.
glossary.gazetted officer: A government official whose appointment, promotion, or transfer is published ("gazetted") in the official Gazette, marking a rank of formal seniority and authority -- here relevant to officers of Mints, Note/Security Printing Presses, and Forensic Departments whose reports can be used as evidence without their personal attendance.
glossary.deponent: The person who makes a deposition or swears an affidavit -- i.e., the individual whose sworn or recorded statement is being relied upon as evidence.
glossary.commissioner of oaths: A person appointed by a High Court or Court of Session specifically empowered to administer oaths and affirmations for affidavits used in judicial proceedings.
glossary.warrant of commitment: A formal document issued by a Court directing that a convicted person be taken into custody and detained in prison to undergo the sentence imposed, used here as one method of proving a previous conviction.
glossary.successor officer: The public servant, scientific expert, or medical officer who currently holds the post previously held by an officer who prepared a document or report but who has since been transferred, retired, died, or become otherwise unavailable -- the successor may give deposition on that document or report in the original officer's place.
glossary.double jeopardy: The legal principle, reflected in section 337, that a person once validly tried and convicted or acquitted of an offence by a competent Court cannot be tried again for the same offence (or substantially the same facts) while that conviction or acquittal stands -- subject to specific statutory exceptions.
glossary.autrefois acquit / autrefois convict: Latin-derived pleas ("previously acquitted" / "previously convicted") that an accused may raise to bar a second trial for the same offence, embodying the double jeopardy protection codified in section 337.
glossary.corporation: As defined in section 342, an incorporated company or other body corporate, including a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 -- capable of being an accused and appointing a representative to stand in for it during an inquiry or trial.
glossary.tender of pardon: A conditional offer by a Chief Judicial Magistrate or a first-class Magistrate to an accomplice, promising immunity from prosecution for a serious offence in exchange for a full and true disclosure of all facts known to him about the offence and everyone else involved -- the accomplice who accepts becomes an approver and must testify as a prosecution witness.
glossary.approver: An accomplice who has accepted a tender of pardon under section 343 or 344 and, in exchange for immunity, is examined as a prosecution witness and must truthfully disclose everything he knows about the offence and all persons involved, on pain of being tried himself if he breaches the condition of pardon.
glossary.legal aid: State-funded legal representation assigned to an accused person who is unrepresented and unable to afford an advocate, mandatory under section 341 once the Court identifies the need -- the practical mechanism giving effect to the constitutional right to a fair trial for indigent accused persons.
glossary.day-to-day trial: The default rule (section 346(1)) that an inquiry or trial must proceed continuously, on successive days, until all attending witnesses have been examined, unless the Court records reasons for adjourning beyond the following day -- aimed at preventing indefinite drift in criminal proceedings.
glossary.local inspection: A Judge's or Magistrate's visit to the scene of an alleged offence, or any other place relevant to properly appreciating the evidence, conducted after due notice to the parties, with a memorandum of observed facts recorded and made part of the case record.
glossary.specimen: A sample of a person's signature, finger impressions, handwriting, or voice, which a first-class Magistrate may order a person (including an accused) to provide for the purposes of an investigation or proceeding, ordinarily only if the person has been arrested in connection with that matter.
glossary.memorandum of arguments: A written note, submitted to the Court by a party after closing oral arguments, setting out concisely and under distinct headings the arguments supporting that party's case; it becomes part of the case record and a copy must be simultaneously given to the opposite party.
glossary.competent witness: A person legally qualified to give evidence in a proceeding; section 353 makes an accused person a competent witness for the defence, meaning he may testify on oath to disprove the charge, but only on his own written request, and his choice not to testify cannot be commented on or used to presume guilt.
glossary.in absentia: Latin for 'in the absence [of the person]' -- a trial, inquiry, or judgment conducted or pronounced without the accused being personally present, permitted under section 356 for a declared proclaimed offender who has absconded to evade trial, subject to strict procedural safeguards (repeated warrant attempts, public notice, a mandatory ninety-day wait, and State-funded defence counsel).
glossary.compounding of offences: A statutorily-permitted settlement of specified criminal offences between the offender and the victim (or another specified person), which has the legal effect of an acquittal; section 359 lists which offences may be compounded freely and which require the Court's permission, and bars compounding altogether where a previous conviction exposes the accused to enhanced punishment.
glossary.withdrawal from prosecution: The discontinuation of a criminal prosecution by the Public Prosecutor or Assistant Public Prosecutor, with the Court's consent, before judgment is pronounced -- resulting in discharge (if before charge) or acquittal (if after charge) of the accused for the withdrawn offence(s), subject to Central Government permission requirements for certain categories of cases and a mandatory hearing for the victim.
glossary.commitment (for trial): The formal act by which a Magistrate transfers a case beyond his own sentencing power to a higher forum -- the Chief Judicial Magistrate or the Court of Session -- so that a heavier or more appropriate sentence can be considered, or because the offence must by law be tried there.
glossary.successor judge or magistrate: A Judge or Magistrate who takes over a part-heard inquiry or trial from a predecessor who has ceased to exercise jurisdiction in it (whether through transfer, promotion, or otherwise); section 365 lets the successor act on evidence already recorded, while preserving a power to re-summon and further examine any witness where the interests of justice require it.
glossary.coinage: Currency in the form of coins (and, by extension under BNS Chapter X, Government stamps) -- offences against coinage include counterfeiting, altering, or dealing in counterfeit coin, treated as serious property-adjacent crimes carrying enhanced procedural consequences for repeat offenders under section 363.
glossary.open court: The default rule that a Criminal Court's proceedings are held in a place accessible to the public generally, subject to the presiding Judge or Magistrate's power to exclude the public (or particular persons) at any stage in a particular case, and subject to the mandatory in-camera rule for rape and specified sexual-offence trials under section 366(2).
glossary.unsound mind: A mental condition that renders an accused person incapable of understanding the proceedings against him or of making his defence; Chapter XXVII (sections 367-378) sets out a dedicated procedure -- medical examination, a capacity finding, possible postponement or discharge, and safeguards around detention or release -- that displaces the ordinary trial process whenever unsoundness of mind is credibly in issue.
glossary.intellectual disability: A disability involving significant limitations in intellectual functioning and adaptive behaviour, treated under Chapter XXVII as distinct from unsoundness of mind but given a parallel procedural track: if it renders the accused incapable of entering a defence, the Magistrate closes the inquiry (rather than postponing it) and deals with the accused under section 369's release/care framework.
glossary.mental healthcare act: The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 -- the central legislation governing the treatment, rights, and institutional care of persons with mental illness in India; BNSS's unsound-mind procedure defers to its rules whenever an accused is ordered detained in a public mental health establishment, ensuring criminal-process detention does not bypass that Act's safeguards.
glossary.sound mind: The mental capacity to know the nature of one's act and to know that it is wrong or contrary to law; section 372 addresses the situation where an accused is of sound mind at the time of inquiry or trial but is found to have been of unsound mind -- and thus incapable of that knowledge -- at the time the act was actually committed.
glossary.security: A formal guarantee -- typically a bond or undertaking, sometimes with a financial or personal surety -- given to a Magistrate or Court as assurance that a person delivered into someone's care will be properly looked after and prevented from causing harm to himself or others, and will be produced for inspection or before the authorities as directed; under section 374, a relative or friend seeking delivery of a person acquitted on unsoundness-of-mind grounds must give such security before the Court will release the person into their care.
glossary.inspector-general of prisons: The senior State official heading the prison administration of a State, responsible for the oversight, inspection, and welfare of persons confined in jails; under BNSS's unsound-mind provisions, the Inspector-General certifies whether a jail-detained accused has become capable of making his defence (section 376) or fit to be released without danger to himself or others (section 377), and the State Government may delegate these certifying functions to a jail's officer in charge under section 375.
glossary.mental health review board: A quasi-judicial body constituted under the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 to review and safeguard the rights of persons receiving mental healthcare, including reviewing admission and detention in mental health establishments; where a section 369 detainee is held in a public mental health establishment rather than a jail, it is this Board -- not the Inspector-General of Prisons -- that certifies capacity to stand trial under section 376.
glossary.bind over: To require a person, by a formal court order backed by a bond or security, to do (or refrain from doing) a specified act -- most commonly, to appear and give evidence at a future date; section 379 empowers a Court to bind over witnesses to appear before the Magistrate to whom it forwards a complaint regarding offences against the administration of justice.
glossary.commission: A body of designated persons formally appointed by an authority (here, the State Government) to investigate a specific question and report back, rather than the authority deciding the matter itself in the first instance; section 377(1) allows the State Government, when transferring a detained person to a public mental health establishment, to appoint a three-member Commission -- one Judicial officer and two medical officers -- to formally inquire into that person's state of mind and report a recommendation on release or detention.
glossary.revision: The supervisory jurisdiction of a superior Court -- the High Court or a Sessions Judge -- to call for and examine the record of a subordinate/inferior Criminal Court's proceeding, to correct errors of jurisdiction, law, or procedure (correctness, legality, or propriety of a finding, sentence, or order, and the regularity of the proceedings), without being a full-fledged appeal on facts (section 438). It cannot be exercised over interlocutory orders (section 438(2)), and is subject to a one-application rule: once a person applies to either the High Court or a Sessions Judge, no further application by that same person will be entertained by the other (sections 438(3), 440(3)). Section 380(2) specifically excludes orders under sections 379-380 from revision, making the appellate Court's decision on whether to lodge a complaint for offences against the administration of justice final and not open to further supervisory challenge.
glossary.costs: The expenses of litigation -- process-fees, witness expenses, advocate's fees, and similar prosecution or application expenses -- that a Court may order one party to pay to another as part of its order; under section 381 a Court may award costs on a section 379 complaint application or section 380 appeal as it thinks just, distinct from the separate cost-shifting power in section 400 for non-cognizable-offence prosecutions.
glossary.false evidence: Evidence given by a witness that he knows or believes to be untrue, or evidence (including a document or other material) fabricated with the intention that it be used as genuine in a judicial proceeding; section 383 lets the very Court before which such evidence was knowingly or wilfully given or fabricated try the witness summarily for it immediately upon delivering judgment in the underlying case, without needing a separate complaint process.
glossary.contempt: Conduct that disrespects, obstructs, or undermines the authority and dignity of a Court -- here, the specific set of offences against public justice (insult, interruption, or intentional obstruction of judicial proceedings, among others under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023) that section 384 allows a Civil, Criminal, or Revenue Court to punish summarily and on the spot when committed in its own view or presence, without the ordinary complaint-and-trial process.
glossary.registrar: An officer appointed under the Registration Act, 1908 to register documents (such as sale deeds, mortgages, and wills) within a defined jurisdiction, verifying execution and maintaining the official record of registered instruments; section 386 lets the State Government deem a Registrar a Civil Court for the limited purpose of exercising the contempt-handling powers under sections 384 and 385 over misconduct occurring in his registration proceedings.
glossary.sub-registrar: A subordinate registering officer under the Registration Act, 1908, exercising registration functions (typically at the taluka/sub-district level) under a Registrar's superintendence; like a Registrar, a Sub-Registrar can be deemed a Civil Court under section 386 when the State Government so directs, solely for handling contempt under sections 384-385.
glossary.apology: An offender's expression of regret and submission to a Court's order or requisition, tendered to the Court's satisfaction; section 387 lets a Court that has punished someone under section 384 (in-Court contempt) or forwarded him for trial under section 385, discharge him or remit his punishment entirely at its discretion once he submits to the Court's requirement or offers a satisfactory apology.
glossary.warrant: A written order issued by a Magistrate or Judge, under his own hand, authorising a specified officer to take a named person into custody -- here, used under section 388 to commit a witness or document-holder who refuses without reasonable excuse to answer questions or produce a document/thing to the custody of a court officer for up to seven days, as an alternative to a direct sentence of simple imprisonment.
glossary.court of small causes: A specialised civil court of limited pecuniary jurisdiction that tries small-value money claims through a simplified, speedy procedure, with normally very limited rights of appeal on the civil side; section 390(3) carves out a specific criminal-appeal route for BNSS summary convictions (sections 383, 384, 388, 389) handed down by such a Court, sending the appeal to the Court of Session for that sessions division rather than following the ordinary civil appellate hierarchy.
glossary.judgment: The formal decision of a Criminal Court disposing of a trial, stating the point(s) for determination, the decision on them, the reasons, and (on conviction) the offence and sentence, or (on acquittal) a direction that the accused be set at liberty; section 392 governs how and when it must be pronounced in open Court, and section 393 governs its required language and contents.
glossary.operative part: The specific portion of a judgment that actually grants relief or imposes a consequence -- the conviction/acquittal and sentence -- as distinct from the reasoning and discussion that precede it; section 392(1)(c) allows a presiding officer to pronounce judgment by reading out only the operative part and explaining the substance in a language the accused or his advocate understands, rather than reading the whole judgment aloud.
glossary.fatal accidents act: The Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 -- a civil statute allowing the legal representatives of a person wrongfully killed to recover damages from the person responsible for the death; section 395(1)(c) lets a Criminal Court, when sentencing someone for causing or abetting a death, direct fine-derived compensation to the persons who would be entitled to recover such damages under that Act, without them having to separately file a civil suit.
glossary.bona fide purchaser: A person who buys property genuinely and in good faith, for value, without knowledge that the seller lacked good title to it -- for instance, someone who innocently buys stolen property without knowing it was stolen; section 395(1)(d) lets a Court compensate such a purchaser out of recovered fine amounts if the property is later restored to its rightful owner, cushioning the innocent buyer's loss.
glossary.abetment: Intentionally instigating, engaging in a conspiracy for, or intentionally aiding the commission of an offence, without necessarily committing the offence itself; section 394(2) extends the residence-notification order to abetment (and conspiracy and attempt) of a qualifying repeat offence, and section 395(1)(c) extends fine-based compensation to cases of abetting a death, not just directly causing it.
glossary.victim compensation scheme: A State-Government scheme (prepared in coordination with the Central Government under section 396) that funds compensation and rehabilitation for crime victims or their dependents, administered case-by-case through the District or State Legal Services Authority, separate from and in addition to any fine-based compensation ordered by the trial Court itself.
glossary.legal services authority: The District Legal Services Authority or State Legal Services Authority -- statutory bodies (under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987) responsible under section 396 for deciding the quantum of victim compensation recommended by a Court, for receiving direct applications where no trial takes place because the offender is untraced, and for completing compensation enquiries within two months.
glossary.rehabilitation: The support -- financial, medical, or otherwise -- needed to help a crime victim or their dependents recover from the loss or injury caused by the offence; section 396 centres the victim compensation scheme explicitly around funding rehabilitation, not merely punishing the offender.
glossary.protection of children from sexual offen: The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (POCSO) -- a special statute criminalizing sexual offences against children; section 397 cross-references its sections 4, 6, 8, and 10 (penalties for penetrative sexual assault, aggravated penetrative sexual assault, sexual assault, and aggravated sexual assault) to extend the mandatory free first-aid/treatment and police-notification duty to child victims of those offences.
glossary.witness protection scheme: A scheme every State Government must prepare and notify under section 398 to ensure the protection of witnesses -- addressing threats, intimidation, or retaliation that could otherwise deter witnesses from testifying truthfully, complementing the victim-focused compensation and treatment provisions of sections 396 and 397.
glossary.admonition: A formal reprimand or caution given by a Court in lieu of any punishment -- section 401(3) allows a Court to release certain minor, first-time offenders (theft, dishonest misappropriation, cheating, or offences punishable with two years' imprisonment or less, or fine only) after due admonition, sparing them a criminal sentence given the trivial nature of the offence or extenuating circumstances.
glossary.recognizance: A formal, court-recorded undertaking (with or without sureties) by which a person binds himself to do or not do a specified act -- such as appearing to receive sentence and keeping the peace -- breach of which allows the Court to issue a warrant for his apprehension; section 401(1) conditions probationary release on the offender entering into such a bond, and section 401(8) ties its breach to re-arrest.
glossary.probation of offenders act: The Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 -- a separate central statute enabling release of certain offenders on probation instead of sentencing them to prison, operating alongside (not displaced by) section 401's own probation/admonition powers; section 401(10) and section 402 both expressly preserve its application.
glossary.juvenile justice act: The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 -- the special statute governing the treatment, training, and rehabilitation of children in conflict with law, whose application section 401(10) expressly preserves alongside BNSS's own probation and admonition provisions, and whose availability a Court must record special reasons for not using under section 402.
glossary.confirmation: The High Court's formal approval of a death sentence passed by a Court of Session, without which the sentence cannot be executed; section 407 makes such submission to the High Court mandatory and automatic, and section 409 sets out the High Court's options on confirmation -- confirm, pass a different lawful sentence, annul the conviction, or acquit.
glossary.annul: To formally cancel or invalidate a conviction, as if it had not been passed, while leaving open the possibility of convicting the accused afresh of a lawful offence or ordering a new trial; section 409(b) gives the High Court this power when reviewing a Court of Session's death sentence submitted for confirmation.
glossary.bench: A panel of two or more Judges of a High Court (or other Court) sitting together to hear and decide a case, as distinct from a Single Judge; section 411 addresses what happens when a death-sentence-confirmation Bench is equally divided in opinion, routing the case to the special procedure in section 433.
glossary.appeal: A statutory right to have a higher Court review a lower Court's judgment, order, or sentence -- available only where this Sanhita or another law specifically provides for it (section 413), with numerous carve-outs and conditions (guilty pleas, petty sentences, victim's right to appeal against acquittal/inadequate compensation, State/Central Government appeals against inadequate sentences, and special leave requirements for acquittal appeals) set out across Chapter XXXI.
glossary.extraordinary original criminal jurisdic: A High Court's power to try certain criminal cases itself as a Court of first instance (rather than only hearing appeals/revisions), historically confined to the three Presidency High Courts (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras) over serious offences within city limits; section 415(1) gives a person convicted on such a trial a direct right of appeal to the Supreme Court.
glossary.supreme court: India's apex Court and final court of appeal, established under Article 124 of the Constitution; within this Sanhita's appellate ladder, it is the direct appeal forum for convictions from a High Court's extraordinary original criminal jurisdiction (section 415(1)) and, separately, for certain High Court reversals of acquittal into a death/life/ten-year-plus sentence (section 420).
glossary.plea of guilty: An accused's formal admission in Court that he committed the offence charged, which if accepted results in conviction on that plea itself, without a full trial; section 416 bars any appeal against a High Court conviction on a guilty plea, and limits appeal from a Sessions/Magistrate guilty-plea conviction to only the extent or legality of the sentence, not the conviction itself.
glossary.central government: The Union Government of India, exercising executive power under the Constitution; within this Chapter it has its own independent power (alongside State Governments) to direct the Public Prosecutor to appeal an inadequate sentence (section 418(2)) or an acquittal (section 419(2)) where the offence was investigated by a Central agency empowered under a Central Act other than this Sanhita, such as the CBI or NIA.
glossary.special leave: The High Court's discretionary permission, which must be separately sought and granted, before an appeal against an order of acquittal can proceed in certain circumstances; section 419(4)-(6) lets a private complainant apply for special leave to appeal an acquittal, subject to strict limitation periods (six months for a public servant complainant, sixty days otherwise), and forecloses any other route to appeal that acquittal if special leave is refused.
glossary.petition of appeal: The written document by which an appeal is formally initiated -- presented by the appellant or his advocate under section 423, ordinarily accompanied by a copy of the judgment or order appealed against unless the Court dispenses with that requirement; a jailed appellant may instead present it to the jail's officer-in-charge under section 424, who forwards it to the proper Appellate Court.
glossary.summary dismissal: An Appellate Court's power under section 425 to dismiss an appeal at the threshold, without a full hearing, if it finds no sufficient ground for interfering after examining the petition of appeal and judgment copy -- subject to safeguards: an appellant under section 423 must get a reasonable hearing opportunity first, a jailed appellant under section 424 must generally get one too (unless the appeal is frivolous or producing him would be disproportionately inconvenient), and no section 424 appeal can be summarily dismissed before the appeal-filing period has expired.
glossary.enhancement of sentence: An appellate outcome where a sentence originally imposed is increased -- available only on an appeal specifically brought for that purpose (typically a State/Central Government appeal under section 418), and only after giving the accused an opportunity to show cause against the proposed enhancement (section 427's first proviso); the Appellate Court also cannot inflict a punishment greater than what the original Court could have imposed for the offence it finds was actually committed (section 427's second proviso).
glossary.additional evidence: New evidence introduced at the appellate stage, beyond what was recorded at trial; section 432 lets the Appellate Court take such evidence itself, or direct a Magistrate (or, if the Appellate Court is a High Court, a Court of Session or Magistrate) to take it, provided the Appellate Court records its reasons for finding it necessary and the accused/his advocate has the right to be present when it is taken.
glossary.abatement of appeal: The automatic lapsing of an appeal, without any decision on its merits, typically triggered by the death of the relevant party; section 435 provides that a State/Central Government appeal (sections 418, 419) finally abates on the accused's death, and any other appeal (except a fine-sentence appeal) finally abates on the appellant's death -- subject to a proviso letting a near relative apply within thirty days for leave to continue a death/imprisonment-sentence appeal.
glossary.reference: A procedure by which a subordinate Court, doubting the validity of a law it must apply to decide a pending case, formally states its opinion and reasons and refers the question to the High Court for decision, rather than deciding the validity question itself (section 436); distinct from an 'appeal' (which challenges an already-decided outcome) in that a reference happens mid-case, before the subordinate Court has itself ruled on the point.
glossary.interlocutory order: An order passed at an intermediate stage of a case, without finally deciding the rights of the parties or disposing of the matter -- section 438(2) expressly places interlocutory orders passed in any appeal, inquiry, trial, or other proceeding outside the scope of the revisional power, meaning parties generally cannot use revision to challenge routine intermediate rulings and must wait for the final order or judgment.
glossary.attorney-general of india: The Government of India's principal law officer and chief legal adviser, appointed under Article 76 of the Constitution; section 446(2) names the Attorney-General of India as one of only two categories of applicants (the other being an interested party) who may move the Supreme Court for a case/appeal transfer between High Courts, and uniquely, his motion need not be supported by affidavit or affirmation.
glossary.advocate-general: A State's principal law officer, appointed under Article 165 of the Constitution to advise the State Government and represent it in legal proceedings; like the Attorney-General of India at the Supreme Court, the Advocate-General of a State is exempted from the affidavit/affirmation-support requirement when moving the High Court (section 447(3)) or Sessions Judge (section 448(3), via cross-reference) for a case-transfer order.
glossary.motion: A formal application made to a superior Court to seek an order -- here, a transfer of a criminal case or appeal under sections 446-448; ordinarily such a motion must be supported by an affidavit or affirmation, except when made by the Attorney-General of India (for Supreme Court transfers) or the Advocate-General of the State (for High Court/Sessions Judge transfers), whose official position substitutes for that evidentiary backing.
glossary.commutation: The substitution of a lesser sentence for a more severe one already imposed, by a competent authority -- e.g., a death sentence commuted to imprisonment for life (section 456). Distinct from 'remission' (reduction of the sentence's duration without changing its character) and 'suspension' (temporary deferral of execution) -- commutation permanently changes the nature of the punishment itself.
glossary.imprisonment for life: A sentence of imprisonment for the remainder of the convict's natural life, subject to any remission or commutation granted under law. It is the mandatory substitute when a death sentence on a pregnant woman is commuted under section 456, and is itself a form of sentence whose execution is governed by sections 457-460 (place of confinement, warrant mechanics, and lodgment).
glossary.civil jail: A place of confinement for persons committed to custody in civil (non-criminal) process, such as under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, used to compel compliance with a civil obligation rather than to punish a criminal offence. Section 457 governs the interplay between civil and criminal confinement when a person already held in a civil jail also becomes liable to imprisonment under this Sanhita. Under section 491(2)'s proviso, a surety who fails to pay a forfeited bond's penalty, where it cannot otherwise be recovered, may similarly be imprisoned in civil jail for up to six months.
glossary.criminal jail: A place of confinement for persons imprisoned or committed to custody under this Sanhita (i.e., in criminal process), as distinct from a civil jail. Under section 457, a person held in a civil jail may be removed to a criminal jail, but must ordinarily be sent back to the civil jail upon release unless a statutory release trigger under Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 section 58 applies.
glossary.state government: The executive government of a State, which under section 457(1) holds the default power to direct the place of confinement for any person liable to be imprisoned or committed to custody under this Sanhita, except where some other law already provides for it.
glossary.jailor: The officer with direct custodial charge of a jail. Under section 460, a warrant for a prisoner's confinement in a jail must be lodged with the jailor, completing the execution chain that begins with the Court forwarding the warrant (section 458) and directing it to the officer in charge of the confining place (section 459).
glossary.arrears of land revenue: Unpaid dues owed to the State on account of land revenue, recoverable through a well-established summary coercive-recovery machinery under revenue law (attachment/sale of the defaulter's property by the Collector, without needing a fresh civil suit). Section 461(1)(b) lets a Court issue a warrant to the Collector authorising him to realise an unpaid fine using this same land-revenue-recovery machinery, against the offender's movable or immovable property -- but section 461(3) bars using it to arrest or imprison the offender.
glossary.rigorous imprisonment: A form of imprisonment involving hard labour, as distinct from simple imprisonment (confinement without compulsory labour). Section 466(3) deems rigorous imprisonment 'severer in kind' than simple imprisonment for the purpose of determining when a new sentence on an escaped convict takes effect immediately versus only after the unexpired portion of the earlier sentence.
glossary.simple imprisonment: A form of imprisonment without compulsory hard labour, as distinct from rigorous imprisonment. Under section 466(3), it is deemed the less severe of the two kinds when comparing sentences for purposes of the escaped-convict rules.
glossary.mercy petition: A petition filed by a death-sentenced convict (or his legal heir/relative) seeking clemency from the Governor (under Article 161 of the Constitution) or the President (under Article 72), the only route for relief once judicial remedies (appeal, review, special leave) are exhausted. Section 472 sets strict timelines -- thirty days to file after being informed of exhaustion of judicial remedies, then sixty days from a Governor's rejection/disposal to escalate to the President -- and makes the eventual Presidential/Gubernatorial order final and immune from judicial appeal or inquiry into how the decision was reached (section 472(7)).
glossary.president: The President of India, who under Article 72 of the Constitution holds the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions of punishment, or to suspend, remit, or commute a sentence -- including, most significantly, a sentence of death. Section 472 channels mercy petitions in death sentence cases to the President (after first going to the Governor), and section 472(7) makes the President's decision final and non-appealable.
glossary.governor: The Governor of a State, who under Article 161 of the Constitution holds a power of pardon, reprieve, respite, or remission of punishment, or to suspend, remit, or commute a sentence, parallel to the President's Article 72 power. Section 472(2) requires a death-sentence mercy petition to be made initially to the Governor, escalating to the President only upon the Governor's rejection or disposal.
glossary.superintendent of jail: The officer in charge of a jail, who under section 472 bears specific procedural duties in death sentence cases: informing the convict of the dismissal of his appeal/review/special leave or of death-sentence confirmation (triggering the thirty-day mercy-petition window), ensuring every convict in a multi-convict case files a mercy petition, and forwarding case records to the government where a convict fails to do so, plus receiving communication of the President's final order within forty-eight hours.
