breakdown.plain_summary: This is a post-release residence-monitoring tool aimed at recidivists: where someone with a prior conviction for a three-year-plus offence is convicted again of a three-year-plus offence (by any Court above a second-class Magistrate), the convicting Court may, at sentencing, order that for up to five years after release, his residence and any change of or absence from it be notified as prescribed by State Government rules. It reaches not just the completed offence but conspiracies to commit it, abetment of it, and attempts at it. The order automatically falls away if the underlying conviction is later set aside, and Appellate Courts / the High Court / Court of Session (in revision) can also make such orders. State Governments prescribe the notification mechanics by rule, and can also make breach of those rules a punishable offence triable by a competent Magistrate in the district of the last notified residence.
essential_elements: Applies where a person previously convicted of a three-year-plus offence is again convicted of a three-year-plus offence, by any Court other than a second-class Magistrate.
The Court may, at sentencing, order residence and any change/absence to be notified for up to five years post-release.
Extends to criminal conspiracies, abetment, and attempts regarding such offences.
The order becomes void if the underlying conviction is set aside on appeal or otherwise.
An Appellate Court, the High Court, or a Court of Session (in revision) may also make such an order.
The State Government prescribes the notification mechanics by rules, which may also criminalize breach, triable by a competent Magistrate in the district of the last notified residence.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a discretionary ("may") supervisory tool distinct from and additional to the sentence itself -- practitioners defending repeat offenders should treat a section 394 order as a live issue at sentencing, separate from arguing against the term of imprisonment, since it survives independently unless the conviction itself is overturned.

sections.title: Order to pay compensation
sections.raw_text:
395. Order to pay compensation.—(1) When a Court imposes a sentence of fine or a sentence
(including a sentence of death) of which fine forms a part, the Court may, when passing judgment, order
the whole or any part of the fine recovered to be applied—
        (a) in defraying the expenses properly incurred in the prosecution;
        (b) in the payment to any person of compensation for any loss or injury caused by the offence,
    when compensation is, in the opinion of the Court, recoverable by such person in a Civil Court;
        (c) when any person is convicted of any offence for having caused the death of another person or
    of having abetted the commission of such an offence, in paying compensation to the persons who are,
    under the Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 (13 of 1855), entitled to recover damages from the person
    sentenced for the loss resulting to them from such death;
        (d) when any person is convicted of any offence which includes theft, criminal misappropriation,
    criminal breach of trust, or cheating, or of having dishonestly received or retained, or of having
    voluntarily assisted in disposing of, stolen property knowing or having reason to believe the same to be
    stolen, in compensating any bona fide purchaser of such property for the loss of the same if such
    property is restored to the possession of the person entitled thereto.
    (2) If the fine is imposed in a case which is subject to appeal, no such payment shall be made before
the period allowed for presenting the appeal has elapsed, or, if an appeal be presented, before the decision
of the appeal.
    (3) When a Court imposes a sentence, of which fine does not form a part, the Court may, when passing
judgment, order the accused person to pay, by way of compensation, such amount as may be specified in
the order to the person who has suffered any loss or injury by reason of the act for which the accused person
has been so sentenced.
    (4) An order under this section may also be made by an Appellate Court or by the High Court or Court
of Session when exercising its powers of revision.
    (5) At the time of awarding compensation in any subsequent civil suit relating to the same matter, the
Court shall take into account any sum paid or recovered as compensation under this section.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the Court's general compensation-from-sentence power. Whenever a fine is imposed (alone, or as part of any sentence including death), the Court may direct the recovered fine towards prosecution expenses, compensating a victim whose loss/injury would otherwise be civilly recoverable, compensating Fatal Accidents Act-eligible dependents where the offence caused death, or compensating a bona fide purchaser of stolen property that has been restored to its rightful owner. Payment out of a fine subject to appeal must wait until the appeal period lapses or the appeal is decided. Separately, even where no fine is imposed at all, the Court can still directly order the accused to pay a specified compensation amount to anyone who suffered loss or injury from the sentenced act. Appellate Courts, the High Court, and the Court of Session (in revision) share this compensation power, and any sum paid/recovered under this section must be credited against compensation later awarded in a related civil suit, preventing double recovery.
essential_elements: Applies whenever a Court imposes a fine (alone or as part of any sentence, including death), or, under sub-section (3), even where no fine is imposed at all.

From a recovered fine, the Court may direct payment toward prosecution expenses, civilly-recoverable victim compensation, Fatal Accidents Act-eligible dependents' compensation (death cases), or bona fide purchaser compensation (property-offence cases where stolen property is restored to its owner).
Payment from a fine in an appealable case must await expiry of the appeal period or the appeal's decision.
Where no fine forms part of the sentence, the Court may still order the accused to pay a specified compensation amount directly to the person who suffered loss or injury.
Appellate Courts, the High Court, and the Court of Session (exercising revision) may also make compensation orders under this section.
Any sum paid/recovered as compensation under this section must be accounted for in any later related civil suit's compensation award.
breakdown.how_to_read: The sub-section (3) power (ordering compensation even absent any fine) is easy to overlook but practically significant -- it means a purely custodial sentence with no fine component can still carry a separate, directly enforceable compensation obligation to the victim.

sections.title: Victim compensation scheme
sections.raw_text:
396. Victim compensation scheme.—(1) Every State Government in co-ordination with the Central
Government shall prepare a scheme for providing funds for the purpose of compensation to the victim or
his dependents who have suffered loss or injury as a result of the crime and who require rehabilitation.
    (2) Whenever a recommendation is made by the Court for compensation, the District Legal Service
Authority or the State Legal Service Authority, as the case may be, shall decide the quantum of
compensation to be awarded under the scheme referred to in sub-section (1).
    (3) If the trial Court, at the conclusion of the trial, is satisfied, that the compensation awarded under
section 395 is not adequate for such rehabilitation, or where the cases end in acquittal or discharge and the
victim has to be rehabilitated, it may make recommendation for compensation.
    (4) Where the offender is not traced or identified, but the victim is identified, and where no trial takes
place, the victim or his dependents may make an application to the State or the District Legal Services
Authority for award of compensation.
    (5) On receipt of such recommendations or on the application under sub-section (4), the State or the
District Legal Services Authority shall, after due enquiry award adequate compensation by completing the
enquiry within two months.
    (6) The State or the District Legal Services Authority, as the case may be, to alleviate the suffering of
the victim, may order for immediate first-aid facility or medical benefits to be made available free of cost
on the certificate of the police officer not below the rank of the officer in charge of the police station or a
Magistrate of the area concerned, or any other interim relief as the appropriate authority deems fit.
    (7) The compensation payable by the State Government under this section shall be in addition to the
payment of fine to the victim under section 65, section 70 and sub-section (1) of section 124 of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (45 of 2023).

breakdown.plain_summary: This creates a State-funded rehabilitation safety net for crime victims, running parallel to (not instead of) the Court's own fine-based compensation power under section 395. States, coordinating with the Centre, must set up a funded scheme; the District or State Legal Services Authority actually fixes the compensation amount, either because the trial Court recommends it (when section 395's fine-based award is inadequate for rehabilitation, or when the case ends in acquittal/discharge but the victim still needs rehabilitation) or because the victim applies directly when the offender was never traced and no trial ever happened. The Authority must complete its enquiry and award compensation within two months, and separately has power to order free immediate first-aid, medical benefits, or other interim relief on a police or Magistrate certificate, to address urgent suffering without waiting for the full award. This compensation stacks on top of, rather than replacing, fine-based victim payments under specific BNS provisions (sections 65, 70, 124(1)).
essential_elements: Every State Government, coordinating with the Centre, must prepare a funded scheme for compensating and rehabilitating crime victims/dependents.
The District or State Legal Services Authority decides the compensation quantum once a Court makes a recommendation.
A trial Court may recommend compensation where a section 395 award is inadequate for rehabilitation, or where the case ends in acquittal/discharge but rehabilitation is still needed.
Where the offender is untraced/unidentified but the victim is identified and no trial occurs, the victim/dependents may apply directly to the Authority.
The Authority must complete its enquiry and award adequate compensation within two months of the recommendation or application.
The Authority may separately order free immediate first-aid/medical benefits or other interim relief, certified by a qualifying police officer or Magistrate.
This State compensation is additional to fine-based victim payments under BNS sections 65, 70, and 124(1).
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the acquittal-proof compensation route -- unlike section 395 (tied to a conviction and a fine), section 396 explicitly covers acquittals, discharges, and even cases where the offender is never caught, making it the correct avenue to invoke when a victim's rehabilitation need survives a failed or impossible prosecution.

sections.title: Treatment of victims
sections.raw_text:
397. Treatment of victims.—All hospitals, public or private, whether run by the Central Government,
the State Government, local bodies or any other person, shall immediately, provide the first-aid or medical
treatment, free of cost, to the victims of any offence covered under section 64, section 65, section
66, section 67, section 68, section 70, section 71 or sub-section (1) of section 124 of the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023 (45 of 2023) or under sections 4, 6, 8 or section 10 of the Protection of Children from Sexual
Offences Act, 2012 (32 of 2012), and shall immediately inform the police of such incident.
key_terms: protection of children from sexual offences act

breakdown.plain_summary: This imposes an absolute, immediate obligation on every hospital -- public, private, Central, State, local-body-run, or otherwise -- to give free first-aid or medical treatment to victims of specified serious BNS offences (broadly, sexual offences and acid-attack-type injuries under sections 64-71 and 124(1)) and specified POCSO offences against children, and to immediately notify the police. No hospital may refuse or delay treatment pending payment, insurance, police formalities, or jurisdictional questions.
essential_elements: Applies to all hospitals regardless of ownership -- Central Government, State Government, local body, or private.
Covers victims of BNS sections 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 70, 71, and 124(1), and POCSO sections 4, 6, 8, and 10.
Requires immediate, free first-aid or medical treatment.
Requires the hospital to immediately inform the police of the incident.
breakdown.how_to_read: This provision is frequently paired with a hospital's independent duty to preserve medico-legal evidence -- practitioners representing victims should treat any hospital's refusal or delay as an actionable lapse in its own right, separate from the underlying criminal prosecution.

sections.title: Witness protection scheme
sections.raw_text:
398. Witness protection scheme.—Every State Government shall prepare and notify a Witness
Protection Scheme for the State with a view to ensure protection of the witnesses.

breakdown.plain_summary: A short but significant mandate: every State Government must prepare and formally notify its own Witness Protection Scheme, aimed at protecting witnesses -- addressing the practical reality that fear of retaliation or intimidation is a major reason witnesses turn hostile or refuse to testify.
essential_elements: Every State Government must prepare and notify a Witness Protection Scheme.
The scheme's stated objective is ensuring protection of witnesses.
breakdown.how_to_read: This section is enabling rather than self-executing -- it does not itself specify what protections are available; practitioners need to check the specific State's notified scheme (or, absent one, the Supreme Court's Witness Protection Scheme, 2018, which has been directed to apply until States notify their own) for the actual mechanics of threat assessment and protection measures.

sections.title: Compensation to persons groundlessly arrested
sections.raw_text:
399. Compensation to persons groundlessly arrested.—(1) Whenever any person causes a police
officer to arrest another person, if it appears to the Magistrate by whom the case is heard that there was no
sufficient ground for causing such arrest, the Magistrate may award such compensation, not exceeding one
thousand rupees, to be paid by the person so causing the arrest to the person so arrested, for his loss of time
and expenses in the matter, as the Magistrate thinks fit.
    (2) In such cases, if more persons than one are arrested, the Magistrate may, in like manner, award to
each of them such compensation, not exceeding one thousand rupees, as such Magistrate thinks fit.
    (3) All compensation awarded under this section may be recovered as if it were a fine, and, if it cannot
be so recovered, the person by whom it is payable shall be sentenced to simple imprisonment for such term
not exceeding thirty days as the Magistrate directs, unless such sum is sooner paid.

breakdown.plain_summary: This deters people from misusing the police to arrest others without sufficient ground. If a private complainant causes a police officer to arrest someone, and the Magistrate hearing the case finds no sufficient ground existed for that arrest, the Magistrate may order the complainant to pay the wrongly-arrested person compensation (capped at one thousand rupees) for lost time and expenses -- with the same cap applying separately to each person if multiple people were groundlessly arrested. The compensation is recovered like a fine, and if it cannot be recovered, the person liable to pay faces simple imprisonment of up to thirty days, which stops the moment the amount is paid.
essential_elements: Applies where a person causes a police officer to arrest another person.
The Magistrate hearing the case must find there was no sufficient ground for the arrest.
Compensation is capped at one thousand rupees per arrested person, payable by the person who caused the arrest.
Compensation covers loss of time and expenses arising from the groundless arrest.
With multiple groundless arrests, the Magistrate may award compensation to each person separately, each up to the cap.
Compensation is recoverable as if it were a fine; non-recovery leads to simple imprisonment of up to thirty days, ending on payment.
breakdown.how_to_read: The one-thousand-rupee cap has not been revised and is nominal by modern standards -- practitioners should treat section 399 as a limited deterrent/symbolic remedy for a groundless private-complaint arrest, not a substitute for a separate civil suit or constitutional remedy for wrongful arrest and detention.

sections.title: Order to pay costs in non-cognizable cases
sections.raw_text:
400. Order to pay costs in non-cognizable cases.—(1) Whenever any complaint of a non-cognizable
offence is made to a Court, the Court, if it convicts the accused, may, in addition to the penalty imposed
upon him, order him to pay to the complainant, in whole or in part, the cost incurred by him in the
prosecution, and may further order that in default of payment, the accused shall suffer simple imprisonment
for a period not exceeding thirty days and such costs may include any expenses incurred in respect of
process-fees, witnesses and advocate's fees which the Court may consider reasonable.
    (2) An order under this section may also be made by an Appellate Court or by the High Court or Court
of Session when exercising its powers of revision.

breakdown.plain_summary: This lets a Court shift the complainant's prosecution costs onto a convicted accused in non-cognizable-offence complaint cases -- on conviction, the Court may order the accused to reimburse the complainant's costs (in whole or part), covering reasonable process-fees, witness expenses, and advocate's fees, on top of whatever penalty is imposed. Default in paying these costs carries its own simple-imprisonment consequence, capped at thirty days. Appellate Courts, the High Court, and the Court of Session (in revision) share this cost-shifting power.
essential_elements: Applies to complaints of non-cognizable offences made to a Court.
On conviction, the Court may order the accused to pay the complainant's prosecution costs, in whole or part, in addition to the penalty.
Costs may include reasonable process-fees, witness expenses, and advocate's fees.
Default in payment may lead to simple imprisonment of up to thirty days.
Appellate Courts, the High Court, and the Court of Session (in revision) may also make such a costs order.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a private-complainant-specific costs shift for non-cognizable offences -- since such offences are typically pursued by direct complaint rather than police investigation, section 400 offsets some of the complainant's own litigation burden when the prosecution succeeds, which is worth flagging as a recoverable head alongside the substantive penalty when drafting a complaint.

sections.title: Order to release on probation of good conduct or after admonition
sections.raw_text:
401. Order to release on probation of good conduct or after admonition.—(1) When any person
not under twenty-one years of age is convicted of an offence punishable with fine only or with imprisonment
for a term of seven years or less, or when any person under twenty-one years of age or any woman is
convicted of an offence not punishable with death or imprisonment for life, and no previous conviction is
proved against the offender, if it appears to the Court before which he is convicted, regard being had to the
age, character or antecedents of the offender, and to the circumstances in which the offence was committed,
that it is expedient that the offender should be released on probation of good conduct, the Court may, instead
of sentencing him at once to any punishment, direct that he be released on his entering into a bond or bail
bond to appear and receive sentence when called upon during such period (not exceeding three years) as
the Court may direct, and in the meantime to keep the peace and be of good behavior:
    Provided that where any first offender is convicted by a Magistrate of the second class not specially
empowered by the High Court, and the Magistrate is of opinion that the powers conferred by this section
should be exercised, he shall record his opinion to that effect, and submit the proceedings to a Magistrate
of the first class, forwarding the accused to, or taking bail for his appearance before, such Magistrate, who
shall dispose of the case in the manner provided by sub-section (2).
    (2) Where proceedings are submitted to a Magistrate of the first class as provided by sub-section (1),
such Magistrate may thereupon pass such sentence or make such order as he might have passed or made if
the case had originally been heard by him, and, if he thinks further inquiry or additional evidence on any
point to be necessary, he may make such inquiry or take such evidence himself or direct such inquiry or
evidence to be made or taken.
    (3) In any case in which a person is convicted of theft, theft in a building, dishonest misappropriation,
cheating or any offence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, punishable with not more than two years'
imprisonment or any offence punishable with fine only and no previous conviction is proved against him,
the Court before which he is so convicted may, if it thinks fit, having regard to the age, character,
antecedents or physical or mental condition of the offender and to the trivial nature of the offence or any
extenuating circumstances under which the offence was committed, instead of sentencing him to any
punishment, release him after due admonition.
    (4) An order under this section may be made by any Appellate Court or by the High Court or Court of
Session when exercising its powers of revision.
    (5) When an order has been made under this section in respect of any offender, the High Court or Court
of Session may, on appeal when there is a right of appeal to such Court, or when exercising its powers of
revision, set aside such order, and in lieu thereof pass sentence on such offender according to law:
    Provided that the High Court or Court of Session shall not under this sub-section inflict a greater
punishment than might have been inflicted by the Court by which the offender was convicted.
    (6) The provisions of sections 140, 143 and 414 shall, so far as may be, apply in the case of sureties
offered in pursuance of the provisions of this section.
    (7) The Court, before directing the release of an offender under sub-section (1), shall be satisfied that
an offender or his surety (if any) has a fixed place of abode or regular occupation in the place for which the
Court acts or in which the offender is likely to live during the period named for the observance of the
conditions.
    (8) If the Court which convicted the offender, or a Court which could have dealt with the offender in
respect of his original offence, is satisfied that the offender has failed to observe any of the conditions of
his recognizance, it may issue a warrant for his apprehension.
    (9) An offender, when apprehended on any such warrant, shall be brought forthwith before the Court
issuing the warrant, and such Court may either remand him in custody until the case is heard or admit him
to bail with a sufficient surety conditioned on his appearing for sentence and such Court may, after hearing
the case, pass sentence.
    (10) Nothing in this section shall affect the provisions of the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958
(20 of 1958), or the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 (2 of 2016) or any other
law for the time being in force for the treatment, training or rehabilitation of youthful offenders.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives Courts a rehabilitative alternative to immediate punishment for first offenders. Two tracks exist: probation (sub-section 1) -- available to adults convicted of fine-only or up-to-seven-year offences, and to under-21s/women convicted of anything short of death/life imprisonment, provided there's no prior conviction and the Court considers it expedient given the offender's age, character, antecedents, and the offence's circumstances -- releases the person on a bond to appear for sentencing if called upon within up to three years, meanwhile keeping the peace and behaving well; and admonition (sub-section 3) -- a simple reprimand-only release for minor property offences (theft, misappropriation, cheating) or offences carrying two years or less/fine only, again with no prior conviction, where the offence is trivial or there are extenuating circumstances. A second-class Magistrate who thinks probation is warranted but lacks the power must refer the case up to a first-class Magistrate. Probation/admonition orders are also available to Appellate Courts and in revision, but can be overturned on appeal/revision in favour of a proper sentence (capped at what the original Court could have imposed). Breach of the bond's conditions triggers a warrant and a return to Court for sentencing. Crucially, none of this displaces the separate Probation of Offenders Act or the Juvenile Justice Act, which remain fully available alongside these powers.
essential_elements: Probation (sub-section 1): available for adults (fine-only/up to 7 years) and under-21s/women (anything short of death/life imprisonment), no prior conviction, Court finds it expedient given age/character/antecedents/circumstances.
Release is on a bond/bail bond to appear for sentencing if called upon, for up to three years, with conditions to keep the peace and be of good behaviour.
A second-class Magistrate inclined to use this power must record that opinion and refer the case to a first-class Magistrate for disposal.

Admonition (sub-section 3): available for minor property offences or offences with a two-year/fine-only ceiling, no prior conviction, where the offence is trivial or there are extenuating circumstances -- results in release with just a reprimand.

Appellate Courts, the High Court, and the Court of Session (in revision) may also make, or set aside and replace, such orders -- replacement sentences cannot exceed what the original Court could have imposed.
Surety provisions (sections 140, 143, 414) apply to sureties offered under this section; the Court must be satisfied the offender/surety has a fixed abode or occupation before releasing him.
Breach of recognizance conditions allows the Court to issue a warrant; the apprehended offender is brought before the Court, which may remand or bail him pending sentencing.
The section does not affect the Probation of Offenders Act, 1958, the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, or any other youthful-offender rehabilitation law.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Not available where the offender has a previous conviction proved against him.
Not available for offences punishable with death or imprisonment for life (for the under-21/women track).
breakdown.how_to_read: This is functionally the BNSS's own first-offender diversion tool, distinct from and supplementary to the Probation of Offenders Act -- practitioners should plead both in the alternative for a youthful or first-time client, since a Court declining one may still be persuaded by the other, and section 402 forces the Court to justify on the record any refusal to use either.

sections.title: Special reasons to be recorded in certain cases
sections.raw_text:
402. Special reasons to be recorded in certain cases.—Where in any case the Court could have dealt
with,—
        (a) an accused person under section 401 or under the provisions of the Probation of Offenders Act,
    1958 (20 of 1958); or
        (b) a youthful offender under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015
    (2 of 2016) or any other law for the time being in force for the treatment, training or rehabilitation of
    youthful offenders,
but has not done so, it shall record in its judgment the special reasons for not having done so.

breakdown.plain_summary: This forces judicial accountability whenever a Court declines to use the rehabilitative options available to it. If a Court could have released the accused under section 401, the Probation of Offenders Act, or the Juvenile Justice Act, but chooses ordinary sentencing instead, it must record special reasons in its judgment explaining why. This creates a reviewable record and nudges Courts to genuinely consider the rehabilitative route before defaulting to punishment.
essential_elements: Applies whenever the Court could have dealt with the accused under section 401, the Probation of Offenders Act, or the Juvenile Justice Act (or other youthful-offender rehabilitation law).
If the Court does not use that route, it must record special reasons for not doing so, in the judgment itself.
breakdown.how_to_read: A judgment sentencing an eligible first offender or minor without any special-reasons discussion of section 401/Probation of Offenders Act/Juvenile Justice Act eligibility is vulnerable on appeal for that omission alone -- always check whether the accused fit the eligibility profile and, if so, whether the trial Court engaged with it at all.

sections.title: Court not to alter judgment

breakdown.plain_summary: This locks in a judgment once signed: apart from correcting a clerical or arithmetical slip, a Court cannot alter or review its own signed judgment or final order, except where some other provision of this Sanhita or another law specifically permits it (such as review, revision, or appeal mechanisms). This preserves finality and prevents a Court from second-guessing its own disposed-of decisions outside the proper channels.
essential_elements: Applies once a Court has signed its judgment or final order disposing of a case.
The Court cannot alter or review that judgment/order thereafter.
The only self-correction allowed is fixing a clerical or arithmetical error.
Other statutory alteration routes (review, revision, appeal, etc.) remain available where separately provided.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the functus officio principle for criminal judgments -- if a substantive error (not merely clerical/arithmetical) is discovered post-signing, the correct route is appeal, revision, or a statutorily provided review, not asking the same Court to simply amend its own judgment.

sections.title: Copy of judgment to be given to accused and other persons
sections.raw_text:
404. Copy of judgment to be given to accused and other persons.—(1) When the accused is
sentenced to imprisonment, a copy of the judgment shall, immediately after the pronouncement of the
judgment, be given to him free of cost.
    (2) On the application of the accused, a certified copy of the judgment, or when he so desires, a
translation in his own language if practicable or in the language of the Court, shall be given to him without
delay, and such copy shall, in every case where the judgment is appealable by the accused, be given free of
cost:
    Provided that where a sentence of death is passed or confirmed by the High Court, a certified copy of
the judgment shall be immediately given to the accused free of cost whether or not he applies for the same.
    (3) The provisions of sub-section (2) shall apply in relation to an order under section 136 as they apply
in relation to a judgment which is appealable by the accused.
    (4) When the accused is sentenced to death by any Court and an appeal lies from such judgment as of
right, the Court shall inform him of the period within which, if he wishes to appeal, his appeal should be
preferred.
    (5) Save as otherwise provided in sub-section (2), any person affected by a judgment or order passed
by a Criminal Court shall, on an application made in this behalf and on payment of the prescribed charges,
be given a copy of such judgment or order or of any deposition or other part of the record:
    Provided that the Court may, if it thinks fit for some special reason, give it to him free of cost:
    Provided further that the Court may, on an application made in this behalf by the Prosecuting Officer,
provide to the Government, free of cost, a certified copy of such judgment, order, deposition or record.
    (6) The High Court may, by rules, provide for the grant of copies of any judgment or order of a Criminal
Court to any person who is not affected by a judgment or order, on payment, by such person, of such fees,
and subject to such conditions, as the High Court may, by such rules, provide.

breakdown.plain_summary: This guarantees access to judgment copies, calibrated by need and urgency. An imprisoned accused gets a free copy immediately on pronouncement, no application needed. Any accused can additionally apply for a certified copy (or a translation into his own language if practicable) without delay, free of cost wherever the judgment is appealable by him -- and a death sentence copy must be given immediately and automatically, application or not, given the stakes. The same free/prompt-copy treatment extends to section 136 orders (peace/good-behaviour security orders). Where a death sentence carries an as-of-right appeal, the Court must proactively inform the accused of the appeal deadline. Beyond the accused, any person affected by a criminal judgment/order can get a copy on application and payment of prescribed charges (with free copies possible for special reasons, and free certified copies to Government on the Prosecuting Officer's request), and the High Court can make rules allowing even unaffected persons to obtain copies on payment of fees.
essential_elements: An accused sentenced to imprisonment gets a free judgment copy immediately after pronouncement, without needing to apply.
On application, a certified copy (or translation if practicable/desired) is given without delay; free of cost wherever the judgment is appealable by the accused.
A death sentence copy (passed or confirmed by the High Court) must be given immediately and free of cost, whether or not applied for.
The same copy-access rules apply to section 136 orders as to appealable judgments.
Where a death-sentence appeal lies as of right, the Court must inform the accused of the appeal-filing deadline.

Any person affected by a criminal judgment/order can obtain a copy on application and payment of prescribed charges, with discretionary free copies for special reasons and mandatory free certified copies to Government on the Prosecuting Officer's request.
The High Court may make rules allowing even unaffected persons to obtain copies, on payment of fees and subject to conditions.
breakdown.how_to_read: The automatic, no-application death-sentence copy rule is a due-process safeguard worth flagging in any capital case file review -- its absence would itself be a procedural irregularity independent of the merits of conviction or sentence.

sections.title: Judgment when to be translated
sections.raw_text:
405. Judgment when to be translated.—The original judgment shall be filed with the record of the
proceedings and where the original is recorded in a language different from that of the Court, and if either
party so requires, a translation thereof into the language of the Court shall be added to such record.

breakdown.plain_summary: A straightforward record-keeping and language-access rule: the original judgment goes onto the case record, and if it was recorded in a language other than the Court's own language, either party can require a translation into the Court's language to be added to the record, ensuring the official record remains usable and comprehensible in the Court's working language.
essential_elements: The original judgment must be filed with the record of proceedings.
If the original judgment's language differs from the language of the Court, either party may require a translation into the Court's language.
That translation is then added to the record.
breakdown.how_to_read: This dovetails with section 404's translation-on-request right for the accused personally -- section 405 is about the official case record generally, while section 404(2) is about giving the accused his own copy in a language he understands; both can be invoked in the same multi-lingual proceeding.

sections.title: Court of Session to send copy of finding and sentence to District Magistrate
sections.raw_text:
406. Court of Session to send copy of finding and sentence to District Magistrate.—In cases tried
by the Court of Session or a Chief Judicial Magistrate, the Court or such Magistrate, as the case may be,
shall forward a copy of its or his finding and sentence (if any) to the District Magistrate within whose local
jurisdiction the trial was held.

breakdown.plain_summary: A simple administrative-coordination rule: whenever a case is tried by the Court of Session or a Chief Judicial Magistrate, that Court/Magistrate must send a copy of the finding and sentence (if any) to the District Magistrate of the district where the trial took place, keeping the district administration informed of judicial outcomes in its territory.
essential_elements: Applies to cases tried by the Court of Session or a Chief Judicial Magistrate.
The trying Court/Magistrate must forward a copy of the finding and sentence (if any) to the District Magistrate of the district where the trial was held.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is purely administrative and does not itself affect the judgment's validity or appealability -- it exists to keep the district's executive administration apprised of serious judicial outcomes within its jurisdiction.

sections.title: Sentence of death to be submitted by Court of Session for confirmation
sections.raw_text:
407. Sentence of death to be submitted by Court of Session for confirmation.—(1) When the Court
of Session passes a sentence of death, the proceedings shall forthwith be submitted to the High Court, and
the sentence shall not be executed unless it is confirmed by the High Court.
    (2) The Court passing the sentence shall commit the convicted person to jail custody under a warrant.

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Chapter XXX with the core safeguard on capital punishment: a Court of Session cannot itself finalize a death sentence. The moment it passes one, the entire proceedings must go forthwith to the High Court, and the sentence cannot be executed unless and until the High Court confirms it -- an automatic, mandatory judicial safety check before any execution, independent of whether the convict even appeals. Meanwhile, the convicted person is committed to jail custody under a warrant pending that confirmation process.
essential_elements: Applies whenever a Court of Session passes a sentence of death.
The proceedings must be submitted forthwith to the High Court.
The death sentence cannot be executed unless confirmed by the High Court.
The convicted person is committed to jail custody under a warrant pending confirmation.
breakdown.how_to_read: This submission is automatic and mandatory, not dependent on the convict filing an appeal -- even an accused who does not wish to appeal still has his death sentence independently scrutinized by the High Court under this confirmation process, reflecting the irreversibility of the punishment.

sections.title: Power to direct further inquiry to be made or additional evidence to be taken
sections.raw_text:
408. Power to direct further inquiry to be made or additional evidence to be taken.—(1) If, when
such proceedings are submitted, the High Court thinks that a further inquiry should be made into, or
additional evidence taken upon, any point bearing upon the guilt or innocence of the convicted person, it
may make such inquiry or take such evidence itself, or direct it to be made or taken by the Court of Session.
    (2) Unless the High Court otherwise directs, the presence of the convicted person may be dispensed
with when such inquiry is made or such evidence is taken.
    (3) When the inquiry or evidence (if any) is not made or taken by the High Court, the result of such
inquiry or evidence shall be certified to such Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: During the confirmation process, the High Court is not limited to the existing trial record -- if it thinks further inquiry or additional evidence is needed on any point going to guilt or innocence, it can conduct that inquiry/take that evidence itself, or direct the Court of Session to do so. The convicted person's presence during this extra inquiry can be dispensed with unless the High Court directs otherwise. If the Court of Session (rather than the High Court itself) conducts the inquiry, it must certify the results back to the High Court.
essential_elements: Applies during the High Court's review of a death-sentence confirmation submission under section 407.
The High Court may order further inquiry or additional evidence on any point bearing on guilt or innocence.
It may conduct that inquiry/evidence-taking itself, or direct the Court of Session to do so.
The convicted person's presence may be dispensed with unless the High Court directs otherwise.
Where the Court of Session conducts the inquiry, it must certify the results to the High Court.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a meaningful, substantive review power, not a rubber-stamp confirmation process -- the High Court can genuinely revisit the guilt/innocence question with fresh evidence, which is why confirmation proceedings are treated as a real second look rather than a formality.

sections.title: Power of High Court to confirm sentence or annul conviction
sections.raw_text:
409. Power of High Court to confirm sentence or annul conviction.—In any case submitted under
section 407, the High Court—
        (a) may confirm the sentence, or pass any other sentence warranted by law; or
        (b) may annul the conviction, and convict the accused of any offence of which the Court of Session
    might have convicted him, or order a new trial on the same or an amended charge; or
        (c) may acquit the accused person:
    Provided that no order of confirmation shall be made under this section until the period allowed for
preferring an appeal has expired, or, if an appeal is presented within such period, until such appeal is
disposed of.

breakdown.plain_summary: This sets out the High Court's full menu of options when a death sentence is submitted for confirmation: confirm the death sentence as passed, or substitute any other legally warranted sentence; annul the conviction altogether and either convict the accused of some other offence the Court of Session could have convicted him of, or order a fresh trial (on the same or an amended charge); or acquit the accused entirely. None of these outcomes are pre-ordained -- confirmation genuinely means the High Court could go any of these directions. Crucially, no confirmation order can be made until the appeal-filing window has expired, or, if an appeal was filed, until that appeal is fully disposed of -- ensuring the confirmation and appeal processes are properly sequenced rather than a confirmation short-circuiting an appeal.
essential_elements: Applies to any death-sentence case submitted to the High Court under section 407.
Option (a): confirm the sentence, or substitute any other sentence warranted by law.
Option (b): annul the conviction and either convict of a lesser/different offence the Sessions Court could have convicted of, or order a new trial on the same or amended charge.
Option (c): acquit the accused person.
No confirmation order may be made until the appeal period has expired, or, if an appeal was filed, until it is disposed of.
breakdown.how_to_read: The confirmation-appeal sequencing proviso is critical -- a High Court cannot confirm a death sentence while a timely appeal against it is still pending; practitioners should treat any premature confirmation order (before appeal disposal) as procedurally void on this ground alone.

sections.title: Confirmation or new sentence to be signed by two Judges
sections.raw_text:
410. Confirmation or new sentence to be signed by two Judges.—In every case so submitted, the
confirmation of the sentence, or any new sentence or order passed by the High Court, shall, when such
Court consists of two or more Judges, be made, passed and signed by at least two of them.

breakdown.plain_summary: Given the irreversible stakes of a death sentence, a single Judge's decision is not enough where the High Court has two or more Judges available -- the confirmation, or any new sentence/order the High Court passes instead, must be made, passed, and signed by at least two Judges, building in a collective-decision safeguard.
essential_elements: Applies where the High Court consists of two or more Judges.
The confirmation of a death sentence, or any new sentence/order passed instead, must be made, passed, and signed by at least two Judges.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is why death-confirmation matters are institutionally routed to a Division Bench rather than a Single Judge -- practitioners should check Bench composition as a threshold procedural point in any confirmation reference.

sections.title: Procedure in case of difference of opinion
sections.raw_text:
411. Procedure in case of difference of opinion.—Where any such case is heard before a Bench of
Judges and such Judges are equally divided in opinion, the case shall be decided in the manner provided by
section 433.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes a procedural gap for death-sentence confirmation cases heard by an evenly-numbered Bench: if the Judges are equally divided in opinion on confirming/annulling the sentence, the matter doesn't stall -- it is resolved using the general tie-breaking mechanism set out in section 433 (typically referral to another Judge), ensuring a definitive outcome even in a capital case.
essential_elements: Applies where a death-sentence confirmation case is heard by a Bench of Judges.
Applies specifically where the Judges are equally divided in opinion.
The case is then decided per the procedure in section 433.
breakdown.how_to_read: This cross-references section 433's general difference-of-opinion mechanism rather than creating a separate rule -- practitioners should read the two sections together when a confirmation Bench splits evenly.

sections.title: Procedure in cases submitted to High Court for confirmation
sections.raw_text:
412. Procedure in cases submitted to High Court for confirmation.—In cases submitted by the
Court of Session to the High Court for the confirmation of a sentence of death, the proper officer of the
High Court shall, without delay, after the order of confirmation or other order has been made by the High
Court, send either physically, or through electronic means, a copy of the order, under the seal of the High
Court and attested with his official signature, to the Court of Session.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes the confirmation-process loop: once the High Court has decided a death-sentence confirmation reference (whichever way it goes -- confirmation or any other order under section 409), the High Court's proper officer must, without delay, send a sealed and signed copy of that order back to the Court of Session, either physically or electronically, so the trial-level Court has the authoritative record of the final outcome.
essential_elements: Applies to death-sentence confirmation cases submitted by the Court of Session to the High Court.
After the High Court makes its order (confirmation or otherwise), its proper officer must send a copy to the Court of Session without delay.
The copy must be under the High Court's seal and attested with the officer's official signature.
Transmission may be physical or electronic.
breakdown.how_to_read: The explicit allowance for electronic transmission reflects the same digitization push seen in section 392's judgment-upload requirements -- practitioners should not assume physical dispatch is the only compliant method.

sections.title: No appeal to lie unless otherwise provided
sections.raw_text:
413. No appeal to lie unless otherwise provided.—No appeal shall lie from any judgment or order of
a Criminal Court except as provided for by this Sanhita or by any other law for the time being in force:
    Provided that the victim shall have a right to prefer an appeal against any order passed by the Court
acquitting the accused or convicting for a lesser offence or imposing inadequate compensation, and such
appeal shall lie to the Court to which an appeal ordinarily lies against the order of conviction of such Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Chapter XXXI with the foundational rule that appeal is a creature of statute, not an inherent right: no appeal lies from any Criminal Court judgment/order unless this Sanhita or some other law specifically creates that right. The significant BNSS-era addition is the proviso: a victim now has an express, independent right to appeal against an acquittal, a conviction for a lesser offence than charged, or inadequate compensation -- routed to whichever Court would ordinarily hear an appeal against that Court's conviction orders. This gives victims direct standing to challenge outcomes they consider too lenient, without depending on the State to appeal on their behalf.
essential_elements: General rule: no appeal lies from a Criminal Court judgment/order except where specifically provided by this Sanhita or another law.
Proviso: a victim has a right to appeal against an order acquitting the accused, convicting for a lesser offence, or imposing inadequate compensation.
The victim's appeal lies to the Court to which an appeal ordinarily lies against that Court's conviction orders.
breakdown.how_to_read: The victim's independent appeal right under the proviso is a notable BNSS-era empowerment -- previously victims largely depended on the State/Public Prosecutor to challenge an inadequate outcome; now a victim's advocate can directly draft and file that appeal without waiting on prosecutorial discretion.

sections.title: Appeal from orders requiring security or refusal to accept or rejecting surety for keeping peace or good behavior
sections.raw_text:
414. Appeal from orders requiring security or refusal to accept or rejecting surety for keeping
peace or good behavior.—Any person, —
        (i) who has been ordered under section 136 to give security for keeping the peace or for good
    behaviour; or
        (ii) who is aggrieved by any order refusing to accept or rejecting a surety under section 140,
may appeal against such order to the Court of Session:
    Provided that nothing in this section shall apply to persons the proceedings against whom are laid before
a Sessions Judge in accordance with the provisions of sub-section (2) or sub-section (4) of section 141.

breakdown.plain_summary: This creates a specific appeal route for the peace/good-behaviour security regime: a person ordered under section 136 to furnish security, or one aggrieved by a section 140 order refusing to accept or rejecting his surety, may appeal to the Court of Session. This does not apply where the proceedings were already laid before a Sessions Judge directly under section 141(2)/(4), since there the Sessions Judge is already the decision-maker and no further appeal within this route is needed.
essential_elements: Available to a person ordered under section 136 to give security for keeping the peace or good behaviour.
Available to a person aggrieved by a section 140 order refusing to accept or rejecting a surety.
The appeal lies to the Court of Session.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Does not apply to persons whose proceedings were laid before a Sessions Judge under section 141(2) or 141(4).
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the appellate counterpart to the section 136/140/141 preventive-security scheme -- practitioners handling a security-for-good-behaviour matter should treat section 414 as the default appeal route unless the case was already escalated to a Sessions Judge at first instance.

sections.title: Appeals from convictions
sections.raw_text:
415. Appeals from convictions.—(1) Any person convicted on a trial held by a High Court in its
extraordinary original criminal jurisdiction may appeal to the Supreme Court.
    (2) Any person convicted on a trial held by a Sessions Judge or an Additional Sessions Judge or on a
trial held by any other Court in which a sentence of imprisonment for more than seven years has been
passed against him or against any other person convicted at the same trial, may appeal to the High Court.
    (3) Save as otherwise provided in sub-section (2), any person,--
        (a) convicted on a trial held by Magistrate of the first class, or of the second class; or
        (b) sentenced under section 364; or
        (c) in respect of whom an order has been made or a sentence has been passed under section 401 by
    any Magistrate,
may appeal to the Court of Session.
    (4) When an appeal has been filed against a sentence passed under section 64, section 65,
section 66, section 67, section 68, section 70 or section 71 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the appeal
shall be disposed of within a period of six months from the date of filing of such appeal.

breakdown.plain_summary: This lays out the core appellate ladder by trial forum. A conviction from a High Court's extraordinary original criminal jurisdiction goes straight to the Supreme Court. A conviction by a Sessions Judge/Additional Sessions Judge, or any Court that has imposed more than seven years' imprisonment (on the appellant or any co-accused at the same trial), goes to the High Court. Everything else by default -- Magistrate of the first or second class convictions, section 364 sentences, or section 401 probation/admonition orders -- goes to the Court of Session. A special fast-track applies to appeals against sentences for specified serious offences (BNS sections 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 70, 71 -- broadly sexual offences), which must be disposed of within six months of filing, reflecting the urgency of resolving such matters for victims and accused alike.
essential_elements: High Court extraordinary original criminal jurisdiction convictions: appeal to the Supreme Court.
Sessions Judge/Additional Sessions Judge convictions, or any conviction with a sentence exceeding seven years (on the appellant or a co-accused at the same trial): appeal to the High Court.
Default route (Magistrate first/second class convictions, section 364 sentences, section 401 orders): appeal to the Court of Session.
Appeals against sentences under BNS sections 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 70, or 71 must be disposed of within six months of filing.
breakdown.how_to_read: The six-month disposal mandate for sexual-offence sentence appeals is a hard timeline worth flagging proactively in case management -- practitioners on either side should track this deadline and be prepared to raise delay as a live issue if the appellate Court is not moving the matter along.

sections.title: No appeal in certain cases when accused pleads guilty
sections.raw_text:
416. No appeal in certain cases when accused pleads guilty.—Notwithstanding anything in section
415, where an accused person has pleaded guilty and has been convicted on such plea, there shall be no
appeal,—
        (i) if the conviction is by a High Court; or
        (ii) if the conviction is by a Court of Session or Magistrate of the first or second class, except as to
    the extent or legality of the sentence.

breakdown.plain_summary: This narrows section 415's general appeal ladder where the accused himself pleaded guilty. A High Court conviction on a guilty plea is simply not appealable at all -- there is nothing to appeal since the accused admitted the offence. Where a Court of Session or a first/second-class Magistrate convicts on a guilty plea, the conviction itself likewise cannot be appealed, but the sentence remains open to challenge on its extent (too harsh) or legality (not authorized by law). The logic is straightforward: a guilty plea concedes the facts and guilt, so only sentencing questions genuinely remain in dispute.
essential_elements: Applies where the accused has pleaded guilty and been convicted on that plea.
High Court guilty-plea convictions: no appeal at all.
Court of Session or Magistrate (first/second class) guilty-plea convictions: no appeal against the conviction, but the sentence's extent or legality may still be appealed.
breakdown.how_to_read: Before advising a client to plead guilty, flag this section explicitly -- it forecloses any later argument that the plea was factually wrong or the conviction unsound; only a sentencing challenge survives, so the plea decision should be treated as effectively final on guilt.

sections.title: No appeal in petty cases
sections.raw_text:
417. No appeal in petty cases.—Notwithstanding anything in section 415, there shall be no appeal by
a convicted person in any of the following cases, namely: —
        (a) where a High Court passes only a sentence of imprisonment for a term not exceeding three
    months or of fine not exceeding one thousand rupees, or of both such imprisonment and fine;
        (b) where a Court of Session passes only a sentence of imprisonment for a term not exceeding three
    months or of fine not exceeding two hundred rupees, or of both such imprisonment and fine;
        (c) where a Magistrate of the first class passes only a sentence of fine not exceeding one hundred
    rupees; or
        (d) where, in a case tried summarily, a Magistrate empowered to act under section 283 passes only
    a sentence of fine not exceeding two hundred rupees:
    Provided that an appeal may be brought against any such sentence if any other punishment is combined
with it, but such sentence shall not be appealable merely on the ground—
        (i) that the person convicted is ordered to furnish security to keep the peace; or
        (ii) that a direction for imprisonment in default of payment of fine is included in the sentence; or
        (iii) that more than one sentence of fine is passed in the case, if the total amount of fine imposed
    does not exceed the amount hereinbefore specified in respect of the case.

breakdown.plain_summary: This filters out trivially minor sentences from clogging the appellate system: where the punishment imposed falls at or below specified low thresholds -- graduated by the sentencing Court's level (three months/one thousand rupees for a High Court, three months/two hundred rupees for a Court of Session, one hundred rupees fine-only for a first-class Magistrate, two hundred rupees fine-only for a summary trial under section 283) -- there is simply no appeal available to the convicted person. But this bar only holds if the sentence is purely within those caps; if any additional punishment is combined with it, the whole sentence becomes appealable again. Three specific features don't by themselves defeat the appeal bar: an accompanying peace-security order, a default-imprisonment direction for unpaid fines, or multiple fine components that together still stay within the relevant cap.
essential_elements: Applies to sentences at or below fixed thresholds, tiered by the sentencing forum: High Court (3 months/Rs. 1,000), Court of Session (3 months/Rs. 200), first-class Magistrate (Rs. 100 fine-only), summary trial under section 283 (Rs. 200 fine-only).
Within those caps, the convicted person has no appeal.
If any other/additional punishment is combined with the capped sentence, the appeal bar is lifted entirely.
The bar is not defeated merely by a peace-security order, a default-imprisonment direction, or multiple fines that together remain within the cap.
breakdown.how_to_read: Always compute the true aggregate sentence before advising a client there's no appeal -- a seemingly petty fine combined with even a minor additional punishment (not covered by the three savings clauses) restores the full right of appeal.

sections.title: Appeal by State Government against sentence
sections.raw_text:
418. Appeal by State Government against sentence.—(1) Save as otherwise provided in
sub-section (2), the State Government may, in any case of conviction on a trial held by any Court other than
a High Court, direct the Public Prosecutor to present an appeal against the sentence on the ground of its
inadequacy—
        (a) to the Court of Session, if the sentence is passed by the Magistrate; and
        (b) to the High Court, if the sentence is passed by any other Court.
    (2) If such conviction is in a case in which the offence has been investigated by any agency empowered
to make investigation into an offence under any Central Act other than this Sanhita, the Central Government
may also direct the Public Prosecutor to present an appeal against the sentence on the ground of its
inadequacy—
        (a) to the Court of Session, if the sentence is passed by the Magistrate; and
        (b) to the High Court, if the sentence is passed by any other Court.
    (3) When an appeal has been filed against the sentence on the ground of its inadequacy, the Court of
Session or, as the case may be, the High Court shall not enhance the sentence except after giving to the
accused a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against such enhancement and while showing cause,
the accused may plead for his acquittal or for the reduction of the sentence.
    (4) When an appeal has been filed against a sentence passed under section 64, section 65,
section 66, section 67, section 68, section 70 or section 71 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the appeal
shall be disposed of within a period of six months from the date of filing of such appeal.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives the prosecution side its own route to challenge a sentence as too lenient. The State Government may direct the Public Prosecutor to appeal a conviction's sentence on grounds of inadequacy (to the Court of Session for Magistrate-passed sentences, to the High Court for sentences passed by any other non-High-Court Court). Where the offence was investigated by a Central agency under a Central Act other than this Sanhita (e.g., CBI, NIA-type agencies), the Central Government independently has the same power. Fairness is preserved on the accused's side: before any sentence enhancement on such an appeal, the accused must get a reasonable opportunity to show cause, during which he may argue for outright acquittal or a reduced sentence rather than just resisting enhancement. The same six-month disposal fast-track for specified sexual-offence sentence appeals (as in section 415(4)) applies here too.
essential_elements: The State Government may direct the Public Prosecutor to appeal a non-High-Court conviction's sentence as inadequate -- to the Court of Session (Magistrate sentences) or the High Court (other Courts' sentences).
The Central Government has an independent, parallel power where the offence was investigated by a Central agency under a Central Act other than this Sanhita.
Before enhancing a sentence on such an appeal, the accused must be given a reasonable opportunity to show cause, and may argue for acquittal or reduction while doing so.
Appeals against sentences under BNS sections 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 70, or 71 must be disposed of within six months of filing.
breakdown.how_to_read: The accused's show-cause right under sub-section (3) is a genuine, substantive safeguard, not a formality -- it means a State-initiated inadequacy appeal can backfire into an acquittal or reduced sentence if the accused makes a strong showing, so the State should weigh this risk before directing such an appeal in a borderline case.

sections.title: Appeal in case of acquittal
sections.raw_text:
419. Appeal in case of acquittal.—(1) Save as otherwise provided in sub-section (2), and subject
to the provisions of sub-sections (3) and (5),—
        (a) the District Magistrate may, in any case, direct the Public Prosecutor to present an appeal to the
    Court of Session from an order of acquittal passed by a Magistrate in respect of a cognizable and non-
    bailable offence;
        (b) the State Government may, in any case, direct the Public Prosecutor to present an appeal to the
    High Court from an original or appellate order of acquittal passed by any Court other than a High Court
    not being an order under clause (a) or an order of acquittal passed by the Court of Session in revision.
    (2) If such an order of acquittal is passed in a case in which the offence has been investigated by any
agency empowered to make investigation into an offence under any Central Act other than this Sanhita, the
Central Government may, subject to the provisions of sub-section (3), also direct the Public Prosecutor to
present an appeal—
        (a) to the Court of Session, from an order of acquittal passed by a Magistrate in respect of a
    cognizable and non-bailable offence;
        (b) to the High Court from an original or appellate order of an acquittal passed by any Court other
    than a High Court not being an order under clause (a) or an order of acquittal passed by the Court of
    Session in revision.
    (3) No appeal to the High Court under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) shall be entertained except
with the leave of the High Court.
    (4) If such an order of acquittal is passed in any case instituted upon complaint and the High Court, on
an application made to it by the complainant in this behalf, grants special leave to appeal from the order of
acquittal, the complainant may present such an appeal to the High Court.
    (5) No application under sub-section (4) for the grant of special leave to appeal from an order of
acquittal shall be entertained by the High Court after the expiry of six months, where the complainant is a
public servant, and sixty days in every other case, computed from the date of that order of acquittal.
    (6) If, in any case, the application under sub-section (4) for the grant of special leave to appeal from an
order of acquittal is refused, no appeal from that order of acquittal shall lie under sub-section (1) or under
sub-section (2).

breakdown.plain_summary: This carefully allocates the power to appeal an acquittal among several state and private actors. The District Magistrate may direct the Public Prosecutor to appeal a Magistrate's acquittal (in cognizable, non-bailable offences) to the Court of Session; the State Government may direct an appeal from other acquittals (original or appellate, from any Court other than a High Court, and not already covered by clause (a) or a Sessions Court revisional acquittal) to the High Court -- and the Central Government has an equivalent independent power where a Central agency investigated the offence. Any appeal to the High Court under either route needs the High Court's leave first. Separately, a private complainant in a complaint-case acquittal can apply to the High Court for special leave to appeal -- but strictly within six months (if the complainant is a public servant) or sixty days (otherwise) of the acquittal, and if special leave is refused, that forecloses any appeal route against that acquittal altogether, including the government-directed routes.
essential_elements: District Magistrate: may direct a Public Prosecutor's appeal to the Court of Session from a Magistrate's acquittal in a cognizable, non-bailable offence.
State Government: may direct a Public Prosecutor's appeal to the High Court from other acquittals (original/appellate, excluding clause (a) and Sessions-Court revisional acquittals).
Central Government: has an independent, parallel power where a Central agency investigated the offence under a Central Act other than this Sanhita.
Any High Court appeal under sub-section (1) or (2) requires the High Court's leave.
A private complainant in a complaint case may separately apply for special leave to appeal the acquittal to the High Court.
Special leave applications must be made within six months (public-servant complainant) or sixty days (otherwise) of the acquittal.
Refusal of special leave forecloses any appeal against that acquittal under any route in this section.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Excludes acquittal orders passed by the Court of Session in revision from the State Government's High Court appeal route.
breakdown.how_to_read: The sub-section (6) finality trap is critical -- a private complainant who applies for and is refused special leave has permanently lost any avenue to challenge that acquittal, even if the government might otherwise have been willing to direct its own appeal, so this route should be pursued carefully and not treated as a low-stakes first attempt.

sections.title: Appeal against conviction by High Court in certain cases
sections.raw_text:
420. Appeal against conviction by High Court in certain cases.—Where the High Court has, on
appeal, reversed an order of acquittal of an accused person and convicted him and sentenced him to death
or to imprisonment for life or to imprisonment for a term of ten years or more, he may appeal to the Supreme
Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives a narrow but vital further appeal right: if a High Court, hearing an appeal against an acquittal, reverses that acquittal and itself convicts and sentences the accused to death, life imprisonment, or ten years or more, the accused may appeal that fresh conviction to the Supreme Court -- recognizing that going from acquitted to severely sentenced in a single appellate step is a significant enough reversal of fortune to warrant one more level of review.
essential_elements: Applies where the High Court, on appeal, reverses an acquittal and itself convicts the accused.
Applies only where the resulting sentence is death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment of ten years or more.
The accused may then appeal to the Supreme Court.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is distinct from section 415(1)'s extraordinary-original-jurisdiction route to the Supreme Court -- section 420 is specifically about a High Court's appellate reversal of an acquittal into a severe sentence, a scenario worth flagging immediately to any client facing such a reversal, since the Supreme Court appeal window and procedure differ from an ordinary High Court appeal.

sections.title: Special right of appeal in certain cases
sections.raw_text:
421. Special right of appeal in certain cases.—Notwithstanding anything in this Chapter, when more
persons than one are convicted in one trial, and an appealable judgment or order has been passed in respect
of any of such persons, all or any of the persons convicted at such trial shall have a right of appeal.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes a potential gap in joint trials: even if a particular convicted person's own situation would not, standing alone, obviously trigger an appeal right under the earlier sections of this Chapter, the fact that an appealable judgment or order has been passed against any one of multiple co-accused convicted at the same trial gives all or any of them a right of appeal. It ensures joint-trial defendants are not left without an appellate remedy due to technical gaps in how the appeal-eligibility rules apply to each individual conviction.
essential_elements: Applies where more than one person is convicted in one trial.
An appealable judgment or order must have been passed in respect of any of those persons.
All or any of the persons convicted at that trial then have a right of appeal.
This right operates notwithstanding anything else in this Chapter (i.e., it is an overriding, gap-filling entitlement).
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a safety-net provision -- practitioners defending multiple co-accused in a joint trial should treat it as confirming that none of their clients are stranded without appeal rights merely because the appealability analysis might otherwise look different person-by-person.

sections.title: Appeal to Court of Session how heard
sections.raw_text:
422. Appeal to Court of Session how heard.—(1) Subject to the provisions of sub-section (2), an
appeal to the Court of Session or Sessions Judge shall be heard by the Sessions Judge or by an Additional
Sessions Judge:
    Provided that an appeal against a conviction on a trial held by a Magistrate of the second class may be
heard and disposed of by the Chief Judicial Magistrate.
    (2) An Additional Sessions Judge or a Chief Judicial Magistrate shall hear only such appeals as the
Sessions Judge of the division may, by general or special order, make over to him or as the High Court
may, by special order, direct him to hear.

breakdown.plain_summary: This assigns who within the Court of Session actually hears an appeal routed there: ordinarily the Sessions Judge or an Additional Sessions Judge, with a special carve-out letting the Chief Judicial Magistrate hear and dispose of appeals against second-class Magistrate convictions. An Additional Sessions Judge or Chief Judicial Magistrate cannot simply pick up any appeal on their own initiative -- they may only hear those specifically made over to them by the Sessions Judge's general or special order, or specially directed by the High Court.
essential_elements: Default: appeals to the Court of Session/Sessions Judge are heard by the Sessions Judge or an Additional Sessions Judge.
Proviso: an appeal against a second-class Magistrate conviction may instead be heard and disposed of by the Chief Judicial Magistrate.
An Additional Sessions Judge or Chief Judicial Magistrate hears only appeals made over to him by the Sessions Judge's order, or specially directed by the High Court.
breakdown.how_to_read: Practitioners should check the relevant Sessions Division's standing orders on case allocation -- an appeal heard by an Additional Sessions Judge or Chief Judicial Magistrate without a valid making-over order or High Court direction is vulnerable to a jurisdictional challenge.

sections.title: Petition of appeal
sections.raw_text:
423. Petition of appeal.—Every appeal shall be made in the form of a petition in writing presented by
the appellant or his advocate, and every such petition shall (unless the Court to which it is presented
otherwise directs) be accompanied by a copy of the judgment or order appealed against.

breakdown.plain_summary: This sets the basic form requirement for every appeal under this Chapter: it must be a written petition, presented either by the appellant himself or his advocate, and it must normally come with a copy of the judgment or order being appealed -- though the Court receiving it can waive that accompanying-copy requirement in a given case.
essential_elements: Every appeal must be made as a written petition.
The petition must be presented by the appellant or his advocate.
It must be accompanied by a copy of the judgment or order appealed against, unless the Court otherwise directs.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Court receiving the petition may direct that the judgment/order copy need not accompany it.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the procedural entry point for the entire appeals Chapter -- practitioners should treat 'petition + judgment copy' as the default filing checklist and only rely on the Court's discretion to waive the copy requirement in genuinely justified circumstances (e.g., certified copy delays).

sections.title: Procedure when appellant in jail
sections.raw_text:
424. Procedure when appellant in jail.—If the appellant is in jail, he may present his petition of
appeal and the copies accompanying the same to the officer in charge of the jail, who shall thereupon
forward such petition and copies to the proper Appellate Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives an incarcerated appellant a practical route to file an appeal without needing to personally appear before or send papers directly to the Appellate Court: he may hand his petition of appeal (and accompanying copies) to the jail's officer-in-charge, who is then obligated to forward them on to the proper Appellate Court.
essential_elements: Applies to an appellant who is in jail.
He may present his petition of appeal and accompanying copies to the jail's officer in charge.
The officer in charge must forward the petition and copies to the proper Appellate Court.
breakdown.how_to_read: This route is expressly cross-referenced by sections 425 and 434 -- e.g., a section 424 filing gets a slightly different (still-protective) summary-dismissal standard than a section 423 filing, so identifying which route an appellant used matters procedurally down the line.

sections.title: Summary dismissal of appeal
sections.raw_text:
425. Summary dismissal of appeal.—(1) If upon examining the petition of appeal and copy of the
judgment received under section 423 or section 424, the Appellate Court considers that there is no sufficient
ground for interfering, it may dismiss the appeal summarily:
    Provided that—
        (a) no appeal presented under section 423 shall be dismissed unless the appellant or his advocate
    has had a reasonable opportunity of being heard in support of the same;
        (b) no appeal presented under section 424 shall be dismissed except after giving the appellant a
    reasonable opportunity of being heard in support of the same, unless the Appellate Court considers that
    the appeal is frivolous or that the production of the accused in custody before the Court would involve
    such inconvenience as would be disproportionate in the circumstances of the case;
        (c) no appeal presented under section 424 shall be dismissed summarily until the period allowed
    for preferring such appeal has expired.

    (2) Before dismissing an appeal under this section, the Court may call for the record of the case.
   (3) Where the Appellate Court dismissing an appeal under this section is a Court of Session or of the
Chief Judicial Magistrate, it shall record its reasons for doing so.
    (4) Where an appeal presented under section 424 has been dismissed summarily under this section and
the Appellate Court finds that another petition of appeal duly presented under section 423 on behalf of the
same appellant has not been considered by it, that Court may, notwithstanding anything contained in section
434, if satisfied that it is necessary in the interests of justice so to do, hear and dispose of such appeal in
accordance with law.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives the Appellate Court a filtering mechanism at the threshold: after examining the petition and judgment copy, if it sees no sufficient ground for interfering, it may dismiss the appeal without a full hearing. But this power is hedged with hearing-opportunity safeguards that differ slightly by filing route (ordinary section 423 filings always get a reasonable hearing opportunity; jail-routed section 424 filings generally do too, unless the appeal is frivolous or producing the accused would be disproportionately inconvenient) and a mandatory waiting period for section 424 filings (no summary dismissal before the appeal period expires). The Court may call for the case record before deciding, and a Court of Session or Chief Judicial Magistrate summarily dismissing an appeal must record its reasons.
