A special repair mechanism in sub-section (4) lets the Court revisit a section 424 summary dismissal if it later discovers a duplicate section 423 petition from the same appellant was never actually considered -- overriding the ordinary finality rule in section 434 where the interests of justice require it.
essential_elements: The Appellate Court may summarily dismiss an appeal if it finds no sufficient ground for interfering, after examining the petition and judgment copy.
Proviso (a): a section 423 appeal cannot be dismissed without giving the appellant/advocate a reasonable hearing opportunity.
Proviso (b): a section 424 (jail-routed) appeal generally needs the same hearing opportunity, unless frivolous or producing the accused would be disproportionately inconvenient.
Proviso (c): a section 424 appeal cannot be summarily dismissed before the appeal-filing period has expired.
The Court may call for the case record before dismissing.
A Court of Session or Chief Judicial Magistrate dismissing summarily must record its reasons.

Sub-section (4): if a section 424 summary dismissal is later found to have overlooked an uncommented-upon section 423 petition from the same appellant, the Court may, in the interests of justice, hear and dispose of that appeal despite section 434's finality rule.
breakdown.how_to_read: The sub-section (4) repair mechanism is a useful, narrow safety valve worth flagging to clients whose jail-routed appeal was summarily dismissed -- if a parallel advocate-filed petition on the same conviction was never actually considered, this section allows a second look notwithstanding ordinary finality.

sections.title: Procedure for hearing appeals not dismissed summarily
sections.raw_text:
426. Procedure for hearing appeals not dismissed summarily.—(1) If the Appellate Court does not
dismiss the appeal summarily, it shall cause notice of the time and place at which such appeal will be heard
to be given—
        (i) to the appellant or his advocate;
        (ii) to such officer as the State Government may appoint in this behalf;
       (iii) if the appeal is from a judgment of conviction in a case instituted upon complaint, to the
    complainant;
        (iv) if the appeal is under section 418 or section 419, to the accused, and shall also furnish such
    officer, complainant and accused with a copy of the grounds of appeal.
     (2) The Appellate Court shall then send for the record of the case, if such record is not already available
in that Court, and hear the parties:
     Provided that if the appeal is only as to the extent or the legality of the sentence, the Court may dispose
of the appeal without sending for the record.
   (3) Where the only ground for appeal from a conviction is the alleged severity of the sentence, the
appellant shall not, except with the leave of the Court, urge or be heard in support of any other ground.

breakdown.plain_summary: Once an appeal survives the summary-dismissal filter, this lays out the full-hearing procedure: notice of the hearing date/place must go to the appellant/advocate, the State-appointed officer (in practice, typically the Public Prosecutor or a designated officer), the complainant (if the conviction arose from a complaint case), and the accused himself (if the appeal is a State/Central Government sentence-enhancement appeal under section 418 or an acquittal appeal under section 419) -- with all of them also getting a copy of the grounds of appeal. The Court then calls for the case record and hears the parties, though it can skip fetching the record if the appeal is confined to the extent or legality of the sentence. And an appellant who has only challenged sentence severity cannot, without the Court's leave, expand into arguing other grounds at the hearing.
essential_elements: Applies once the Appellate Court has decided not to dismiss the appeal summarily.

Notice of the hearing time/place, with a copy of the grounds of appeal, must go to: the appellant/advocate; the State Government's designated officer; the complainant (if a complaint case conviction); and the accused (if the appeal is under section 418 or 419).
The Court sends for the case record (unless the appeal is only about sentence extent/legality) and hears the parties.
If the appeal's only ground was sentence severity, the appellant needs the Court's leave to argue any other ground.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The record need not be sent for if the appeal is confined to the extent or legality of the sentence.
breakdown.how_to_read: The differentiated notice list is a checklist worth verifying in practice -- a State/Central Government sentence-enhancement or acquittal appeal specifically requires notice to the accused himself (not just his advocate), since he stands to lose more from that particular appeal than from an ordinary appeal against his own conviction.

sections.title: Powers of Appellate Court
sections.raw_text:
427. Powers of Appellate Court.—After perusing such record and hearing the appellant or his
advocate, if he appears, and the Public Prosecutor if he appears, and in case of an appeal under section 418
or section 419, the accused, if he appears, the Appellate Court may, if it considers that there is no sufficient
ground for interfering, dismiss the appeal, or may—
        (a) in an appeal from an order of acquittal, reverse such order and direct that further inquiry be
    made, or that the accused be re-tried or committed for trial, as the case may be, or find him guilty and
    pass sentence on him according to law;
        (b) in an appeal from a conviction—
             (i) reverse the finding and sentence and acquit or discharge the accused, or order him to be
        re-tried by a Court of competent jurisdiction subordinate to such Appellate Court or committed for
        trial; or
            (ii) alter the finding, maintaining the sentence; or
             (iii) with or without altering the finding, alter the nature or the extent, or the nature and extent,
        of the sentence, but not so as to enhance the same;
        (c) in an appeal for enhancement of sentence—
             (i) reverse the finding and sentence and acquit or discharge the accused or order him to be
        re-tried by a Court competent to try the offence; or
            (ii) alter the finding maintaining the sentence; or
             (iii) with or without altering the finding, alter the nature or the extent, or, the nature and extent,
        of the sentence, so as to enhance or reduce the same;
        (d) in an appeal from any other order, alter or reverse such order;
        (e) make any amendment or any consequential or incidental order that may be just or proper:
    Provided that the sentence shall not be enhanced unless the accused has had an opportunity of showing
cause against such enhancement:
     Provided further that the Appellate Court shall not inflict greater punishment for the offence which in
its opinion the accused has committed, than might have been inflicted for that offence by the Court passing
the order or sentence under appeal.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the heart of the Appellate Court's substantive authority, giving it a distinct menu of powers depending on what kind of appeal is before it. On an acquittal appeal, it can reverse the acquittal and order further inquiry, retrial, committal for trial, or itself convict and sentence. On a conviction appeal, it can reverse and acquit/discharge/order retrial or committal, alter the finding while keeping the sentence, or alter the sentence's nature/extent -- but never enhance it in an ordinary conviction appeal. On a sentence-enhancement appeal, it has full symmetric power to enhance or reduce. On any other order, it can alter or reverse it, and it always has a residual power to make just and proper amendments or consequential/incidental orders. Two protective provisos constrain enhancement power generally: the accused must get a chance to show cause before any enhancement, and the Appellate Court can never impose a harsher punishment than the original Court could have imposed for the offence it now finds was actually committed.
essential_elements: Threshold: after perusing the record and hearing the appellant/advocate, Public Prosecutor, and (for section 418/419 appeals) the accused, the Court may dismiss if there is no sufficient ground for interfering.
(a) Acquittal appeal: reverse and order further inquiry/retrial/committal, or convict and sentence.
(b) Conviction appeal: reverse and acquit/discharge/retry/commit; or alter the finding keeping the sentence; or alter the sentence's nature/extent without enhancing it.
(c) Sentence-enhancement appeal: reverse and acquit/discharge/retry; or alter the finding keeping the sentence; or alter the sentence's nature/extent, enhancing or reducing it.
(d) Appeal from any other order: alter or reverse it.
(e) Residual power to make any just and proper amendment or consequential/incidental order.
Proviso 1: no sentence enhancement without giving the accused an opportunity to show cause.
Proviso 2: the Appellate Court cannot inflict greater punishment for the offence it finds committed than the original Court could have imposed for that offence.
breakdown.how_to_read: The asymmetry between (b) and (c) is the key structural point to internalize: an ordinary conviction appeal by the accused can never result in a harsher sentence, while a dedicated enhancement appeal under section 418 can cut either way (enhance or reduce) -- so which section an appeal is filed under determines the ceiling on downside risk for the accused.

sections.title: Judgments of subordinate Appellate Court
sections.raw_text:
428. Judgments of subordinate Appellate Court.—The rules contained in Chapter XXIX as to the
judgment of a Criminal Court of original jurisdiction shall apply, so far as may be practicable, to the
judgment in appeal of a Court of Session or Chief Judicial Magistrate:
    Provided that, unless the Appellate Court otherwise directs, the accused shall not be brought up, or
required to attend, to hear judgment delivered.

breakdown.plain_summary: This extends the Chapter XXIX judgment-writing rules (pronouncement, content, language requirements, etc., originally designed for a trial Court's judgment) to appellate judgments delivered by a Court of Session or Chief Judicial Magistrate, applying them as far as practicable given the appellate context. A practical relief is built in: unlike a trial Court's judgment, the accused need not be brought up or required to attend to hear the appellate judgment delivered, unless the Appellate Court specifically directs otherwise.
essential_elements: Chapter XXIX's judgment rules apply, so far as practicable, to appellate judgments of a Court of Session or Chief Judicial Magistrate.
Unless the Appellate Court directs otherwise, the accused need not be brought up or required to attend to hear the judgment delivered.
breakdown.how_to_read: This section only covers Sessions/Chief Judicial Magistrate appellate judgments -- High Court appellate judgments are governed by the High Court's own procedure (including its Rules) rather than being routed through this cross-reference.

sections.title: Order of High Court on appeal to be certified to lower Court
sections.raw_text:
429. Order of High Court on appeal to be certified to lower Court.—(1) Whenever a case is decided
on appeal by the High Court under this Chapter, it shall certify its judgment or order to the Court by which
the finding, sentence or order appealed against was recorded or passed and if such Court is that of a Judicial
Magistrate other than the Chief Judicial Magistrate, the High Court's judgment or order shall be sent through
the Chief Judicial Magistrate, and if such Court is that of an Executive Magistrate, the High Court's
judgment or order shall be sent through the District Magistrate.
    (2) The Court to which the High Court certifies its judgment or order shall thereupon make such orders
as are conformable to the judgment or order of the High Court; and if necessary, the record shall be amended
in accordance therewith.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes the loop after a High Court decides an appeal: it must certify its judgment or order back to the Court whose decision was appealed from. There's a routing nuance for Magistrate-level cases -- if the original Court was a Judicial Magistrate (other than the Chief Judicial Magistrate), the certified order is routed through the Chief Judicial Magistrate; if it was an Executive Magistrate, it's routed through the District Magistrate. Whichever Court ultimately receives the certified order must then make conforming orders and, if necessary, amend its own record to match the High Court's decision.
essential_elements: Applies whenever the High Court decides a case on appeal under this Chapter.
The High Court must certify its judgment/order to the Court that recorded/passed the appealed-from finding, sentence, or order.
If the original Court was a Judicial Magistrate (not Chief Judicial Magistrate), certification is routed through the Chief Judicial Magistrate.
If the original Court was an Executive Magistrate, certification is routed through the District Magistrate.
The receiving Court must make conforming orders and, if necessary, amend its record accordingly.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the High-Court-level counterpart to section 412's death-confirmation certification mechanism -- both exist to ensure the lower Court's official record is actually updated to reflect the higher Court's final word, not left inconsistent with it.

sections.title: Suspension of sentence pending appeal; release of appellant on bail
sections.raw_text:
430. Suspension of sentence pending appeal; release of appellant on bail.—(1) Pending any appeal
by a convicted person, the Appellate Court may, for reasons to be recorded by it in writing, order that the
execution of the sentence or order appealed against be suspended and, also, if he is in confinement, that he
be released on bail, or on his own bond or bail bond:
     Provided that the Appellate Court shall, before releasing on his own bond or bail bond a convicted
person who is convicted of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life or imprisonment for
a term of not less than ten years, shall give opportunity to the Public Prosecutor for showing cause in writing
against such release:
    Provided further that in cases where a convicted person is released on bail it shall be open to the Public
Prosecutor to file an application for the cancellation of the bail.
     (2) The power conferred by this section on an Appellate Court may be exercised also by the High Court
in the case of an appeal by a convicted person to a Court subordinate thereto.
    (3) Where the convicted person satisfies the Court by which he is convicted that he intends to present
an appeal, the Court shall,—
        (i) where such person, being on bail, is sentenced to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three
    years; or
        (ii) where the offence of which such person has been convicted is a bailable one, and he is on bail,
order that the convicted person be released on bail, unless there are special reasons for refusing bail, for
such period as will afford sufficient time to present the appeal and obtain the orders of the Appellate Court
under sub-section (1); and the sentence of imprisonment shall, so long as he is so released on bail, be
deemed to be suspended.
     (4) When the appellant is ultimately sentenced to imprisonment for a term or to imprisonment for life,
the time during which he is so released shall be excluded in computing the term for which he is so sentenced.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives a convicted person facing imprisonment a route to seek release pending appeal, so that a conviction under challenge doesn't automatically mean immediate incarceration for the appeal's full duration. The Appellate Court can, with written reasons, suspend execution of the sentence/order and release the appellant on bail or bond -- though for the most serious sentences (death, life, or ten-plus years) it must first give the Public Prosecutor a chance to show cause in writing against release on the appellant's own bond/bail bond, and the Prosecutor can separately move to cancel bail once granted. A High Court holds this same power over appeals to Courts subordinate to it. Separately, the trial Court itself (not just the Appellate Court) has a duty in narrower circumstances -- where the convict was already on bail and got three years or less, or was convicted of a bailable offence and is on bail -- to grant bail pending appeal for long enough to actually get to the Appellate Court, absent special reasons to refuse; the sentence is deemed suspended during that period. If the appellant is ultimately sentenced to a term or life imprisonment, the time spent released on bail is excluded when computing the sentence term.
essential_elements: The Appellate Court may, with written reasons, suspend the appealed sentence/order and release the appellant on bail or bond, pending appeal.
For death/life/ten-plus-year sentences, the Public Prosecutor must first get a chance to show cause in writing against release on the appellant's own bond/bail bond.
The Public Prosecutor may separately apply for cancellation of bail once granted.
A High Court holds the same power for appeals to Courts subordinate to it.

The trial Court itself must grant bail pending appeal (absent special reasons) where the convict, already on bail, is sentenced to three years or less, or was convicted of a bailable offence and is on bail -- for long enough to present the appeal and get the Appellate Court's orders; the sentence is deemed suspended during that period.
Time spent released under sub-section (3) is excluded when computing an ultimate term or life sentence.
breakdown.how_to_read: The sub-section (3) trial-Court-level bail entitlement is a frequently-used, time-sensitive provision -- practitioners representing a convict who was on bail and got three years or less (or a bailable-offence conviction) should raise it immediately at sentencing, since it operates as a near-automatic bridge to the appeal stage rather than requiring a separate Appellate Court application in the first instance.

sections.title: Arrest of accused in appeal from acquittal
sections.raw_text:
431. Arrest of accused in appeal from acquittal.—When an appeal is presented under section 419,
the High Court may issue a warrant directing that the accused be arrested and brought before it or any
subordinate Court, and the Court before which he is brought may commit him to prison pending the disposal
of the appeal or admit him to bail.

breakdown.plain_summary: Since an acquitted accused is, by definition, a free person, this gives the High Court a mechanism to actually secure his presence once an acquittal appeal under section 419 is filed: it may issue a warrant for his arrest and production before it or a subordinate Court. Whichever Court he is brought before can then either commit him to custody pending the appeal's disposal or admit him to bail -- so arrest does not automatically mean continued detention through the appeal.
essential_elements: Applies once an appeal against acquittal is presented under section 419.
The High Court may issue a warrant for the accused's arrest and production before it or a subordinate Court.
The Court before which he is brought may commit him to prison pending disposal of the appeal, or admit him to bail.
breakdown.how_to_read: This power is discretionary, not automatic -- filing an acquittal appeal does not by itself re-arrest the accused; the High Court must affirmatively issue a warrant, and even then the receiving Court retains the choice between custody and bail.

sections.title: Appellate Court may take further evidence or direct it to be taken
sections.raw_text:
432. Appellate Court may take further evidence or direct it to be taken.—(1) In dealing with any
appeal under this Chapter, the Appellate Court, if it thinks additional evidence to be necessary, shall record
its reasons and may either take such evidence itself, or direct it to be taken by a Magistrate or, when the
Appellate Court is a High Court, by a Court of Session or a Magistrate.
    (2) When the additional evidence is taken by the Court of Session or the Magistrate, it or he shall certify
such evidence to the Appellate Court, and such Court shall thereupon proceed to dispose of the appeal.
    (3) The accused or his advocate shall have the right to be present when the additional evidence is taken.
   (4) The taking of evidence under this section shall be subject to the provisions of Chapter XXV, as if it
were an inquiry.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives the Appellate Court the same kind of evidence-supplementing power the High Court has in death-confirmation cases (section 408): if it thinks additional evidence is genuinely necessary to decide the appeal, it must record its reasons and can either take that evidence itself or direct a Magistrate (or, if it is itself a High Court, a Court of Session or Magistrate) to take it. Where a subordinate Court takes the evidence, it must certify the results back to the Appellate Court, which then proceeds to dispose of the appeal. The accused or his advocate has a guaranteed right to be present during this evidence-taking, and the whole process is governed by Chapter XXV's inquiry rules as if it were an inquiry.
essential_elements: Applies when the Appellate Court, dealing with any appeal under this Chapter, thinks additional evidence is necessary.
The Appellate Court must record its reasons for finding additional evidence necessary.
It may take the evidence itself, or direct a Magistrate (or, if it is a High Court, a Court of Session or Magistrate) to take it.
Evidence taken by a subordinate Court/Magistrate must be certified back to the Appellate Court, which then disposes of the appeal.
The accused or his advocate has the right to be present when the additional evidence is taken.
The evidence-taking is subject to Chapter XXV's provisions, as if it were an inquiry.
breakdown.how_to_read: The mandatory reasoned-order requirement is a real check on this power -- an Appellate Court cannot simply call for additional evidence on a whim; practitioners should scrutinize whether genuine necessity was recorded before such evidence is admitted, since this reopens the evidentiary record at the appellate stage.

sections.title: Procedure where Judges of Court of appeal are equally divided
sections.raw_text:
433. Procedure where Judges of Court of appeal are equally divided.—When an appeal under this
Chapter is heard by a High Court before a Bench of Judges and they are divided in opinion, the appeal, with
their opinions, shall be laid before another Judge of that Court, and that Judge, after such hearing as he
thinks fit, shall deliver his opinion, and the judgment or order shall follow that opinion:
    Provided that if one of the Judges constituting the Bench, or, where the appeal is laid before another
Judge under this section, that Judge, so requires, the appeal shall be re-heard and decided by a larger Bench
of Judges.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the general tie-breaking mechanism that section 411 (death-confirmation cases) cross-references. When a High Court Bench hearing an appeal splits evenly in opinion, the matter is not left unresolved: the appeal and both opinions go before another Judge of that Court, who hears it as he thinks fit and delivers his own opinion, which then becomes the controlling judgment or order. But there is a built-in escalation valve -- either an original Bench Judge or the referee Judge himself can require the appeal to instead be re-heard and decided by a larger Bench, rather than resolved by a single tie-breaking Judge.
essential_elements: Applies when a High Court Bench hearing an appeal under this Chapter is equally divided in opinion.
The appeal, with both opinions, is laid before another Judge of that Court.
That Judge hears the matter as he thinks fit and delivers his opinion, which the judgment/order then follows.
Proviso: if an original Bench Judge, or the referee Judge himself, requires it, the appeal is instead re-heard and decided by a larger Bench.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the mechanism directly cross-referenced by section 411 for a divided death-confirmation Bench -- practitioners should read the two sections together whenever a two-Judge Bench splits on any matter under this Chapter, capital or otherwise.

sections.title: Finality of judgments and orders on appeal
sections.raw_text:
434. Finality of judgments and orders on appeal.—Judgments and orders passed by an Appellate
Court upon an appeal shall be final, except in the cases provided for in section 418, section 419,
sub-section (4) of section 425 or Chapter XXXII:
   Provided that notwithstanding the final disposal of an appeal against conviction in any case, the
Appellate Court may hear and dispose of, on the merits,—
    (a) an appeal against acquittal under section 419, arising out of the same case; or
    (b) an appeal for the enhancement of sentence under section 418, arising out of the same case.

breakdown.plain_summary: This establishes finality as the default rule for appellate outcomes: once an Appellate Court decides an appeal, that judgment/order is final, closing off further challenge -- except through the specific escape routes this Sanhita itself carves out: a State/Central Government sentence-enhancement appeal (section 418), an acquittal appeal (section 419), the sub-section (4) repair mechanism for an overlooked section 423 petition after a section 424 summary dismissal (section 425), or the reference-and-revision jurisdiction of Chapter XXXII. A specific proviso clarifies that finality of a conviction appeal in a given case doesn't block a separate, still-pending section 418 enhancement appeal or section 419 acquittal appeal arising from that same case -- both can still be heard and decided on their merits even after the conviction appeal is finally disposed of.
essential_elements: General rule: an Appellate Court's judgment/order on appeal is final.
Exceptions: section 418 (enhancement appeals), section 419 (acquittal appeals), section 425(4) (overlooked petition repair), and Chapter XXXII (reference and revision).

Proviso: final disposal of a conviction appeal in a case does not prevent the Appellate Court from separately hearing and deciding, on the merits, a related section 419 acquittal appeal or section 418 enhancement appeal arising from the same case.
breakdown.how_to_read: This finality rule is why reference/revision (Chapter XXXII) functions as the residual safety valve in the system -- when none of the enumerated appeal-specific exceptions apply and an appellate order is otherwise final, revision jurisdiction becomes the practical avenue to challenge a Sessions Judge's or subordinate Court's order.

sections.title: Abatement of appeals
sections.raw_text:
435. Abatement of appeals.—(1) Every appeal under section 418 or section 419 shall finally abate on
the death of the accused.
    (2) Every other appeal under this Chapter (except an appeal from a sentence of fine) shall finally abate
on the death of the appellant:
    Provided that where the appeal is against a conviction and sentence of death or of imprisonment, and
the appellant dies during the pendency of the appeal, any of his near relatives may, within thirty days of the
death of the appellant, apply to the Appellate Court for leave to continue the appeal; and if leave is granted,
the appeal shall not abate.
     Explanation.—In this section, "near relative" means a parent, spouse, lineal descendant, brother or
sister.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes Chapter XXXI by addressing what happens to a pending appeal when a party dies. A State/Central Government appeal for enhanced sentence or against acquittal (sections 418, 419) simply and finally abates if the accused dies -- there is no one left to enhance the sentence against or reconvict. For any other appeal (except one only about a fine, which can still matter for estate/recovery purposes), the appellant's death finally abates the appeal too -- but with an important safeguard: if the appeal was against a conviction carrying a death sentence or imprisonment, a near relative (parent, spouse, lineal descendant, brother, or sister) can apply within thirty days of the appellant's death for leave to continue the appeal, and if granted, the appeal survives rather than abating. This protects the deceased's reputation, family, and any consequences (like property forfeiture) that might still turn on whether the conviction stands.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1): a section 418 or 419 appeal finally abates on the death of the accused.
Sub-section (2): every other appeal under this Chapter (except a fine-sentence appeal) finally abates on the appellant's death.
Proviso: for a conviction-and-death/imprisonment-sentence appeal, a near relative may apply within thirty days of the appellant's death for leave to continue it; if granted, it does not abate.
'Near relative' is defined as a parent, spouse, lineal descendant, brother, or sister.
breakdown.how_to_read: Practitioners for the family of a deceased appellant should treat the thirty-day window as a hard, easily-missed deadline -- the right to continue a serious conviction appeal (and thereby clear the deceased's name or protect estate consequences) is lost if no near relative applies for leave within that period.

sections.title: Reference to High Court
sections.raw_text:
436. Reference to High Court.—(1) Where any Court is satisfied that a case pending before it involves
a question as to the validity of any Act, Ordinance or Regulation or of any provision contained in an Act,
Ordinance or Regulation, the determination of which is necessary for the disposal of the case, and is of
opinion that such Act, Ordinance, Regulation or provision is invalid or inoperative, but has not been so
declared by the High Court to which that Court is subordinate or by the Supreme Court, the Court shall
state a case setting out its opinion and the reasons therefor, and refer the same for the decision of the High
Court.
    Explanation.—In this section, "Regulation" means any Regulation as defined in the General Clauses
Act, 1897 (10 of 1897), or in the General Clauses Act of a State.
    (2) A Court of Session may, if it thinks fit in any case pending before it to which the provisions of sub-
section (1) do not apply, refer for the decision of the High Court any question of law arising in the hearing
of such case.
   (3) Any Court making a reference to the High Court under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) may,
pending the decision of the High Court thereon, either commit the accused to jail or release him on bail to
appear when called upon.

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Chapter XXXII by giving a Court facing a genuine legal-validity doubt a formal escape hatch instead of ruling on that doubt itself. If a Court hearing a pending case believes a statute, Ordinance, Regulation, or provision it must apply is invalid or inoperative -- and no controlling High Court or Supreme Court has already so declared -- it must state a case (its opinion plus reasons) and refer the validity question to the High Court, rather than deciding it unilaterally. Separately, a Court of Session has a broader, purely discretionary power to refer any question of law (not just validity questions) to the High Court in a pending case. While either kind of reference is pending, the referring Court may commit the accused to jail or release him on bail to appear when called upon, keeping the underlying case from stalling entirely.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1): mandatory reference where a Court believes a law/provision it must apply to a pending case is invalid or inoperative, and no High Court/Supreme Court has already so declared -- the Court must state its opinion and reasons and refer it to the High Court.
Explanation: 'Regulation' takes the General Clauses Act, 1897 (or a State's General Clauses Act) definition.
Sub-section (2): a Court of Session may, at its discretion, refer any other question of law arising in a pending case to the High Court.
Sub-section (3): pending the High Court's decision on a reference, the referring Court may commit the accused to jail or release him on bail to appear when called upon.
breakdown.how_to_read: The mandatory-versus-discretionary split matters -- a subordinate Court has no choice but to refer a genuine validity question under sub-section (1), while a Court of Session's sub-section (2) power over other legal questions is purely optional, so counsel should not assume every doubtful legal question automatically gets referred.

sections.title: Disposal of case according to decision of High Court
sections.raw_text:
437. Disposal of case according to decision of High Court.—(1) When a question has been so
referred, the High Court shall pass such order thereon as it thinks fit, and shall cause a copy of such order
to be sent to the Court by which the reference was made, which shall dispose of the case conformably to
the said order.
    (2) The High Court may direct by whom the costs of such reference shall be paid.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes the reference loop: once the High Court decides the referred question, it passes whatever order it thinks fit and sends a copy back to the referring Court, which must then dispose of the underlying case in conformity with that order. The High Court also has the power to direct who bears the costs of the reference itself.
essential_elements: The High Court passes such order on the referred question as it thinks fit.
A copy of that order is sent to the referring Court, which must dispose of the case conformably to it.
The High Court may direct by whom the reference costs shall be paid.
breakdown.how_to_read: The referring Court has no discretion to depart from the High Court's answer -- once the order comes back, disposal 'conformably' to it is mandatory, making the reference genuinely binding rather than merely advisory.

sections.title: Calling for records to exercise powers of revision
sections.raw_text:
438. Calling for records to exercise powers of revision.—(1) The High Court or any Sessions Judge
may call for and examine the record of any proceeding before any inferior Criminal Court situate within its
or his local jurisdiction for the purpose of satisfying itself or himself as to the correctness, legality or
propriety of any finding, sentence or order, recorded or passed, and as to the regularity of any proceedings
of such inferior Court, and may, when calling, for such record, direct that the execution of any sentence or
order be suspended, and if the accused is in confinement that he be released on his own bond or bail bond
pending the examination of the record.
    Explanation.—All Magistrates, whether Executive or Judicial, and whether exercising original or
appellate jurisdiction, shall be deemed to be inferior to the Sessions Judge for the purposes of this sub-
section and of section 439.
    (2) The powers of revision conferred by sub-section (1) shall not be exercised in relation to any
interlocutory order passed in any appeal, inquiry, trial or other proceeding.
    (3) If an application under this section has been made by any person either to the High Court or to the
Sessions Judge, no further application by the same person shall be entertained by the other of them.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the core grant of revisional jurisdiction: the High Court or any Sessions Judge may call for and examine the record of any proceeding before an inferior Criminal Court within its/his local jurisdiction, to check the correctness, legality, or propriety of any finding, sentence, or order, and the regularity of the proceedings generally. While calling for the record, the reviewing authority can suspend execution of a sentence/order and, if the accused is confined, release him on his own bond or bail bond pending the record's examination. The Explanation clarifies that all Magistrates -- Executive or Judicial, original or appellate -- count as 'inferior' to the Sessions Judge for this purpose. Two important limits apply: revision cannot touch interlocutory orders passed in any appeal, inquiry, trial, or other proceeding, and once a person has applied to either the High Court or a Sessions Judge under this section, that same person cannot make a further application to the other of them -- a one-shot rule against forum-shopping between the two revisional authorities.
essential_elements: The High Court, or any Sessions Judge, may call for and examine the record of any proceeding before an inferior Criminal Court within its/his local jurisdiction.
Purpose: to check correctness, legality, or propriety of any finding, sentence, or order, and the regularity of proceedings.
The reviewing authority may suspend execution of a sentence/order and release a confined accused on bond/bail bond pending the record's examination.
Explanation: all Magistrates (Executive/Judicial, original/appellate) are deemed inferior to the Sessions Judge for this section and section 439.
Sub-section (2): revisional power cannot be exercised over interlocutory orders passed in any appeal, inquiry, trial, or other proceeding.
Sub-section (3): if a person has applied to either the High Court or the Sessions Judge under this section, no further application by that same person will be entertained by the other.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Interlocutory orders are excluded from revisional scrutiny.
A person cannot apply to both the High Court and the Sessions Judge under this section -- only one, not both.
breakdown.how_to_read: The one-application rule in sub-section (3) is a critical strategic checkpoint -- practitioners must choose carefully whether to approach the Sessions Judge or go straight to the High Court, since an unsuccessful application to one forecloses trying the other on the same matter.

sections.title: Power to order inquiry
sections.raw_text:
439. Power to order inquiry.—On examining any record under section 438 or otherwise, the High
Court or the Sessions Judge may direct the Chief Judicial Magistrate by himself or by any of the Magistrates
subordinate to him to make, and the Chief Judicial Magistrate may himself make or direct any subordinate
Magistrate to make, further inquiry into any complaint which has been dismissed under section 226 or sub-
section (4) of section 227, or into the case of any person accused of an offence who has been discharged:
    Provided that no Court shall make any direction under this section for inquiry into the case of any
person who has been discharged unless such person has had an opportunity of showing cause why such
direction should not be made.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives the revisional authorities a specific corrective tool for premature dismissals and discharges: after examining a record (whether under section 438 or otherwise), the High Court or Sessions Judge may direct the Chief Judicial Magistrate -- himself or through a subordinate Magistrate -- to conduct further inquiry into a complaint that was dismissed under section 226 or section 227(4), or into the case of an accused who was discharged. The Chief Judicial Magistrate can also make this direction on his own initiative or through a subordinate Magistrate. But a discharged person cannot be subjected to a further-inquiry direction without first getting a chance to show cause against it.
essential_elements: Applies on examination of a record under section 438 or otherwise.

The High Court or Sessions Judge may direct the Chief Judicial Magistrate (himself or via a subordinate Magistrate) to make further inquiry into a complaint dismissed under section 226 or section 227(4), or into a discharged accused's case.
The Chief Judicial Magistrate may also himself make, or direct a subordinate Magistrate to make, such further inquiry.
Proviso: no direction for further inquiry into a discharged person's case may be made without giving that person an opportunity to show cause against it.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a narrow, targeted revisional remedy -- it only reopens complaint dismissals and discharges, not full-blown acquittals or convictions, and always with the discharged person's show-cause right as a mandatory procedural safeguard.

sections.title: Sessions Judge's powers of revision
sections.raw_text:
440. Sessions Judge's powers of revision.—(1) In the case of any proceeding the record of which has
been called for by himself, the Sessions Judge may exercise all or any of the powers which may be exercised
by the High Court under sub-section (1) of section 442.
    (2) Where any proceeding by way of revision is commenced before a Sessions Judge under
sub-section (1), the provisions of sub-sections (2), (3), (4) and (5) of section 442 shall, so far as may be,
apply to such proceeding and references in the said sub-sections to the High Court shall be construed as
references to the Sessions Judge.
    (3) Where any application for revision is made by or on behalf of any person before the Sessions Judge,
the decision of the Sessions Judge thereon in relation to such person shall be final and no further proceeding
by way of revision at the instance of such person shall be entertained by the High Court or any other Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: This equips the Sessions Judge with the same substantive revisional powers the High Court has under section 442(1), for any proceeding whose record the Sessions Judge has himself called for -- and applies section 442's procedural sub-sections (2) through (5) to Sessions Judge-level revision proceedings, reading those provisions' references to the High Court as references to the Sessions Judge instead. Crucially, once a person's revision application has been decided by the Sessions Judge, that decision is final as to that person, and no further revision at that same person's instance can be entertained by the High Court or any other Court -- reinforcing the one-shot rule already set out in section 438(3) from the other direction.
essential_elements: The Sessions Judge may exercise all or any of the High Court's section 442(1) revisional powers, for proceedings whose record he has himself called for.
Section 442(2)-(5)'s procedural provisions apply to Sessions Judge-level revision, with 'High Court' read as 'Sessions Judge'.
A Sessions Judge's decision on a person's revision application is final as to that person; no further revision at that person's instance may be entertained by the High Court or any other Court.
breakdown.how_to_read: Sections 438(3) and 440(3) work together as a matched pair enforcing the same finality principle from both ends -- once a litigant has chosen and exhausted the Sessions Judge route, section 440(3) independently blocks any further attempt at the High Court, even setting aside section 438(3)'s prior-application bar.

sections.title: Power of Additional Sessions Judge
sections.raw_text:
441. Power of Additional Sessions Judge.—An Additional Sessions Judge shall have and may
exercise all the powers of a Sessions Judge under this Chapter in respect of any case which may be
transferred to him by or under any general or special order of the Sessions Judge.

breakdown.plain_summary: This confirms that an Additional Sessions Judge is not a lesser authority when it comes to reference and revision matters -- he has and may exercise the full powers of a Sessions Judge under this Chapter, but only for cases actually transferred to him by the Sessions Judge's general or special order. The power flows from delegation, not independent original authority.
essential_elements: An Additional Sessions Judge has all the powers of a Sessions Judge under this Chapter (Reference and Revision).
This applies only to cases transferred to him by or under a general or special order of the Sessions Judge.
breakdown.how_to_read: Practitioners should verify the underlying transfer order when a matter is being handled by an Additional Sessions Judge under this Chapter -- without a valid general or special order from the Sessions Judge, the Additional Sessions Judge would lack this delegated authority.

sections.title: High Court's powers of revision
sections.raw_text:
442. High Court's powers of revision.—(1) In the case of any proceeding the record of which has
been called for by itself or which otherwise comes to its knowledge, the High Court may, in its discretion,
exercise any of the powers conferred on a Court of Appeal by sections 427, 430, 431 and 432 or on a Court
of Session by section 344, and, when the Judges composing the Court of revision are equally divided in
opinion, the case shall be disposed of in the manner provided by section 433.

    (2) No order under this section shall be made to the prejudice of the accused or other person unless he
has had an opportunity of being heard either personally or by advocate in his own defence.
    (3) Nothing in this section shall be deemed to authorise a High Court to convert a finding of acquittal
into one of conviction.
    (4) Where under this Sanhita an appeal lies and no appeal is brought, no proceeding by way of revision
shall be entertained at the instance of the party who could have appealed.
    (5) Where under this Sanhita an appeal lies but an application for revision has been made to the High
Court by any person and the High Court is satisfied that such application was made under the erroneous
belief that no appeal lies thereto and that it is necessary in the interests of justice so to do, the High Court
may treat the application for revision as a petition of appeal and deal with the same accordingly.

breakdown.plain_summary: This spells out the substantive content of the High Court's revisional power referenced by section 438: for any proceeding whose record it has called for, or which otherwise comes to its knowledge, the High Court may in its discretion exercise any of the Appellate Court's powers under sections 427, 430, 431, and 432, or a Court of Session's powers under section 344, with a divided-Bench tie broken per section 433. Several important limits apply: no order can be made to the accused's/another person's prejudice without giving him a hearing opportunity (personally or by advocate); the High Court cannot use revision to convert an acquittal into a conviction (a hard substantive limit, since that would effectively bypass the acquittal-appeal safeguards in section 419); revision is unavailable to a party who had an appeal right but chose not to use it (revision is not a backdoor around a missed appeal); and, as a fairness safety valve, if someone mistakenly filed for revision believing no appeal lay when one actually did, the High Court may -- in the interests of justice -- simply treat that revision application as a petition of appeal instead.
essential_elements: The High Court may, in its discretion, exercise any of the Appellate Court's powers under sections 427, 430, 431, 432, or a Court of Session's powers under section 344, over any proceeding whose record it has called for or that otherwise comes to its knowledge.
A divided-opinion revision Bench is resolved per section 433.
No prejudicial order may be made without giving the affected person a hearing opportunity (personally or by advocate).
The High Court cannot convert an acquittal into a conviction via revision.
Revision is not available to a party who had an appeal right under this Sanhita but did not appeal.
If a revision application was mistakenly filed under the erroneous belief that no appeal lay, the High Court may, in the interests of justice, treat it as a petition of appeal instead.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The acquittal-to-conviction conversion bar means an acquittal can only be reversed via a proper section 419 acquittal appeal, never through revision.
A party who could have appealed but didn't is barred from using revision as a substitute route.
breakdown.how_to_read: The sub-section (5) rescue mechanism is worth invoking proactively for a client who mistakenly filed a revision application in a case where an appeal actually lay -- rather than losing the remedy entirely to a limitation/wrong-forum technicality, counsel can ask the High Court to treat it as a petition of appeal in the interests of justice.

sections.title: Power of High Court to withdraw or transfer revision cases
sections.raw_text:
443. Power of High Court to withdraw or transfer revision cases.—(1) Whenever one or more
persons convicted at the same trial makes or make application to a High Court for revision and any other
person convicted at the same trial makes an application to the Sessions Judge for revision, the High Court
shall decide, having regard to the general convenience of the parties and the importance of the questions
involved, which of the two Courts should finally dispose of the applications for revision and when the High
Court decides that all the applications for revision should be disposed of by itself, the High Court shall
direct that the applications for revision pending before the Sessions Judge be transferred to itself and where
the High Court decides that it is not necessary for it to dispose of the applications for revision, it shall direct
that the applications for revision made to it be transferred to the Sessions Judge.
    (2) Whenever any application for revision is transferred to the High Court, that Court shall deal with
the same as if it were an application duly made before itself.
    (3) Whenever any application for revision is transferred to the Sessions Judge, that Judge shall deal
with the same as if it were an application duly made before himself.
    (4) Where an application for revision is transferred by the High Court to the Sessions Judge, no further
application for revision shall lie to the High Court or to any other Court at the instance of the person or
persons whose applications for revision have been disposed of by the Sessions Judge.

breakdown.plain_summary: This prevents split, inconsistent outcomes when co-accused from the same trial file revision applications at different levels -- some to the High Court, others to the Sessions Judge. The High Court must decide, weighing the parties' general convenience and the importance of the legal questions involved, which single Court should finally dispose of all the applications, and then direct the necessary transfers (pulling Sessions-Judge-level applications up to itself, or pushing its own applications down to the Sessions Judge) so that one forum handles the whole matter. A transferred application is simply treated as if it had been originally and duly filed before the receiving Court. And where the High Court pushes applications down to the Sessions Judge, section 438(3)'s one-application logic is reinforced: no further revision lies to the High Court or any other Court for a person whose application was disposed of by the Sessions Judge.
essential_elements: Applies when co-accused from the same trial have revision applications pending in different forums (some at the High Court, some at the Sessions Judge).
The High Court decides which single Court should dispose of all applications, considering party convenience and the importance of the questions involved.
It may transfer Sessions-Judge-level applications to itself, or transfer its own applications down to the Sessions Judge.
A transferred application is treated as if duly made before the receiving Court.
Where the High Court transfers applications down to the Sessions Judge, no further revision lies to the High Court or any other Court for persons whose applications the Sessions Judge disposed of.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a consolidation mechanism aimed at co-accused from a single trial -- it prevents the same underlying trial record from being scrutinized inconsistently by two different revisional authorities at once.

sections.title: Option of Court to hear parties
sections.raw_text:
444. Option of Court to hear parties.—Save as otherwise expressly provided by this Sanhita, no party
has any right to be heard either personally or by an advocate before any Court exercising its powers of
revision; but the Court may, if it thinks fit, when exercising such powers, hear any party either personally
or by an advocate.

breakdown.plain_summary: This clarifies that a full oral hearing is not an automatic entitlement in revision proceedings, unlike an appeal: unless this Sanhita expressly says otherwise, no party has a right to be heard, personally or through an advocate, before a Court exercising revisional powers. But the Court retains full discretion to hear any party if it thinks fit -- so hearings do happen in practice, just as a matter of the Court's choice rather than the party's entitlement.
essential_elements: Default rule: no party has a right to be heard (personally or by advocate) before a Court exercising revisional powers, unless this Sanhita expressly provides otherwise.
The Court may, at its discretion, still choose to hear any party personally or by advocate.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Section 442(2)'s prejudicial-order hearing requirement is itself one of the 'expressly provided' exceptions -- a hearing becomes mandatory there specifically because a prejudicial order is contemplated.
breakdown.how_to_read: Practitioners should not assume an automatic right to argue a revision petition orally -- while Courts commonly do grant a hearing as a matter of practice and fairness, section 444 confirms this is discretionary except where another provision (like section 442(2) for prejudicial orders) makes it mandatory.

sections.title: High Court's order to be certified to lower Court
sections.raw_text:
445. High Court's order to be certified to lower Court.—When a case is revised under this Chapter
by the High Court or a Sessions Judge, it or he shall, in the manner provided by section 429, certify its
decision or order to the Court by which the finding, sentence or order revised was recorded or passed, and
the Court to which the decision or order is so certified shall thereupon make such orders as are conformable
to the decision so certified, and, if necessary, the record shall be amended in accordance therewith.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes Chapter XXXII by extending the same certification-and-conforming-order mechanism used for appeals (section 429) to revision outcomes: whichever authority revised the case -- High Court or Sessions Judge -- must certify its decision or order, in the section 429 manner, to the Court whose finding/sentence/order was revised. That receiving Court must then make orders conforming to the certified decision, amending its record if necessary.
essential_elements: Applies whenever a case is revised under this Chapter by the High Court or a Sessions Judge.
The revising authority certifies its decision/order, in the manner provided by section 429, to the Court whose finding/sentence/order was revised.
The receiving Court must make conforming orders and amend its record if necessary.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the third instance of the same certify-and-conform pattern in this Sanhita (after section 412 for death confirmations and section 429 for appeals) -- practitioners can rely on this consistent mechanism whenever a higher authority's decision needs to actually be implemented at the level where the case originated.

sections.title: Power of Supreme Court to transfer cases and appeals
sections.raw_text:
446. Power of Supreme Court to transfer cases and appeals.—(1) Whenever it is made to appear to
the Supreme Court that an order under this section is expedient for the ends of justice, it may direct that any
particular case or appeal be transferred from one High Court to another High Court or from a Criminal
Court subordinate to one High Court to another Criminal Court of equal or superior jurisdiction subordinate
to another High Court.
    (2) The Supreme Court may act under this section only on the application of the Attorney-General of
India or of a party interested, and every such application shall be made by motion, which shall, except when
the applicant is the Attorney-General of India or the Advocate-General of the State, be supported by
affidavit or affirmation.
    (3) Where any application for the exercise of the powers conferred by this section is dismissed, the
Supreme Court may, if it is of opinion that the application was frivolous or vexatious, order the applicant
to pay by way of compensation to any person who has opposed the application such sum as it may consider
appropriate in the circumstances of the case.

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Chapter XXXIII by giving the Supreme Court the highest-level power to move a criminal case or appeal across State/High-Court boundaries -- from one High Court (or a Court subordinate to it) to another High Court (or an equal-or-superior Court subordinate to it) -- whenever expedient for the ends of justice. This power can only be triggered by the Attorney-General of India or an interested party, via a formal motion that must generally be backed by an affidavit or affirmation, except when the applicant is himself the Attorney-General of India or a State's Advocate-General (whose official position substitutes for sworn backing). A deterrent against misuse is built in: if the Supreme Court dismisses an application and finds it was frivolous or vexatious, it can order the applicant to pay compensation to whoever opposed the application.
essential_elements: The Supreme Court may transfer a case/appeal between High Courts, or between Criminal Courts subordinate to different High Courts, whenever expedient for the ends of justice.
Only the Attorney-General of India or an interested party may apply, by motion.
The motion must be supported by affidavit or affirmation, except when made by the Attorney-General of India or a State's Advocate-General.
If an application is dismissed and found frivolous or vexatious, the Supreme Court may order the applicant to pay compensation to a person who opposed it.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the highest and broadest inter-State transfer power in the Sanhita -- reserved for genuinely cross-High-Court transfer needs; a transfer within a single High Court's jurisdiction is instead handled at the High Court or Sessions Judge level under sections 447-448.

sections.title: Power of High Court to transfer cases and appeals
sections.raw_text:
447. Power of High Court to transfer cases and appeals.—(1) Whenever it is made to appear to the
High Court—
         (a) that a fair and impartial inquiry or trial cannot be had in any Criminal Court subordinate thereto;
    or
         (b) that some question of law of unusual difficulty is likely to arise; or
       (c) that an order under this section is required by any provision of this Sanhita, or will tend to the
    general convenience of the parties or witnesses, or is expedient for the ends of justice,
it may order—
        (i) that any offence be inquired into or tried by any Court not qualified under sections 197 to 205
    (both inclusive), but in other respects competent to inquire into or try such offence;
       (ii) that any particular case or appeal, or class of cases or appeals, be transferred from a Criminal
    Court subordinate to its authority to any other such Criminal Court of equal or superior jurisdiction;
         (iii) that any particular case be committed for trial to a Court of Session; or
         (iv) that any particular case or appeal be transferred to and tried before itself.
    (2) The High Court may act either on the report of the lower Court, or on the application of a party
interested, or on its own initiative:
    Provided that no application shall lie to the High Court for transferring a case from one Criminal Court
to another Criminal Court in the same sessions division, unless an application for such transfer has been
made to the Sessions Judge and rejected by him.

   (3) Every application for an order under sub-section (1) shall be made by motion, which shall, except
when the applicant is the Advocate-General of the State, be supported by affidavit or affirmation.
    (4) When such application is made by an accused person, the High Court may direct him to execute a
bond or bail bond for the payment of any compensation which the High Court may award under
sub-section (7).
     (5) Every accused person making such application shall give to the Public Prosecutor notice in writing
of the application, together with a copy of the grounds on which it is made; and no order shall be made on
the merits of the application unless at least twenty-four hours have elapsed between the giving of such
notice and the hearing of the application.
    (6) Where the application is for the transfer of a case or appeal from any subordinate Court, the High
Court may, if it is satisfied that it is necessary so to do in the interest of justice, order that, pending the
disposal of the application the proceedings in the subordinate Court shall be stayed, on such terms as the
High Court may think fit to impose:
    Provided that such stay shall not affect the subordinate Court's power of remand under section 346.
    (7) Where an application for an order under sub-section (1) is dismissed, the High Court may, if it is of
opinion that the application was frivolous or vexatious, order the applicant to pay by way of compensation
to any person who has opposed the application such sum as it may consider proper in the circumstances of
the case.
    (8) When the High Court orders under sub-section (1) that a case be transferred from any Court for trial
before itself, it shall observe in such trial the same procedure which that Court would have observed if the
case had not been so transferred.
    (9) Nothing in this section shall be deemed to affect any order of the Government under section 218.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives the High Court a wide-ranging, multi-purpose transfer power over cases within its own jurisdiction, triggered by any of three grounds: fair/impartial inquiry or trial being impossible in the subordinate Court, an unusually difficult legal question likely arising, or a transfer being required by this Sanhita, convenient for parties/witnesses, or expedient for justice generally. It can then order an otherwise-unqualified Court to try the offence, transfer a case/appeal (or a whole class of them) to an equal-or-superior subordinate Court, commit a case to a Court of Session, or pull the case up to try itself. It may act on a lower Court's report, a party's application, or its own initiative -- though a same-sessions-division transfer application must first go to (and be rejected by) the Sessions Judge before the High Court will entertain it. Applications proceed by motion (affidavit/affirmation-backed, except for the Advocate-General); an accused applicant may be required to post a compensation bond; the accused must give the Public Prosecutor 24 hours' advance notice with grounds; the High Court can stay the subordinate proceedings pending disposal (without disturbing that Court's remand power under section 346); frivolous/vexatious applications can trigger a compensation order; a case transferred up to the High Court itself is tried using the original Court's procedure; and none of this disturbs any Government transfer order under section 218.
essential_elements: Grounds: (a) fair/impartial inquiry or trial impossible in a subordinate Court; (b) an unusually difficult legal question likely to arise; (c) required by this Sanhita, convenient for parties/witnesses, or expedient for justice.

Orders available: (i) direct an otherwise-unqualified Court to try the offence; (ii) transfer a case/appeal/class of cases to an equal-or-superior subordinate Court; (iii) commit a case for trial to a Court of Session; (iv) transfer a case/appeal to and try it before itself.
The High Court may act on a lower Court's report, a party's application, or its own initiative.
A same-sessions-division transfer application must first be made to, and rejected by, the Sessions Judge before it can go to the High Court.
Applications proceed by motion, generally affidavit/affirmation-backed (except for the Advocate-General).
An accused applicant may be required to execute a compensation bond/bail bond.
The accused must give the Public Prosecutor 24 hours' written notice with grounds before a merits hearing.
The High Court may stay subordinate-Court proceedings pending disposal, without affecting that Court's section 346 remand power.
A frivolous/vexatious application, if dismissed, may trigger a compensation order against the applicant.
A case transferred to and tried before the High Court itself follows the original Court's procedure.
This section does not affect any Government transfer order under section 218.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Same-sessions-division transfers require a prior rejected application to the Sessions Judge before the High Court will entertain one.
The stay power under sub-section (6) does not override the subordinate Court's remand power under section 346.
breakdown.how_to_read: The 24-hour advance-notice requirement to the Public Prosecutor in sub-section (5) is a hard procedural floor -- an accused's transfer application cannot be decided on the merits before that window has run, so practitioners should factor this into hearing-date planning.

sections.title: Power of Sessions Judge to transfer cases and appeals
sections.raw_text:
448. Power of Sessions Judge to transfer cases and appeals.—(1) Whenever it is made to appear to
a Sessions Judge that an order under this sub-section is expedient for the ends of justice, he may order that
any particular case be transferred from one Criminal Court to another Criminal Court in his sessions
division.
    (2) The Sessions Judge may act either on the report of the lower Court, or on the application of a party
interested, or on his own initiative.
     (3) The provisions of sub-sections (3), (4), (5), (6), (7) and (9) of section 447 shall apply in relation to
an application to the Sessions Judge for an order under sub-section (1) as they apply in relation to an
application to the High Court for an order under sub-section (1) of section 447, except that sub-section (7)
of that section shall so apply as if for the word "sum" occurring therein, the words "sum not exceeding ten
thousand rupees" were substituted.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives the Sessions Judge a parallel but narrower transfer power confined to his own sessions division: whenever expedient for the ends of justice, he may transfer a case from one Criminal Court to another within that division, acting on a lower Court's report, a party's application, or his own initiative. Most of section 447's procedural machinery (motion/affidavit requirements, notice to the Public Prosecutor, stay power, frivolous-application compensation, and the Government-order savings clause) is imported wholesale, with one capped modification: a Sessions Judge's frivolous-application compensation order is limited to a sum not exceeding ten thousand rupees, unlike the High Court's uncapped discretion under section 447(7).
essential_elements: The Sessions Judge may transfer a case from one Criminal Court to another within his own sessions division, whenever expedient for the ends of justice.
He may act on a lower Court's report, a party's application, or his own initiative.
Section 447(3), (4), (5), (6), (7), and (9) apply correspondingly, with 'sum' in (7) capped at 'a sum not exceeding ten thousand rupees'.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This power is confined to transfers within the Sessions Judge's own sessions division -- cross-division or cross-High-Court transfers require the High Court (section 447) or Supreme Court (section 446).
The frivolous-application compensation ceiling is ten thousand rupees at the Sessions Judge level, uncapped at the High Court level.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the first-line, most localized transfer remedy -- practitioners seeking a same-division transfer should approach the Sessions Judge first, both because it is the natural forum and because section 447's own proviso requires a rejected Sessions Judge application before the High Court will even entertain a same-division transfer request.

sections.title: Withdrawal of cases and appeals by Sessions Judges
sections.raw_text:
449. Withdrawal of cases and appeals by Sessions Judges.—(1) A Sessions Judge may withdraw
any case or appeal from, or recall any case or appeal which he has made over to a Chief Judicial Magistrate
subordinate to him.
   (2) At any time before the trial of the case or the hearing of the appeal has commenced before the
Additional Sessions Judge, a Sessions Judge may recall any case or appeal which he has made over to any
Additional Sessions Judge.
    (3) Where a Sessions Judge withdraws or recalls case or appeal under sub-section (1) or
sub-section (2), he may either try the case in his own Court or hear the appeal himself, or make it over in
accordance with the provisions of this Sanhita to another Court for trial or hearing, as the case may be.

breakdown.plain_summary: Separate from formal inter-Court transfers, this gives the Sessions Judge internal administrative control over case allocation within his own establishment. He may at any time withdraw a case/appeal from, or recall one made over to, a Chief Judicial Magistrate subordinate to him. For an Additional Sessions Judge, the recall power is time-limited -- it can only be exercised before the trial or appeal hearing has actually commenced before that Additional Sessions Judge, respecting proceedings already underway. Once withdrawn or recalled, the Sessions Judge has full flexibility: try/hear it himself, or make it over to another Court per this Sanhita's rules.
essential_elements: The Sessions Judge may withdraw or recall a case/appeal made over to a Chief Judicial Magistrate subordinate to him, at any time.
The Sessions Judge may recall a case/appeal made over to an Additional Sessions Judge, but only before trial/hearing has commenced before that Additional Sessions Judge.
After withdrawal/recall, the Sessions Judge may try/hear the matter himself, or make it over to another Court per this Sanhita.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Recall from an Additional Sessions Judge is time-barred once trial/hearing has actually begun before him.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is purely an internal case-management tool for the Sessions Judge's own division, distinct from the formal section 447/448 transfer procedures with their notice, affidavit, and stay requirements -- no motion or hearing is required to withdraw or recall a case under this section.

sections.title: Withdrawal of cases by Judicial Magistrates
sections.raw_text:
450. Withdrawal of cases by Judicial Magistrates.—(1) Any Chief Judicial Magistrate may
withdraw any case from, or recall any case which he has made over to, any Magistrate subordinate to him,
and may inquire into or try such case himself, or refer it for inquiry or trial to any other such Magistrate
competent to inquire into or try the same.
    (2) Any Judicial Magistrate may recall any case made over by him under sub-section (2) of section 212
to any other Magistrate and may inquire into or try such cases himself.

breakdown.plain_summary: This extends the same kind of internal case-management flexibility to the Judicial Magistrate level. A Chief Judicial Magistrate may withdraw a case from, or recall a case made over to, any subordinate Magistrate, and then either handle it himself or refer it to another competent Magistrate. Separately, any Judicial Magistrate who made over a case to another Magistrate under section 212(2) may recall it and handle it himself.
essential_elements: A Chief Judicial Magistrate may withdraw or recall a case from a subordinate Magistrate, and inquire/try it himself or refer it to another competent Magistrate.
Any Judicial Magistrate may recall a case he made over under section 212(2) to another Magistrate, and inquire/try it himself.
breakdown.how_to_read: This mirrors section 449's Sessions-Judge-level mechanism one tier down -- together, sections 449-451 form a consistent internal-reallocation scheme running from the Sessions Judge through Judicial and Executive Magistrates.

sections.title: Making over or withdrawal of cases by Executive Magistrates
sections.raw_text:
451. Making over or withdrawal of cases by Executive Magistrates.—Any District Magistrate or
Sub-divisional Magistrate may—
   (a) make over, for disposal, any proceeding which has been started before him, to any Magistrate
subordinate to him;
    (b) withdraw any case from, or recall any case which he has made over to, any Magistrate subordinate
to him, and dispose of such proceeding himself or refer it for disposal to any other Magistrate.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes out the Chapter XXXIII toolkit by extending the same making-over/withdrawal/recall logic already given to Judicial Magistrates (section 450) to Executive Magistrates: a District Magistrate or Sub-divisional Magistrate may (a) make over any proceeding started before him to a subordinate Magistrate for disposal, or (b) withdraw a case from, or recall a case he had made over to, a subordinate Magistrate, and then either dispose of it himself or refer it to a different Magistrate.
essential_elements: A District Magistrate or Sub-divisional Magistrate may make over any proceeding started before him to a subordinate Magistrate for disposal.
He may also withdraw a case from, or recall a case he made over to, a subordinate Magistrate.
After withdrawal or recall, he may dispose of the proceeding himself or refer it to any other Magistrate.
breakdown.how_to_read: Sections 448-451 together form a complete internal case-reallocation toolkit spanning every tier of the Chapter XXXIII apparatus -- Sessions Judges (448, 449), Chief Judicial/Judicial Magistrates (450), and Executive Magistrates (451) -- each empowered to redistribute their own caseload among their subordinates without needing to invoke the higher transfer powers of Chapter XXXIII's earlier sections (446-448).

sections.title: Reasons to be recorded
sections.raw_text:
452. Reasons to be recorded.—A Sessions Judge or Magistrate making an order under section 448,
section 449, section 450 or section 451 shall record his reasons for making it.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the accountability backstop for the entire internal case-reallocation toolkit: any Sessions Judge or Magistrate making an order under sections 448 (Sessions Judge's transfer power), 449 (Sessions Judge's withdrawal power), 450 (Judicial Magistrates' withdrawal power), or 451 (Executive Magistrates' making-over/withdrawal power) must record his reasons for making it, ensuring these internal reallocation decisions remain transparent and reviewable rather than being made silently.
essential_elements: Applies to orders made under sections 448, 449, 450, or 451.
The Sessions Judge or Magistrate making such an order must record his reasons for making it.
breakdown.how_to_read: This closes Chapter XXXIII -- the reasons-recorded requirement means a litigant who suspects an unfair transfer, withdrawal, or make-over decision can point to the recorded reasons (or their absence) as a ground for challenge.

sections.title: Execution of order passed under section 409
sections.raw_text:
453. Execution of order passed under section 409.—When in a case submitted to the High Court for
the confirmation of a sentence of death, the Court of Session receives the order of confirmation or other
order of the High Court thereon, it shall cause such order to be carried into effect by issuing a warrant or
taking such other steps as may be necessary.

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Chapter XXXIV (Execution, Suspension, Remission and Commutation of Sentences), Part A (Death sentences), by closing the loop on the section 409 death-sentence confirmation reference procedure: once the Court of Session -- which had submitted the case to the High Court for confirmation -- receives the High Court's order of confirmation (or whatever other order the High Court makes on the reference), it must cause that order to be carried into effect, issuing a warrant or taking whatever other steps are necessary.
essential_elements: Applies where a case was submitted to the High Court for confirmation of a death sentence (section 409).
Once the Court of Session receives the High Court's confirmation order (or other order), it must carry that order into effect.
This is done by issuing a warrant or taking such other steps as may be necessary.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the death-sentence-specific instance of the certify-and-conform pattern seen throughout this Sanhita (sections 412, 429, 445) -- the Court of Session that tried the case is also the Court that must implement the High Court's final word on confirmation.

sections.title: Execution of sentence of death passed by High Court
sections.raw_text:
454. Execution of sentence of death passed by High Court.—When a sentence of death is passed by
the High Court in appeal or in revision, the Court of Session shall, on receiving the order of the High Court,
cause the sentence to be carried into effect by issuing a warrant.

breakdown.plain_summary: This covers the companion scenario to section 453: rather than a trial-court death sentence merely being confirmed, the High Court itself imposes the death sentence for the first time -- either in appeal (e.g., enhancing a lesser sentence, or overturning an acquittal into a conviction with a death sentence) or in revision. In that scenario too, the Court of Session, on receiving the High Court's order, must cause the sentence to be carried into effect by issuing a warrant.
essential_elements: Applies when the High Court itself passes a sentence of death, whether in appeal or in revision.
The Court of Session, on receiving the High Court's order, must cause the sentence to be carried into effect by issuing a warrant.
breakdown.how_to_read: Note the contrast with section 442(3)'s hard bar on a High Court converting an acquittal into a conviction via revision -- a death sentence passed by the High Court "in revision" under this section must therefore arise from revising a sentence already imposed upon a conviction (e.g., enhancing a lesser sentence to death), not from manufacturing a fresh conviction out of an acquittal.

sections.title: Postponement of execution of sentence of death in case of appeal to Supreme Court
sections.raw_text:
455. Postponement of execution of sentence of death in case of appeal to Supreme
Court.—(1) Where a person is sentenced to death by the High Court and an appeal from its judgment lies
to the Supreme Court under sub-clause (a) or sub-clause (b) of clause (1) of article 134 of the Constitution,
the High Court shall order the execution of the sentence to be postponed until the period allowed for
preferring such appeal has expired, or if, an appeal is preferred within that period, until such appeal is
disposed of.
     (2) Where a sentence of death is passed or confirmed by the High Court, and the person sentenced
makes an application to the High Court for the grant of a certificate under article 132 or under sub-clause
