(c) of clause (1) of article 134 of the Constitution, the High Court shall order the execution of the sentence
to be postponed until such application is disposed of by the High Court, or if a certificate is granted on such
application, until the period allowed for preferring an appeal to the Supreme Court on such certificate has
expired.
    (3) Where a sentence of death is passed or confirmed by the High Court, and the High Court is satisfied
that the person sentenced intends to present a petition to the Supreme Court for the grant of special leave
to appeal under article 136 of the Constitution, the High Court shall order the execution of the sentence to
be postponed for such period as it considers sufficient to enable him to present such petition.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is a life-and-death procedural safeguard: it ensures a death sentence is never carried out while a genuine avenue to the Supreme Court remains open or pending. Three scenarios are covered. First, where an appeal lies to the Supreme Court as of right under Article 134(1)(a) or (b) of the Constitution (typically because the High Court reversed an acquittal into a death sentence, or withdrew and tried the case itself imposing death), the High Court must postpone execution until the appeal period expires, or, if an appeal is filed, until it is disposed of. Second, where the person seeks a certificate of fitness to appeal under Article 132 or Article 134(1)(c), execution is postponed until that certificate application is decided, and if granted, until the further appeal period expires. Third, even without any of those formal routes, if the High Court is satisfied the condemned person intends to seek special leave to appeal under Article 136 (the Supreme Court's discretionary appellate jurisdiction), it must still postpone execution long enough for that petition to actually be filed.
essential_elements: Where an appeal lies to the Supreme Court as of right under Article 134(1)(a)/(b) of the Constitution, the High Court must postpone execution until the appeal period expires, or until a timely-filed appeal is disposed of.

Where the person applies to the High Court for a certificate under Article 132 or Article 134(1)(c), execution must be postponed until that application is disposed of, and if a certificate is granted, until the appeal period on it expires.

Where the High Court is satisfied the person intends to petition the Supreme Court for special leave to appeal under Article 136, it must postpone execution for a period sufficient to allow presentation of that petition.
breakdown.how_to_read: All three limbs are protective and cumulative in spirit -- even the third, 'softest' scenario (mere intention to seek Article 136 special leave, with no certificate and no appeal-as-of-right) still triggers a mandatory postponement, reflecting the Sanhita's insistence that the constitutional right to seek Supreme Court review of a death sentence must never be foreclosed by hasty execution.

sections.title: Commutation of sentence of death on pregnant woman
sections.raw_text:
456. Commutation of sentence of death on pregnant woman.—If a woman sentenced to death is
found to be pregnant, the High Court shall commute the sentence to imprisonment for life.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes Part A (Death sentences) of Chapter XXXIV with an absolute, mandatory humanitarian safeguard: if a woman sentenced to death is found to be pregnant, the High Court shall (not may) commute the sentence to imprisonment for life. There is no discretion here -- pregnancy triggers automatic commutation, reflecting the law's refusal to visit capital punishment upon an unborn child.
essential_elements: Applies where a woman sentenced to death is found to be pregnant.
The High Court shall commute the sentence to imprisonment for life -- this is mandatory, not discretionary.
breakdown.how_to_read: The word 'shall' here is doing real work -- unlike many discretionary 'may' powers scattered through this Chapter, this is a hard rule with no carve-out; practitioners representing a pregnant woman under sentence of death should raise this immediately and expect automatic relief rather than needing to argue for it.

sections.title: Power to appoint place of imprisonment
sections.raw_text:
457. Power to appoint place of imprisonment.—(1) Except when otherwise provided by any law for
the time being in force, the State Government may direct in what place any person liable to be imprisoned
or committed to custody under this Sanhita shall be confined.
    (2) If any person liable to be imprisoned or committed to custody under this Sanhita is in confinement
in a civil jail, the Court or Magistrate ordering the imprisonment or committal may direct that the person
be removed to a criminal jail.
    (3) When a person is removed to a criminal jail under sub-section (2), he shall, on being released
therefrom, be sent back to the civil jail, unless either—
        (a) three years have elapsed since he was removed to the criminal jail, in which case he shall be
    deemed to have been released from the civil jail under section 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
    (5 of 1908); or
        (b) the Court which ordered his imprisonment in the civil jail has certified to the officer in charge
    of the criminal jail that he is entitled to be released under section 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure,
    1908 (5 of 1908).

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Part B (Imprisonment) of Chapter XXXIV. Sub-section (1) gives the State Government the default power to designate the place of confinement for anyone liable to be imprisoned or committed to custody under this Sanhita, unless some other law already provides for it. Sub-sections (2) and (3) handle a specific cross-over scenario: someone already confined in a civil jail (typically for civil-process reasons, such as a civil-court committal) who also becomes liable to imprisonment or committal under this (criminal) Sanhita -- the Court or Magistrate may direct his removal to a criminal jail. But that removal is not permanent: on release from the criminal-jail term, he must ordinarily be sent back to the civil jail to complete whatever civil confinement he still owes, unless either three years have elapsed since the removal (in which case the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, section 58 deems him already released from the civil jail), or the civil court has certified his section 58 CPC release entitlement to the criminal jail's officer in charge.
essential_elements: Default rule: the State Government may direct the place of confinement for anyone liable to imprisonment/custody under this Sanhita, unless another law already governs it.
If such a person is already confined in a civil jail, the Court/Magistrate ordering the imprisonment/committal may direct removal to a criminal jail.
On release from the criminal jail, the person must ordinarily be sent back to the civil jail.
Exception: no return to civil jail if three years have elapsed since removal (deemed released under CPC section 58) or the civil court has certified his section 58 CPC release entitlement.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The return-to-civil-jail default is displaced by either the three-year lapse or a civil court's section 58 CPC release certification.
breakdown.how_to_read: This section is a good illustration of the Sanhita's interlock with the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 -- a person can simultaneously owe time to both a civil and a criminal confinement, and this provision ensures the criminal detention doesn't silently erase the civil one (or vice versa) without a proper statutory release trigger.

sections.title: Execution of sentence of imprisonment
sections.raw_text:
458. Execution of sentence of imprisonment.—(1) Where the accused is sentenced to imprisonment
for life or to imprisonment for a term in cases other than those provided for by section 453, the Court
passing the sentence shall forthwith forward a warrant to the jail or other place in which he is, or is to be,
confined, and, unless the accused is already confined in such jail or other place, shall forward him to such
jail or other place, with the warrant:
    Provided that where the accused is sentenced to imprisonment till the rising of the Court, it shall not be
necessary to prepare or forward a warrant to a jail, and the accused may be confined in such place as the
Court may direct.
    (2) Where the accused is not present in Court when he is sentenced to such imprisonment as is
mentioned in sub-section (1), the Court shall issue a warrant for his arrest for the purpose of forwarding
him to the jail or other place in which he is to be confined; and in such case, the sentence shall commence
on the date of his arrest.

breakdown.plain_summary: This sets out the mechanics for actually putting an imprisonment sentence into effect (for sentences other than death-sentence confirmations under section 453, which follow their own execution procedure). Where the accused is sentenced to life imprisonment or a term of imprisonment, the Court must forthwith forward a warrant to the confining jail/place, and, if the accused isn't already confined there, must forward him to that jail/place along with the warrant. A practical carve-out applies for the trivial 'imprisonment till the rising of the Court' sentence -- no warrant or jail forwarding is needed; the Court can simply direct where he's held for that short duration. Separately, if the accused isn't present in Court at the moment of sentencing, the Court must issue an arrest warrant to bring him in for confinement, and in that scenario the sentence's clock starts running only from the date of his arrest (not from the date of the in-absentia sentencing).
essential_elements: For life or term imprisonment (other than section 453 death-sentence-confirmation cases), the Court must forthwith forward a warrant to the confining jail/place and forward the accused there if not already confined.
Exception: for imprisonment till the rising of the Court, no warrant/jail forwarding is required -- the Court may direct confinement at a place of its choosing.
If the accused is not present when sentenced, the Court must issue an arrest warrant to bring him to confinement, and the sentence commences from the date of arrest.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The 'till the rising of the Court' proviso dispenses with the warrant/jail-forwarding formality entirely.
In-absentia sentencing shifts the sentence's start date from the sentencing date to the arrest date.
breakdown.how_to_read: The in-absentia commencement-on-arrest rule is important for limitation and remission calculations -- counsel should always confirm whether a client was physically present at sentencing, since that determines whether the sentence clock started on the sentencing date or only later, upon actual arrest.

sections.title: Direction of warrant for execution
sections.raw_text:
459. Direction of warrant for execution.—Every warrant for the execution of a sentence of
imprisonment shall be directed to the officer in charge of the jail or other place in which the prisoner is, or
is to be, confined.

breakdown.plain_summary: A short mechanical provision: every warrant for executing an imprisonment sentence must be directed to the officer in charge of the jail or other confining place -- ensuring the person with actual custodial authority (rather than, say, a generic police officer) is the one formally instructed to receive and hold the prisoner.
essential_elements: Every warrant executing an imprisonment sentence must be directed to the officer in charge of the jail (or other confining place) where the prisoner is or is to be confined.
breakdown.how_to_read: This works together with section 458's warrant-forwarding mechanics and section 460's lodging rule to form a tight three-step execution chain: forward the warrant (458), address it correctly (459), and lodge it with the right custodian (460).

sections.title: Warrant with whom to be lodged
sections.raw_text:
460. Warrant with whom to be lodged.—When the prisoner is to be confined in a jail, the warrant
shall be lodged with the jailor.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes Part B (Imprisonment) of Chapter XXXIV with the final mechanical step: when the prisoner is to be confined in a jail, the execution warrant must be lodged with the jailor -- the officer with direct custodial responsibility for the jail -- completing the chain from sentencing (458) through addressing (459) to actual lodgment (460).
essential_elements: Applies when the prisoner is to be confined in a jail.
The warrant must be lodged with the jailor.
breakdown.how_to_read: Part C ('Levy of fine') begins immediately after this section, shifting Chapter XXXIV's focus from imprisonment mechanics to the machinery for collecting monetary fines imposed as (or alongside) sentences.

sections.title: Warrant for levy of fine
sections.raw_text:
461. Warrant for levy of fine.—(1) When an offender has been sentenced to pay a fine, but no such
payment has been made, the Court passing the sentence may take action for the recovery of the fine in either
or both of the following ways, that is to say, it may—
        (a) issue a warrant for the levy of the amount by attachment and sale of any movable property
    belonging to the offender;
         (b) issue a warrant to the Collector of the district, authorising him to realise the amount as arrears
    of land revenue from the movable or immovable property, or both, of the defaulter:
    Provided that, if the sentence directs that in default of payment of the fine, the offender shall be imprisoned,
and if such offender has undergone the whole of such imprisonment in default, no Court shall issue such warrant
unless, for special reasons to be recorded in writing, it considers it necessary so to do, or unless it has made an
order for the payment of expenses or compensation out of the fine under section 395.

    (2) The State Government may make rules regulating the manner in which warrants under clause (a) of
sub-section (1) are to be executed, and for the summary determination of any claims made by any person
other than the offender in respect of any property attached in execution of such warrant.
    (3) Where the Court issues a warrant to the Collector under clause (b) of sub-section (1), the Collector
shall realise the amount in accordance with the law relating to recovery of arrears of land revenue, as if
such warrant were a certificate issued under such law:
    Provided that no such warrant shall be executed by the arrest or detention in prison of the offender.

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Part C (Levy of fine) of Chapter XXXIV, giving a Court two alternative (or combinable) coercive routes to actually collect an unpaid fine, beyond simply letting the offender serve out a default-imprisonment term. First, the Court may issue a warrant for attachment and sale of the offender's movable property. Second, it may issue a warrant to the district Collector authorising recovery as arrears of land revenue from the offender's movable or immovable property -- leveraging the revenue department's own established recovery machinery. A protective proviso applies where default imprisonment was already fully served: the Court cannot then issue a fine-recovery warrant unless it records special reasons, or has already ordered expenses/compensation payable out of the fine under section 395 -- preventing double jeopardy-like stacking of full default imprisonment plus property seizure without justification. The State Government may make rules on how attachment warrants are executed and how third-party property claims are summarily decided. And critically, when the Collector-route warrant is used, recovery follows ordinary land-revenue-recovery law, but can never involve arresting or imprisoning the offender -- that coercive tool is reserved exclusively for the attachment/sale route or the original default-sentence itself.
essential_elements: Applies when a fine sentence remains unpaid.
The Court may issue a warrant for attachment and sale of the offender's movable property.
Alternatively (or additionally), the Court may issue a warrant to the district Collector to realise the amount as arrears of land revenue from movable or immovable property.
If default imprisonment for non-payment has already been fully served, a fresh recovery warrant needs either recorded special reasons or a pre-existing section 395 expenses/compensation order.
The State Government may make rules on executing attachment warrants and summarily deciding third-party property claims.
A Collector-route warrant is executed per land-revenue-recovery law but can never involve arrest or imprisonment of the offender.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The special-reasons/section-395-order requirement applies only where default imprisonment for the fine has already been fully undergone.
The Collector-route recovery warrant absolutely excludes arrest or detention of the offender, regardless of what ordinary land-revenue-recovery law might otherwise permit against other defaulters.
breakdown.how_to_read: The two recovery routes (attachment/sale vs. Collector/land-revenue) are not mutually exclusive -- 'either or both' in sub-section (1) -- so a Court can pursue both simultaneously against different classes of the offender's property for maximum recovery efficiency.

sections.title: Effect of such warrant
sections.raw_text:
462. Effect of such warrant.—A warrant issued under clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 461 by
any Court may be executed within the local jurisdiction of such Court, and it shall authorise the attachment
and sale of any such property outside such jurisdiction, when it is endorsed by the District Magistrate within
whose local jurisdiction such property is found.

breakdown.plain_summary: This solves the territorial-reach problem for an attachment-and-sale warrant issued under section 461(1)(a): such a warrant is directly executable only within the issuing Court's own local jurisdiction. But the offender's property may sit elsewhere. The fix is an endorsement mechanism -- if the District Magistrate of the district where the property is actually located endorses the warrant, it becomes executable there too, extending the warrant's reach without requiring a fresh warrant from a different Court.
essential_elements: A section 461(1)(a) attachment-and-sale warrant is directly executable within the issuing Court's own local jurisdiction.
For property located outside that jurisdiction, the warrant becomes executable there once endorsed by the District Magistrate of the district where the property is found.
breakdown.how_to_read: This endorsement mechanism mirrors similar cross-jurisdictional endorsement patterns used elsewhere in this Sanhita (e.g., for warrants of arrest) -- always check whether a warrant has the necessary District Magistrate endorsement before treating it as enforceable against out-of-jurisdiction property.

sections.title: Warrant for levy of fine issued by a Court in any territory to which this Sanhita does not extend
sections.raw_text:
463. Warrant for levy of fine issued by a Court in any territory to which this Sanhita does not
extend.—Notwithstanding anything in this Sanhita or in any other law for the time being in force, when an
offender has been sentenced to pay a fine by a Criminal Court in any territory to which this Sanhita does
not extend and the Court passing the sentence issues a warrant to the Collector of a district in the territories
to which this Sanhita extends, authorising him to realise the amount as if it were an arrear of land revenue,
such warrant shall be deemed to be a warrant issued under clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 461 by a
Court in the territories to which this Sanhita extends, and the provisions of sub-section (3) of the said section
as to the execution of such warrant shall apply accordingly.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is a cross-territory recognition provision, overriding anything else in this Sanhita or any other law (a non-obstante opening). Where a Criminal Court sits in territory where this Sanhita doesn't apply, but sentences an offender to a fine, and that Court sends a Collector-route recovery warrant into territory where this Sanhita does apply, the receiving territory must treat that warrant exactly as if it were a domestic section 461(1)(b) warrant -- with section 461(3)'s execution rules (including the no-arrest/no-imprisonment safeguard) applying in full.
essential_elements: Applies to a fine-recovery warrant issued by a Criminal Court in territory where this Sanhita does not extend.
Where such a warrant is sent to a Collector of a district where this Sanhita does extend, it is deemed a section 461(1)(b) warrant issued by a domestic Court.
Section 461(3)'s execution provisions (including the no-arrest/no-imprisonment bar) apply to it accordingly.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a narrow but practically important cross-border enforcement bridge -- without it, a fine sentence from a non-extending territory's Court would have no mechanism for enforcement against property located within Sanhita territory.

sections.title: Suspension of execution of sentence of imprisonment
sections.raw_text:
464. Suspension of execution of sentence of imprisonment.—(1) When an offender has been
sentenced to fine only and to imprisonment in default of payment of the fine, and the fine is not paid
forthwith, the Court may—
        (a) order that the fine shall be payable either in full on or before a date not more than thirty days
    from the date of the order, or in two or three installments, of which the first shall be payable on or
    before a date not more than thirty days from the date of the order and the other or others at an interval
    or at intervals, as the case may be, of not more than thirty days;
         (b) suspend the execution of the sentence of imprisonment and release the offender, on the
    execution by the offender of a bond or bail bond, as the Court thinks fit, conditioned for his appearance
    before the Court on the date or dates on or before which payment of the fine or the installments thereof,
    as the case may be, is to be made; and if the amount of the fine or of any installment, as the case may
    be, is not realised on or before the latest date on which it is payable under the order, the Court may
    direct the sentence of imprisonment to be carried into execution at once.
    (2) The provisions of sub-section (1) shall be applicable also in any case in which an order for the
payment of money has been made on non-recovery of which imprisonment may be awarded and the money
is not paid forthwith; and, if the person against whom the order has been made, on being required to enter
into a bond such as is referred to in that sub-section, fails to do so, the Court may at once pass sentence of
imprisonment.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives an offender sentenced to a fine (with default imprisonment) breathing room to pay in installments rather than going straight to jail: the Court may set a payment schedule -- full payment within thirty days, or two-to-three installments each spaced up to thirty days apart -- and suspend the default-imprisonment sentence, releasing the offender on a bond/bail bond conditioned on appearing to make each payment. Miss a payment deadline, and the Court may immediately execute the suspended imprisonment sentence. The same installment-and-suspension mechanism extends to any other Sanhita order requiring payment of money on pain of imprisonment for non-payment (e.g., maintenance-type orders) -- and if the person refuses to even execute the required bond, the Court may skip straight to passing the imprisonment sentence.
essential_elements: Applies to an offender sentenced to fine only, with imprisonment in default of payment, where the fine isn't paid forthwith.
The Court may set a payment schedule (full payment within 30 days, or 2-3 installments spaced up to 30 days apart) and suspend default imprisonment, releasing the offender on a bond/bail bond.
Missing a payment deadline lets the Court immediately execute the suspended imprisonment sentence.
The same mechanism applies to any other money-payment order under this Sanhita backed by a default-imprisonment threat.
Refusal to execute the required bond lets the Court pass the imprisonment sentence at once.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a debtor-friendly procedural safety valve -- counsel for a fine-sentenced client unable to pay immediately should proactively request an installment order under this section rather than letting default imprisonment simply take effect.

sections.title: Who may issue warrant
sections.raw_text:
465. Who may issue warrant.—Every warrant for the execution of a sentence may be issued either by
the Judge or Magistrate who passed the sentence, or by his successor-in-office.

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Part D (General provisions regarding execution) of Chapter XXXIV with a simple continuity rule: a sentence-execution warrant may be issued not only by the Judge or Magistrate who originally passed the sentence, but equally by whoever has succeeded him in that office -- ensuring a transfer, retirement, or reassignment of the original judicial officer doesn't stall execution of a valid sentence.
essential_elements: A sentence-execution warrant may be issued by the Judge/Magistrate who passed the sentence.
It may equally be issued by that officer's successor-in-office.
breakdown.how_to_read: This continuity-of-office principle recurs throughout this Sanhita wherever a procedural act is tied to a specific judicial officer rather than the Court as an institution -- it prevents administrative churn from becoming a loophole that stalls enforcement.

sections.title: Sentence on escaped convict when to take effect
sections.raw_text:
466. Sentence on escaped convict when to take effect.—(1) When a sentence of death, imprisonment
for life or fine is passed under this Sanhita on an escaped convict, such sentence shall, subject to the
provisions hereinbefore contained, take effect immediately.
   (2) When a sentence of imprisonment for a term is passed under this Sanhita on an escaped
convict, —

        (a) if such sentence is severer in kind than the sentence which such convict was undergoing when
    he escaped, the new sentence shall take effect immediately;
        (b) if such sentence is not severer in kind than the sentence which such convict was undergoing
    when he escaped, the new sentence shall take effect after he has suffered imprisonment for a further
    period equal to that which, at the time of his escape, remained unexpired of his former sentence.
    (3) For the purposes of sub-section (2), a sentence of rigorous imprisonment shall be deemed to be
severer in kind than a sentence of simple imprisonment.

breakdown.plain_summary: This addresses the timing question for a fresh sentence imposed on someone who escaped from custody while serving an earlier sentence. If the new sentence is death, life imprisonment, or a fine, it takes effect immediately -- no stacking question arises. But for a new term-of-years imprisonment sentence, timing depends on a severity comparison with the sentence he was serving when he escaped: if the new sentence is severer in kind (e.g., rigorous vs. the simple imprisonment he was escaping from), it takes effect immediately, running alongside/replacing the old one in effect. If it's not severer, the new sentence only starts after he has first served out whatever period remained unexpired of his original sentence at the moment of escape -- ensuring the escape doesn't let him simply substitute a fresh, no-worse sentence for the time he still owed.
essential_elements: A death, life-imprisonment, or fine sentence passed on an escaped convict takes effect immediately.
A term-of-years imprisonment sentence that is severer in kind than the sentence being served at escape takes effect immediately.
A term-of-years sentence that is not severer in kind takes effect only after the convict serves the remaining unexpired period of his former sentence.
Rigorous imprisonment is deemed severer in kind than simple imprisonment for this comparison.
breakdown.how_to_read: This section works together with section 467 (sentence on offender already sentenced for another offence) and section 469 (the saving clause) to form a complete scheme preventing an escape, or a fresh conviction during an existing sentence, from ever operating to reduce the total time a person actually owes to the State.

sections.title: Sentence on offender already sentenced for another offence
sections.raw_text:
467. Sentence on offender already sentenced for another offence.—(1) When a person already
undergoing a sentence of imprisonment is sentenced on a subsequent conviction to imprisonment or
imprisonment for life, such imprisonment or imprisonment for life shall commence at the expiration of the
imprisonment to which he has been previously sentenced, unless the Court directs that the subsequent
sentence shall run concurrently with such previous sentence:
    Provided that where a person who has been sentenced to imprisonment by an order under section 141
in default of furnishing security is, whilst undergoing such sentence, sentenced to imprisonment for an
offence committed prior to the making of such order, the latter sentence shall commence immediately.
   (2) When a person already undergoing a sentence of imprisonment for life is sentenced on a subsequent
conviction to imprisonment for a term or imprisonment for life, the subsequent sentence shall run
concurrently with such previous sentence.

breakdown.plain_summary: This sets the default rule for stacking multiple imprisonment sentences on the same person. Ordinarily (sub-section (1)), if someone already serving an imprisonment sentence is sentenced again (imprisonment or life imprisonment) on a later, separate conviction, the new sentence begins only after the earlier one ends -- consecutive, not concurrent -- unless the Court expressly orders the sentences to run concurrently. A carve-out applies for a person imprisoned under section 141 merely for failing to furnish security (a preventive, non-punitive detention): if he's then sentenced for an actual offence committed before that section 141 order, the offence-based sentence starts immediately rather than waiting out the security-default detention. Sub-section (2) flips the default for the specific case where the person is already serving life imprisonment: any subsequent sentence (term or further life imprisonment) must run concurrently with it -- because a term sentence can't meaningfully be served 'after' a life sentence.
essential_elements: Default: a subsequent imprisonment/life-imprisonment sentence on someone already serving imprisonment starts only after the earlier sentence ends (consecutive), unless the Court directs concurrent running.
Exception: if the earlier sentence was mere section 141 default-of-security detention, a later sentence for an offence committed before that order starts immediately.
Special rule: if the person is already serving life imprisonment, any subsequent sentence must run concurrently with it.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The consecutive-by-default rule can be displaced by an express Court direction for concurrent running.
The section 141 default-detention carve-out and the already-serving-life-imprisonment rule are both exceptions that override the general consecutive default.
breakdown.how_to_read: Practitioners seeking concurrent sentencing for a client facing multiple convictions must make an affirmative request and secure an express Court direction -- concurrency is not the default outcome except in the life-imprisonment scenario of sub-section (2).

sections.title: Period of detention undergone by accused to be set off against sentence of imprisonment
sections.raw_text:
468. Period of detention undergone by accused to be set off against sentence of imprisonment.—
Where an accused person has, on conviction, been sentenced to imprisonment for a term, not being
imprisonment in default of payment of fine, the period of detention, if any, undergone by him during the
investigation, inquiry or trial of the same case and before the date of such conviction, shall be set off against
the term of imprisonment imposed on him on such conviction, and the liability of such person to undergo
imprisonment on such conviction shall be restricted to the remainder, if any, of the term of imprisonment
imposed on him:
    Provided that in cases referred to in section 475, such period of detention shall be set off against the
period of fourteen years referred to in that section.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the mandatory pre-trial-detention set-off rule: where a convicted person is sentenced to a term of imprisonment (excluding default-of-fine imprisonment), any time he already spent in detention during the investigation, inquiry, or trial of that same case -- before conviction -- must be credited against (set off) the sentence term, so he only has to actually serve the remainder, if any. For the specific section 475 scenario (life imprisonment imposed for a death-eligible offense, or a death sentence commuted to life imprisonment), the same set-off applies against the fourteen-year minimum-actual-service period fixed by that section, rather than against the notional 'life' term itself.
essential_elements: Applies to a term-of-imprisonment sentence on conviction, excluding default-of-fine imprisonment.
Pre-conviction detention during investigation, inquiry, or trial of the same case is set off against the sentence term.
The person's remaining imprisonment liability is restricted to whatever term (if any) remains after the set-off.
For section 475 cases, the set-off applies against that section's fourteen-year minimum-service period instead.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Default-of-fine imprisonment is expressly excluded from this set-off entitlement.
breakdown.how_to_read: This set-off is not discretionary -- 'shall be set off' -- so counsel should always compute and flag the client's pre-conviction custody period at sentencing to ensure the Court's sentence correctly reflects time already served.

sections.title: Saving
sections.raw_text:
469. Saving.—(1) Nothing in section 466 or section 467 shall be held to excuse any person from any
part of the punishment to which he is liable upon his former or subsequent conviction.
    (2) When an award of imprisonment in default of payment of a fine is annexed to a substantive sentence
of imprisonment and the person undergoing the sentence is after its execution to undergo a further
substantive sentence or further substantive sentences of imprisonment, effect shall not be given to the award
of imprisonment in default of payment of the fine until the person has undergone the further sentence or
sentences.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is a protective clarification ensuring sections 466 and 467's sequencing/concurrency rules are never misread as excusing any part of a person's total punishment liability -- they govern only timing and stacking order, not whether punishment is owed at all. Sub-section (2) then sequences a specific interaction: where default-of-fine imprisonment is attached to a substantive imprisonment sentence, and the person still has further substantive imprisonment sentences to serve after that one, the default-of-fine imprisonment is held back until all the further substantive sentences are completed -- so fine-default time doesn't get inserted ahead of other substantive sentences still owed.
essential_elements: Sections 466 and 467 never excuse any part of a person's punishment liability -- they only govern sequencing/timing.

Where default-of-fine imprisonment is annexed to a substantive sentence, and further substantive imprisonment sentences remain to be served after it, the default-of-fine imprisonment is deferred until those further substantive sentences are completed.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a savings/anti-erosion clause -- always read it alongside sections 466 and 467 to confirm that a favorable sequencing outcome under those sections isn't being mistaken for an actual reduction in total punishment owed.

sections.title: Return of warrant on execution of sentence
sections.raw_text:
470. Return of warrant on execution of sentence.—When a sentence has been fully executed, the
officer executing it shall return the warrant to the Court from which it is issued, with an endorsement under
his hand certifying the manner in which the sentence has been executed.

breakdown.plain_summary: A closing accountability step in the execution chain: once a sentence has been fully carried out, the executing officer must return the warrant to the issuing Court, with a signed endorsement certifying exactly how the sentence was executed -- creating a formal record that closes the loop and confirms compliance.
essential_elements: Once a sentence has been fully executed, the executing officer must return the warrant to the issuing Court.
The return must include a signed endorsement certifying the manner in which the sentence was executed.
breakdown.how_to_read: This return-and-certify step is the final link in the chain that began with sections 458-459 (forwarding and directing the warrant) and 465 (who may issue it) -- together they form a complete, auditable execution lifecycle from sentencing to confirmed completion.

sections.title: Money ordered to be paid recoverable as a fine
sections.raw_text:
471. Money ordered to be paid recoverable as a fine.—Any money (other than a fine) payable by
virtue of any order made under this Sanhita, and the method of recovery of which is not otherwise expressly
provided for, shall be recoverable as if it were a fine:
    Provided that section 461 shall, in its application to an order under section 400, by virtue of this section,
be construed as if in the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 461, after the words and figures "under section
395", the words and figures "or an order for payment of costs under section 400" had been inserted.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes Part D (General provisions regarding execution) with a default recovery mechanism: any money payable under a Sanhita order (other than a fine itself) that has no other express recovery method specified is simply treated and recovered as if it were a fine, plugging into the entire section 461-464 fine-recovery machinery (attachment/sale, Collector-route land-revenue recovery, installment suspension). A specific drafting fix is included for section 400 costs orders -- section 461's proviso (which normally references only section 395 expenses/compensation orders as an exception to the default-imprisonment-already-served bar) is deemed amended to also reference section 400 costs orders, ensuring costs orders get the same treatment.
essential_elements: Any money payable under a Sanhita order, other than a fine, with no other express recovery method, is recoverable as if it were a fine.
This plugs such orders into the full section 461-464 fine-recovery machinery.
A specific proviso extends section 461's section 395 cross-reference to also cover section 400 costs orders.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a catch-all default-recovery provision -- whenever a Sanhita order requires payment of money and you can't find a bespoke recovery mechanism elsewhere in the Sanhita, section 471 supplies one by routing it through the fine-recovery machinery.

sections.title: Mercy petition in death sentence cases
sections.raw_text:
472. Mercy petition in death sentence cases.—(1) A convict under the sentence of death or his legal
heir or any other relative may, if he has not already submitted a petition for mercy, file a mercy petition
before the President of India under article 72 or the Governor of the State under article 161 of the
Constitution within a period of thirty days from the date on which the Superintendent of the jail, —
       (i) informs him about the dismissal of the appeal, review or special leave to appeal by the Supreme
    Court; or
        (ii) informs him about the date of confirmation of the sentence of death by the High Court and the
    time allowed to file an appeal or special leave in the Supreme Court has expired.
    (2) The petition under sub-section (1) may, initially be made to the Governor and on its rejection or
disposal by the Governor, the petition shall be made to the President within a period of sixty days from the
date of rejection or disposal of such petition.
    (3) The Superintendent of the jail or officer in charge of the jail shall ensure, that every convict, in case
there are more than one convict in a case, also files the mercy petition within a period of sixty days and on
non-receipt of such petition from the other convicts, Superintendent of the jail shall send the names,
addresses, copy of the record of the case and all other details of the case to the Central Government or the
State Government for consideration along with the said mercy petition.
    (4) The Central Government shall, on receipt of the mercy petition seek the comments of the State
Government and consider the petition along with the records of the case and make recommendations to the
President in this behalf, as expeditiously as possible, within a period of sixty days from the date of receipt
of comments of the State Government and records from Superintendent of the Jail.
    (5) The President may, consider, decide and dispose of the mercy petition and, in case there are more
than one convict in a case, the petitions shall be decided by the President together in the interests of justice.
    (6) Upon receipt of the order of the President on the mercy petition, the Central Government shall
within forty-eight hours, communicate the same to the Home Department of the State Government and the
Superintendent of the jail or officer in charge of the jail.
    (7) No appeal shall lie in any Court against the order of the President or of the Governor made
under article 72 or article 161 of the Constitution and it shall be final, and any question as to the arriving of
the decision by the President or the Governor shall not be inquired into in any Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Part E (Suspension, remission and commutation of sentences) with a detailed, timeline-driven procedure for the executive clemency route in death sentence cases -- the last resort after judicial remedies are exhausted. A death-sentenced convict (or his legal heir/relative) gets thirty days from being informed of either the Supreme Court's dismissal of his appeal/review/special leave, or the expiry of his time to approach the Supreme Court after High Court confirmation, to file a mercy petition. The petition goes first to the Governor; if rejected or disposed of, the convict has sixty days to escalate to the President. Where multiple convicts share a case, the jail Superintendent must ensure all of them file, and must proactively forward case details to the Government for any convict who doesn't. The Central Government must gather State Government comments and make recommendations to the President within sixty days of receiving those comments and records. The President decides -- and for multiple convicts in the same case, must decide all their petitions together, in the interests of justice (avoiding inconsistent clemency outcomes for co-convicts). Once decided, the Central Government must notify the State's Home Department and the jail Superintendent within forty-eight hours. And critically, sub-section (7) makes the President's or Governor's clemency decision completely final and unappealable -- no Court may even inquire into how the decision was reached.
essential_elements: A death-row convict (or his legal heir/relative) may file a mercy petition within 30 days of being informed of judicial-remedy exhaustion (Supreme Court dismissal, or expiry of the appeal window after High Court confirmation).
The petition goes first to the Governor; upon rejection/disposal, the convict has 60 days to escalate to the President.
The jail Superintendent must ensure all co-convicts in a multi-convict case file mercy petitions, forwarding case details to the Government for any who don't, within 60 days.
The Central Government must seek State Government comments and make recommendations to the President within 60 days of receiving those comments and records.
The President decides the petition(s); multiple convicts in the same case must have their petitions decided together.
The Central Government must communicate the President's order to the State Home Department and jail Superintendent within 48 hours.
The President's or Governor's order is final, unappealable, and immune even from judicial inquiry into how the decision was reached.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Sub-section (7)'s finality bar is absolute -- it excludes both appeal and any inquiry into the decision-making process, not just review on the merits.
breakdown.how_to_read: The strict, cascading timelines here (30 days to file, 60 days Governor-to-President escalation, 60 days for Central Government recommendations, 48 hours for post-decision communication) are the practical heart of this section -- missing any deadline can have irreversible consequences in a death-sentence case, so counsel must track each trigger date precisely.

sections.title: Power to suspend or remit sentences
sections.raw_text:
473. Power to suspend or remit sentences.—(1) When any person has been sentenced to punishment
for an offence, the appropriate Government may, at any time, without conditions or upon any conditions
which the person sentenced accepts, suspend the execution of his sentence or remit the whole or any part
of the punishment to which he has been sentenced.
    (2) Whenever an application is made to the appropriate Government for the suspension or remission of
a sentence, the appropriate Government may require the presiding Judge of the Court before or by which
the conviction was had or confirmed, to state his opinion as to whether the application should be granted or
refused, together with his reasons for such opinion and also to forward with the statement of such opinion
a certified copy of the record of the trial or of such record thereof as exists.
    (3) If any condition on which a sentence has been suspended or remitted is, in the opinion of the
appropriate Government, not fulfilled, the appropriate Government may cancel the suspension or remission,
and thereupon the person in whose favour the sentence has been suspended or remitted may, if at large, be
arrested by any police officer, without warrant and remanded to undergo the unexpired portion of the
sentence.
    (4) The condition on which a sentence is suspended or remitted under this section may be one to be
fulfilled by the person in whose favour the sentence is suspended or remitted, or one independent of his
will.
    (5) The appropriate Government may, by general rules or special orders, give directions as to the
suspension of sentences and the conditions on which petitions should be presented and dealt with:
    Provided that in the case of any sentence (other than a sentence of fine) passed on a person above the
age of eighteen years, no such petition by the person sentenced or by any other person on his behalf shall
be entertained, unless the person sentenced is in jail, and—
         (a) where such petition is made by the person sentenced, it is presented through the officer in charge
    of the jail; or
        (b) where such petition is made by any other person, it contains a declaration that the person
    sentenced is in jail.
    (6) The provisions of the above sub-sections shall also apply to any order passed by a Criminal Court
under any section of this Sanhita or of any other law, which restricts the liberty of any person or imposes
any liability upon him or his property.
    (7) In this section and in section 474, the expression "appropriate Government" means,—
        (a) in cases where the sentence is for an offence against, or the order referred to in sub-section (6)
    is passed under, any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the Union extends, the
    Central Government;
        (b) in other cases, the Government of the State within which the offender is sentenced or the said
    order is passed.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the general executive clemency power (distinct from the death-sentence-specific mercy petition of section 472), letting the appropriate Government suspend execution of, or remit whole or part of, any sentence -- with or without conditions the sentenced person accepts. Before deciding, the Government may seek the trial/confirming Judge's opinion and reasons, along with the trial record. If an accepted condition is later breached, the Government may cancel the suspension/remission, and the person may be arrested without warrant by any police officer and remanded to serve out the unexpired sentence -- conditions can bind the person's own conduct, or be entirely independent of his will (e.g., a change in law or circumstance). The Government may set general rules for how suspension petitions are handled, but a protective proviso requires that (for non-fine sentences on adults) such petitions only be entertained if the sentenced person is actually in jail, and channeled either through the jail officer-in-charge (if filed by the sentenced person) or with a declaration of jail-custody (if filed by someone else) -- preventing petitions from persons who are, say, absconding or out on bail from clogging this clemency channel. The same framework extends to any liberty-restricting or liability-imposing order under this Sanhita or any other law, not just formal sentences. And sub-section (7) defines 'appropriate Government' for both this section and section 474: Central Government for Union-executive-power matters, State Government otherwise.
essential_elements: The appropriate Government may, at any time, suspend execution of a sentence or remit it wholly/partly, with or without conditions the sentenced person accepts.
The Government may seek the presiding/confirming Judge's opinion and the trial record before deciding.
Breach of a suspension/remission condition lets the Government cancel it; the person may then be arrested without warrant and remanded to serve the unexpired sentence.
Conditions may bind the sentenced person's own conduct or be independent of his will.

The Government may make general rules on suspension petitions; for non-fine adult sentences, petitions are entertained only if the person is in jail, via the jail officer-in-charge or with a declaration of custody.
The same framework applies to any liberty-restricting or property-liability-imposing order under this Sanhita or other law.
'Appropriate Government' means the Central Government for Union-executive-power matters, and the State Government otherwise.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The jail-custody filing requirement doesn't apply to fine sentences or to persons below eighteen years of age.
breakdown.how_to_read: This general suspension/remission power under section 473 operates alongside, not instead of, the death-sentence-specific mercy petition machinery of section 472 -- the two exist for overlapping but distinct scenarios (all sentences generally, versus death sentences specifically via Presidential/Gubernatorial constitutional power).

sections.title: Power to commute sentence

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives the appropriate Government a structured ladder of commutation options -- substituting a lesser kind of punishment for a harsher one already imposed -- and, notably, this power can be exercised without the sentenced person's consent (unlike the conditions-based suspension/remission scheme of section 473, where the person must accept any conditions). Five specific commutation moves are authorized: death down to life imprisonment; life imprisonment down to a term of at least seven years; a term of seven-plus years down to a term of at least three years; a term of less than seven years down to a fine; and rigorous imprisonment down to simple imprisonment for whatever term the person could have received.
essential_elements: The appropriate Government may commute a sentence without the sentenced person's consent.
Death may be commuted to imprisonment for life.
Imprisonment for life may be commuted to a term of not less than seven years.
A term of seven years or more may be commuted to a term of not less than three years.
A term of less than seven years may be commuted to a fine.
Rigorous imprisonment may be commuted to simple imprisonment for any term the person might have received.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This commutation power expressly does not require the sentenced person's consent -- a sharp contrast to section 473's suspension/remission conditions, which the person must accept.
breakdown.how_to_read: Note the minimum floors built into each commutation step (not less than seven years for life imprisonment, not less than three years for a seven-plus-year term) -- commutation is not a blank cheque to reduce a sentence to any lesser amount; it must land within the specific bands this section fixes.

sections.title: Restriction on powers of remission or commutation in certain cases
sections.raw_text:
475. Restriction on powers of remission or commutation in certain cases.—Notwithstanding
anything contained in section 473, where a sentence of imprisonment for life is imposed on conviction of a
person for an offence for which death is one of the punishments provided by law, or where a sentence of
death imposed on a person has been commuted under section 474 into one of imprisonment for life, such
person shall not be released from prison unless he had served at least fourteen years of imprisonment.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is a hard floor overriding section 473's general remission power (non-obstante opening) for two specific categories of life-imprisonment cases: (1) where life imprisonment was imposed for an offence for which death was also an available punishment, or (2) where a death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment under section 474. In either scenario, the person cannot be released from prison until he has actually served at least fourteen years -- no remission, however generous, can bring actual release below that fourteen-year floor. This is the section referenced by section 468's proviso, which directs pre-conviction detention to be set off against this fourteen-year period rather than against a notional 'life' term.
essential_elements: Applies where life imprisonment is imposed for a death-eligible offence, or where a death sentence is commuted to life imprisonment under section 474.
In either case, the person cannot be released from prison until he has served at least fourteen years of imprisonment.
This overrides section 473's general remission power to that extent.
breakdown.how_to_read: This fourteen-year floor is a frequently litigated benchmark in Indian sentencing practice -- always check whether a life sentence falls into one of these two triggering categories before assuming ordinary remission policies can shorten actual custody below fourteen years.

sections.title: Concurrent power of Central Government in case of death sentences
sections.raw_text:
476. Concurrent power of Central Government in case of death sentences.—The powers conferred
by sections 473 and 474 upon the State Government may, in the case of sentences of death, also be exercised
by the Central Government.

breakdown.plain_summary: A short but important jurisdictional extension: the suspension/remission power (section 473) and the commutation power (section 474), which the definitions in section 473(7) generally assign to the 'appropriate Government' (Central or State depending on the matter), are both made concurrently exercisable by the Central Government specifically in death-sentence cases -- regardless of which government would otherwise be the 'appropriate' one. This gives the Union an additional, non-exclusive layer of clemency authority over the gravest class of sentence.
essential_elements: The powers under sections 473 (suspend/remit) and 474 (commute) that belong to the State Government may, for death sentences specifically, also be exercised by the Central Government.
This is a concurrent power -- it supplements rather than displaces the State Government's own authority.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read alongside section 477, which imposes the reverse constraint -- requiring the State Government to secure the Central Government's concurrence before acting in certain other categories of cases -- together these two sections calibrate the Union-State balance of clemency power under this Chapter.

sections.title: State Government to act after concurrence with Central Government in certain cases
sections.raw_text:
477. State Government to act after concurrence with Central Government in certain cases.—(1)
The powers conferred by sections 473 and 474 upon the State Government to remit or commute a sentence,
in any case where the sentence is for an offence—
        (a) which was investigated by any agency empowered to make investigation into an offence under
    any Central Act other than this Sanhita; or
        (b) which involved the misappropriation or destruction of, or damage to, any property belonging to
    the Central Government; or
        (c) which was committed by a person in the service of the Central Government while acting or
    purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty,
shall not be exercised by the State Government except after concurrence with the Central Government.
    (2) No order of suspension, remission or commutation of sentences passed by the State Government in
relation to a person, who has been convicted of offences, some of which relate to matters to which the
executive power of the Union extends, and who has been sentenced to separate terms of imprisonment
which are to run concurrently, shall have effect unless an order for the suspension, remission or
commutation, as the case may be, of such sentences has also been made by the Central Government in
relation to the offences committed by such person with regard to matters to which the executive power of
the Union extends.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes Chapter XXXIV Part E by fencing off three categories of cases where the State Government's ordinary section 473/474 power is not free-standing but requires the Central Government's concurrence first: (a) offences investigated by a Central-Act investigating agency other than this Sanhita (e.g., a CBI-type body), (b) offences involving misappropriation, destruction of, or damage to Central Government property, and (c) offences committed by a Central Government servant acting or purporting to act in official duty. Sub-section (2) handles a related concurrent-sentences scenario: where a person convicted of multiple offences -- some touching matters within the Union's executive power -- is serving concurrently-running separate terms, a State Government suspension/remission/commutation order has no effect at all unless the Central Government has made a matching order for the Union-related offences. In effect, the State cannot unilaterally free (or reduce the sentence of) someone whose concurrent sentence includes a Union-matter component, without the Centre's matching action.
essential_elements: For offences in categories (a) investigated by a non-Sanhita Central-Act agency, (b) involving Central Government property, or (c) committed by a Central Government servant in official duty, the State Government's section 473/474 powers require prior Central Government concurrence.

Where a person is serving concurrently-running separate sentences, some relating to Union-executive-power matters, a State Government suspension/remission/commutation order takes effect only if the Central Government has made a matching order for the Union-related offences.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Sub-section (1)'s three categories are cumulative constraints on the State Government's power, not a complete list of Central Government involvement -- section 476 separately gives the Central Government its own concurrent power in death-sentence cases.
breakdown.how_to_read: Practitioners seeking executive clemency in a case touching Central Government property, a Central investigating agency, or a Central Government employee's official conduct should anticipate a two-government approval process, not a single State-level application -- and where concurrent sentences straddle Union and State matters, relief on the Union-linked offence must be separately secured from the Centre for any State-level order to actually take effect.

sections.title: In what cases bail to be taken
sections.raw_text:
478. In what cases bail to be taken.—(1) When any person other than a person accused of a non-
bailable offence is arrested or detained without warrant by an officer in charge of a police station, or appears
or is brought before a Court, and is prepared at any time while in the custody of such officer or at any stage
of the proceeding before such Court to give bail, such person shall be released on bail:
    Provided that such officer or Court, if he or it thinks fit, may, and shall, if such person is indigent and
is unable to furnish surety, instead of taking bail bond from such person, discharge him on his executing a
bond for his appearance as hereinafter provided.
    Explanation.—Where a person is unable to give bail bond within a week of the date of his arrest, it
shall be a sufficient ground for the officer or the Court to presume that he is an indigent person for the
purposes of this proviso:
    Provided further that nothing in this section shall be deemed to affect the provisions of sub-section (3)
of section 135 or section 492.
    (2) Notwithstanding anything in sub-section (1), where a person has failed to comply with the
conditions of the bond or bail bond as regards the time and place of attendance, the Court may refuse to
release him on bail, when on a subsequent occasion in the same case he appears before the Court or is
brought in custody and any such refusal shall be without prejudice to the powers of the Court to call upon
any person bound by such bond or bail bond to pay the penalty thereof under section 491.

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Chapter XXXV (Provisions as to Bail and Bonds) with the baseline rule for bailable offences: anyone other than a person accused of a non-bailable offence, if arrested/detained without warrant or brought before a Court, and prepared to give bail, shall be released on bail -- this is mandatory, not discretionary, for bailable offences. A protective proviso addresses indigency: an indigent person unable to furnish surety must be discharged on a personal bond instead of a surety-backed bail bond, so poverty alone cannot keep a bailable-offence accused in custody. The Explanation makes this practical by creating a presumption of indigency if the person cannot arrange a bail bond within a week of arrest -- officers and Courts don't need a formal indigency inquiry; the passage of a week without bail being furnished is itself sufficient. A further proviso preserves sections 135(3) and 492 untouched. Sub-section (2) is a conduct-based exception: if the person previously breached bond/bail-bond conditions on timing or place of attendance, the Court may refuse bail on a later appearance in the same case -- though this refusal doesn't affect the Court's separate power under section 491 to enforce the bond penalty against whoever was bound by it.
essential_elements: For any person other than one accused of a non-bailable offence, arrested/detained without warrant or brought before a Court, and prepared to give bail: release on bail is mandatory.
An indigent person unable to furnish surety must instead be discharged on a personal bond for appearance.
Inability to furnish a bail bond within a week of arrest creates a presumption of indigency for this purpose.
Sections 135(3) and 492 remain unaffected by this section.

Exception: if the person previously breached bond/bail-bond attendance conditions, the Court may refuse bail on a subsequent appearance in the same case, without prejudice to the section 491 bond-penalty enforcement power.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The indigency proviso and its week-long presumption soften the mandatory bail rule into a practical, surety-free release mechanism for those who cannot afford one.
The sub-section (2) conduct exception displaces the otherwise-mandatory bail entitlement where the person has a track record of non-compliance with attendance conditions in the same case.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the default bailable-offence rule -- contrast with section 480's far more conditional non-bailable-offence framework; always first check whether the offence is bailable, since that single classification determines which of these two very different regimes applies.

sections.title: Maximum period for which under trial prisoner can be detained
sections.raw_text:
479. Maximum period for which under trial prisoner can be detained.—(1) Where a person has,
during the period of investigation, inquiry or trial under this Sanhita of an offence under any law (not being
an offence for which the punishment of death or life imprisonment has been specified as one of the
punishments under that law) undergone detention for a period extending up to one-half of the maximum
period of imprisonment specified for that offence under that law, he shall be released by the Court on bail:
    Provided that where such person is a first-time offender (who has never been convicted of any offence
in the past) he shall be released on bond by the Court, if he has undergone detention for the period extending
up to one-third of the maximum period of imprisonment specified for such offence under that law:
    Provided further that the Court may, after hearing the Public Prosecutor and for reasons to be recorded
by it in writing, order the continued detention of such person for a period longer than one-half of the said
period or release him on bail bond instead of his bond:
    Provided also that no such person shall in any case be detained during the period of investigation,
inquiry or trial for more than the maximum period of imprisonment provided for the said offence under that
law.
    Explanation.—In computing the period of detention under this section for granting bail, the period of
detention passed due to delay in proceeding caused by the accused shall be excluded.
    (2) Notwithstanding anything in sub-section (1), and subject to the third proviso thereof, where an
investigation, inquiry or trial in more than one offence or in multiple cases are pending against a person, he
shall not be released on bail by the Court.
    (3) The Superintendent of jail, where the accused person is detained, on completion of one-half or one-
third of the period mentioned in sub-section (1), as the case may be, shall forthwith make an application in
writing to the Court to proceed under sub-section (1) for the release of such person on bail.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the significant default-bail-on-prolonged-detention safeguard for under trial prisoners, excluding offences carrying death or life imprisonment as one of their possible punishments. If pre-conviction detention during investigation, inquiry, or trial reaches one-half of the offence's maximum imprisonment period, the Court shall release the person on bail -- mandatory once that threshold is crossed. A more generous first proviso favors first-time offenders (never previously convicted of any offence): they must be released on bond once detention reaches just one-third of the maximum period. A second proviso lets the Court push past the one-half threshold, but only after hearing the Public Prosecutor and recording written reasons, and even then it may substitute a bail bond for a personal bond rather than outright continued detention. A third, absolute proviso caps detention at the offence's full maximum imprisonment period no matter what -- this ceiling cannot be extended by any Court order. An Explanation ensures fairness in computing the detention period: delay caused by the accused himself (e.g., seeking adjournments) is excluded from the count, so an accused can't manufacture entitlement to release by deliberately stalling. Sub-section (2) carves out multi-offence/multi-case defendants from this whole release scheme (subject to the absolute third-proviso cap still applying). Sub-section (3) places an affirmative duty on the jail Superintendent: on completion of the relevant one-half or one-third period, he must proactively apply in writing to the Court for the prisoner's release -- the safeguard isn't meant to depend on the accused or his counsel remembering to apply.
essential_elements: Excludes offences for which death or life imprisonment is one of the specified punishments.
Default: detention reaching one-half of the offence's maximum imprisonment period triggers mandatory release on bail.
First-time offenders: detention reaching one-third of the maximum period triggers mandatory release on bond.
The Court may extend detention beyond one-half (after hearing the Public Prosecutor and recording reasons), or release on bail bond instead of personal bond.
Absolute cap: detention can never exceed the offence's maximum imprisonment period.
Delay caused by the accused is excluded when computing the detention period.
Persons facing investigation/inquiry/trial for more than one offence or in multiple cases are excluded from this release scheme, subject to the absolute cap still applying.
The jail Superintendent must proactively apply in writing to the Court for release once the relevant threshold period is completed.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Death/life-imprisonment-eligible offences fall entirely outside this section's release mechanism.
The second proviso's extension power is conditioned on hearing the Public Prosecutor and recording written reasons -- it is not an unconditional discretion.
The third proviso's absolute cap cannot be overridden even by a reasoned Court order under the second proviso.
Sub-section (2) removes the release entitlement entirely for persons facing multiple pending offences/cases, though still subject to the absolute cap.
breakdown.how_to_read: This provision operationalizes the constitutional concern against indefinite pre-trial detention -- practitioners representing long-detained undertrial clients should track the detention clock precisely (excluding accused-caused delay) and be ready to invoke the Superintendent's independent section 479(3) duty to apply for release if defence counsel's own application has not yet been filed.

sections.title: When bail may be taken in case of non-bailable offence
sections.raw_text:
480. When bail may be taken in case of non-bailable offence.—(1) When any person accused of, or
suspected of, the commission of any non-bailable offence is arrested or detained without warrant by an
officer in charge of a police station or appears or is brought before a Court other than the High Court or
Court of Session, he may be released on bail, but—
       (i) such person shall not be so released if there appear reasonable grounds for believing that he has
    been guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life;
        (ii) such person shall not be so released if such offence is a cognizable offence and he had been
    previously convicted of an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment for
    seven years or more, or he had been previously convicted on two or more occasions of a cognizable
    offence punishable with imprisonment for three years or more but less than seven years:
    Provided that the Court may direct that a person referred to in clause (i) or clause (ii) be released on
bail if such person is a child or is a woman or is sick or infirm:
    Provided further that the Court may also direct that a person referred to in clause (ii) be released on bail
if it is satisfied that it is just and proper so to do for any other special reason:
    Provided also that the mere fact that an accused person may be required for being identified by
witnesses during investigation or for police custody beyond the first fifteen days shall not be sufficient
ground for refusing to grant bail if he is otherwise entitled to be released on bail and gives an undertaking
that he shall comply with such directions as may be given by the Court:
    Provided also that no person shall, if the offence alleged to have been committed by him is punishable
with death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for seven years or more, be released on bail by the Court
under this sub-section without giving an opportunity of hearing to the Public Prosecutor.
    (2) If it appears to such officer or Court at any stage of the investigation, inquiry or trial, as the case
may be, that there are not reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed a non-bailable
offence, but that there are sufficient grounds for further inquiry into his guilt, the accused shall, subject to
the provisions of section 492 and pending such inquiry, be released on bail, or, at the discretion of such
officer or Court, on the execution by him of a bond for his appearance as hereinafter provided.
    (3) When a person accused or suspected of the commission of an offence punishable with imprisonment
which may extend to seven years or more or of an offence under Chapter VI, Chapter VII or Chapter XVII
of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 or abetment of, or conspiracy or attempt to commit, any such offence,
is released on bail under sub-section (1), the Court shall impose the conditions,--
       (a) that such person shall attend in accordance with the conditions of the bond executed under this
    Chapter;
        (b) that such person shall not commit an offence similar to the offence of which he is accused, or
    suspected, of the commission of which he is suspected; and
        (c) that such person shall not directly or indirectly make any inducement, threat or promise to any
    person acquainted with the facts of the case so as to dissuade him from disclosing such facts to the
    Court or to any police officer or tamper with the evidence,
and may also impose, in the interests of justice, such other conditions as it considers necessary.
    (4) An officer or a Court releasing any person on bail under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2), shall
record in writing his or its reasons or special reasons for so doing.
    (5) Any Court which has released a person on bail under sub-section (1) or sub-section (2), may, if it
considers it necessary so to do, direct that such person be arrested and commit him to custody.
    (6) If, in any case triable by a Magistrate, the trial of a person accused of any non-bailable offence is
not concluded within a period of sixty days from the first date fixed for taking evidence in the case, such
person shall, if he is in custody during the whole of the said period, be released on bail to the satisfaction
of the Magistrate, unless for reasons to be recorded in writing, the Magistrate otherwise directs.
    (7) If, at any time, after the conclusion of the trial of a person accused of a non-bailable offence and
before judgment is delivered, the Court is of opinion that there are reasonable grounds for believing that
the accused is not guilty of any such offence, it shall release the accused, if he is in custody, on the execution
by him of a bond for his appearance to hear judgment delivered.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the detailed, conditional non-bailable-offence bail framework -- the counterpart to section 478's largely mandatory bailable-offence rule. Sub-section (1) starts from discretionary 'may' release before a Court other than the High Court or Court of Session, but immediately carves out two categories where release is barred outright: (i) reasonable grounds of guilt for a death/life-imprisonment-punishable offence, and (ii) a cognizable offence where the accused has serious prior convictions (death/life/7+-years, or two-plus prior 3-to-7-year cognizable convictions). Four provisos soften this bar: courts may still release category (i)/(ii) persons who are children, women, sick, or infirm; may release category (ii) persons for other special reasons if just and proper; mere need for witness identification or extended police custody beyond fifteen days isn't itself sufficient to refuse bail (if otherwise entitled, with an undertaking to comply with Court directions); and for the most serious offences (death/life/7+-years) bail cannot be granted without first hearing the Public Prosecutor. Sub-section (2) covers the flip scenario -- insufficient grounds to believe the accused guilty of the non-bailable offence but grounds for further inquiry -- triggering release on bail or bond (subject to section 492) pending that inquiry. Sub-section (3) makes bail conditions mandatory (not merely permissible) for serious offences (7+-year imprisonment, or BNS Chapters VI/VII/XVII offences, or their abetment/conspiracy/attempt): attendance per the bond, no similar offence, and no witness inducement/threat/tampering, plus any other conditions the Court considers necessary in the interests of justice. Sub-section (4) requires written reasons for every release decision. Sub-section (5) lets the Court later re-arrest and re-commit a person it released, if it considers this necessary. Sub-section (6) is a speedy-trial safeguard for Magistrate-triable cases: if trial isn't concluded within sixty days from the first evidence-taking date, an in-custody accused must be released on bail unless the Magistrate records reasons otherwise. Sub-section (7) provides a pre-judgment release where the Court, after trial concludes but before delivering judgment, believes there are reasonable grounds the accused is not guilty -- the accused is released on bond pending the judgment itself.
essential_elements: Sub-section (1): before a Court other than High Court/Court of Session, bail is discretionary for non-bailable offences, subject to bars for (i) reasonable grounds of a death/life-imprisonment offence and (ii) cognizable offences with specified serious prior convictions.

Four provisos soften the bars: release for children/women/sick/infirm persons; release for special reasons in category (ii); witness-identification/extended-custody needs alone don't justify refusal; mandatory Public Prosecutor hearing before bail in death/life/7+-year cases.
Sub-section (2): insufficient grounds of guilt but grounds for further inquiry triggers release on bail or bond pending inquiry, subject to section 492.

Sub-section (3): mandatory bail conditions (attendance, no similar offence, no witness tampering/inducement) for 7+-year offences and BNS Chapters VI/VII/XVII offences (and their abetment/conspiracy/attempt), plus any other conditions in the interests of justice.
Sub-section (4): written reasons required for every release under sub-sections (1) or (2).
Sub-section (5): the Court may later direct arrest and recommitment to custody of a person it had released.
