Sub-section (6): Magistrate-triable case not concluded within sixty days of the first evidence date triggers mandatory bail for an in-custody accused, absent recorded reasons otherwise.
Sub-section (7): reasonable grounds of not-guilty after trial conclusion but before judgment triggers release on bond pending judgment.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The category (i)/(ii) bars in sub-section (1) are themselves subject to four provisos permitting release in defined circumstances.
Sub-section (2)'s release-pending-inquiry route is expressly made subject to section 492.
Sub-section (6)'s sixty-day mandatory-bail rule can be displaced by the Magistrate recording reasons for continued detention.
breakdown.how_to_read: This section's seven sub-sections operate as a layered decision tree -- practitioners should work through it in sequence: first classify the offence's severity and the accused's prior record to locate which bar (if any) applies, then check whether a proviso reopens the door, before turning to the separate procedural safeguards in sub-sections (3) through (7) that apply once bail is actually granted or a trial drags on.

sections.title: Bail to require accused to appear before next Appellate Court
sections.raw_text:
481. Bail to require accused to appear before next Appellate Court.—(1) Before conclusion of the
trial and before disposal of the appeal, the Court trying the offence or the Appellate Court, as the case may
be, shall require the accused to execute a bond or bail bond, to appear before the higher Court as and when
such Court issues notice in respect of any appeal or petition filed against the judgment of the respective
Court and such bond shall be in force for six months.
    (2) If such accused fails to appear, the bond stand forfeited and the procedure under section 491 shall
apply.

breakdown.plain_summary: This ensures bail doesn't simply evaporate when a case moves to a higher forum. Before the trial concludes, and again before an appeal is disposed of, the trying Court or the Appellate Court must require the accused to execute a bond or bail bond binding him to appear before the next higher Court whenever it issues notice on an appeal or petition against the judgment -- and this bond stays in force for six months. If the accused then fails to appear as required, the bond is forfeited and the standard forfeiture procedure under section 491 (show-cause, penalty recovery, potential civil-jail imprisonment for a defaulting surety) kicks in.
essential_elements: Before conclusion of trial and before disposal of an appeal, the Court must require the accused to execute a bond/bail bond to appear before the higher Court on notice of any appeal/petition.
The bond remains in force for six months.
Failure to appear as required forfeits the bond, triggering the section 491 forfeiture procedure.
breakdown.how_to_read: This section bridges the trial-level and appellate-level bail regimes -- practitioners should track the six-month validity window and ensure a fresh bond is executed if appellate proceedings outlast it, to avoid an unintended lapse in the accused's bail status.

sections.title: Direction for grant of bail to person apprehending arrest
sections.raw_text:
482. Direction for grant of bail to person apprehending arrest.—(1) When any person has reason
to believe that he may be arrested on an accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence, he may
apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction under this section; and that Court may, if it
thinks fit, direct that in the event of such arrest, he shall be released on bail.
    (2) When the High Court or the Court of Session makes a direction under sub-section (1), it may include
such conditions in such directions in the light of the facts of the particular case, as it may think fit,
including—
        (i) a condition that the person shall make himself available for interrogation by a police officer as
    and when required;
        (ii) a condition that the person shall not, directly or indirectly, make any inducement, threat or
    promise to any person acquainted with the facts of the case so as to dissuade him from disclosing such
    facts to the Court or to any police officer;
        (iii) a condition that the person shall not leave India without the previous permission of the Court;
        (iv) such other condition as may be imposed under sub-section (3) of section 480, as if the bail were
    granted under that section.
    (3) If such person is thereafter arrested without warrant by an officer in charge of a police station on
such accusation, and is prepared either at the time of arrest or at any time while in the custody of such
officer to give bail, he shall be released on bail; and if a Magistrate taking cognizance of such offence
decides that a warrant should be issued in the first instance against that person, he shall issue a bailable
warrant in conformity with the direction of the Court under sub-section (1).
    (4) Nothing in this section shall apply to any case involving the arrest of any person on accusation of
having committed an offence under section 65 and sub-section (2) of section 70 of the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the anticipatory bail provision -- a person who reasonably believes he may be arrested on a non-bailable offence accusation can apply to the High Court or Court of Session for a direction that, should the arrest happen, he be released on bail. The Court has discretion ('may, if it thinks fit') whether to grant this protective direction at all. If granted, the Court can attach conditions tailored to the case, including a menu of four suggested types: availability for police interrogation, no inducement/threat/tampering with witnesses, no leaving India without Court permission, and any other condition otherwise available under section 480(3) as if bail had been granted there. Sub-section (3) operationalizes the direction: if the person is later arrested without warrant on that accusation and is prepared to give bail, he must be released on bail; and if a Magistrate taking cognizance instead decides a warrant should issue in the first instance, that warrant must be a bailable warrant consistent with the Court's earlier direction -- so the anticipatory protection survives even a formal warrant route. Sub-section (4) is a hard carve-out: this entire anticipatory-bail mechanism does not apply to accusations under section 65 or section 70(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (aggravated sexual offences against children and gang rape of a woman under eighteen) -- no anticipatory bail is available for these offences.
essential_elements: A person reasonably apprehending arrest on a non-bailable offence accusation may apply to the High Court or Court of Session for an anticipatory-bail direction.
The Court has discretion whether to grant the direction, and may attach conditions (interrogation availability, no witness tampering, no leaving India, or other section 480(3)-type conditions).
If later arrested without warrant and prepared to give bail, the person shall be released on bail.
If a Magistrate instead issues a warrant in the first instance, it must be a bailable warrant consistent with the Court's direction.
This section does not apply at all to accusations under BNS section 65 or section 70(2).
exceptions_and_qualifications: Grant of the direction is discretionary, not automatic, even where the applicant reasonably apprehends arrest.
The absolute carve-out for BNS section 65/70(2) accusations means anticipatory bail is categorically unavailable for those offences, regardless of the case's individual facts.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the anticipatory bail mechanism -- practitioners should note it is available only from the High Court or Court of Session (never a Magistrate), and must flag the absolute section 65/70(2) bar at the outset, since no argument on individual facts can overcome that categorical exclusion.

sections.title: Special powers of High Court or Court of Session regarding bail
sections.raw_text:
483. Special powers of High Court or Court of Session regarding bail.—(1) A High Court or Court
of Session may direct,—
        (a) that any person accused of an offence and in custody be released on bail, and if the offence is of the
    nature specified in sub-section (3) of section 480, may impose any condition which it considers necessary
    for the purposes mentioned in that sub-section;
        (b) that any condition imposed by a Magistrate when releasing any person on bail be set aside or
    modified:
    Provided that the High Court or the Court of Session shall, before granting bail to a person who is
accused of an offence which is triable exclusively by the Court of Session or which, though not so triable,
is punishable with imprisonment for life, give notice of the application for bail to the Public Prosecutor
unless it is, for reasons to be recorded in writing, of opinion that it is not practicable to give such notice:
    Provided further that the High Court or the Court of Session shall, before granting bail to a person who
is accused of an offence triable under section 65 or sub-section (2) of section 70 of the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023, give notice of the application for bail to the Public Prosecutor within a period of fifteen days
from the date of receipt of the notice of such application.
    (2) The presence of the informant or any person authorised by him shall be obligatory at the time of
hearing of the application for bail to the person under section 65 or sub-section (2) of section 70 of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
    (3) A High Court or Court of Session may direct that any person who has been released on bail under
this Chapter be arrested and commit him to custody.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives the High Court and Court of Session a broader, supervisory bail power beyond what a Magistrate can do: they may release any accused-and-in-custody person on bail (imposing section 480(3)-type conditions where relevant), or set aside/modify conditions a Magistrate has already imposed. Two provisos add procedural safeguards for serious-offence bail applications: first, before granting bail in a Court-of-Session-exclusive or life-imprisonment-punishable offence, the Public Prosecutor must be given notice of the application, unless the Court records in writing that notice isn't practicable; second, for BNS section 65/70(2) offences specifically, notice to the Public Prosecutor is mandatory within fifteen days of the bail application's receipt -- no 'not practicable' escape valve here. Sub-section (2) makes the informant's (or his authorised representative's) presence obligatory at the bail hearing itself for these same section 65/70(2) cases, giving the victim's side a guaranteed voice at that hearing. Sub-section (3) confirms these Courts retain a standing power to later re-arrest and re-commit to custody anyone released on bail under this Chapter, if circumstances warrant.
essential_elements: High Court/Court of Session may release any accused-and-in-custody person on bail, with section 480(3)-type conditions where applicable, or set aside/modify a Magistrate's bail conditions.
For Court-of-Session-exclusive or life-imprisonment-punishable offences, Public Prosecutor notice is required before granting bail, unless the Court records reasons that notice is impracticable.
For BNS section 65/70(2) offences, Public Prosecutor notice is mandatory within fifteen days of the application's receipt -- no impracticability exception.
The informant's (or authorised representative's) presence is obligatory at bail hearings for BNS section 65/70(2) offences.
The High Court/Court of Session may direct arrest and recommitment to custody of any person previously released on bail under this Chapter.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The first proviso's Public-Prosecutor-notice requirement can be waived by the Court recording written reasons of impracticability -- but this escape valve is unavailable for the second proviso's BNS section 65/70(2) category.
breakdown.how_to_read: The layered notice requirements here -- general 'unless impracticable' versus absolute for the most serious sexual offences against children/minors -- reflect a deliberate legislative tightening for that specific category; practitioners on either side of a section 65/70(2) bail application should build the fifteen-day notice and informant-presence requirements into their hearing timeline from the outset.

sections.title: Amount of bond and reduction thereof
sections.raw_text:
484. Amount of bond and reduction thereof.—(1) The amount of every bond executed under this
Chapter shall be fixed with due regard to the circumstances of the case and shall not be excessive.
    (2) The High Court or the Court of Session may direct that the bail required by a police officer or
Magistrate be reduced.

breakdown.plain_summary: A short but consequential fairness safeguard: whenever a bond is executed under this Chapter, its monetary amount must be fixed with due regard to the case's actual circumstances and must not be excessive -- bail conditions cannot be set punitively high simply to keep someone in custody in substance while nominally offering bail. Sub-section (2) gives the High Court or Court of Session an express oversight power to reduce a bail amount that a police officer or Magistrate has fixed, providing a direct avenue of relief where a lower authority's bond amount is unreasonably steep.
essential_elements: Every bond's amount must be fixed with due regard to the case's circumstances and must not be excessive.
The High Court or Court of Session may direct reduction of a bail amount fixed by a police officer or Magistrate.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the go-to provision when a bail amount, though nominally granted, is set so high as to be effectively a denial of bail -- counsel should move the High Court or Court of Session under sub-section (2) rather than treating an excessive bond amount as unchallengeable simply because bail was 'granted' in name.

sections.title: Bond of accused and sureties
sections.raw_text:
485. Bond of accused and sureties.—(1) Before any person is released on bond or bail bond, a bond
for such sum of money as the police officer or Court, as the case may be, thinks sufficient shall be executed
by such person, and, when he is released on bond or bail bond, by one or more sufficient sureties conditioned
that such person shall attend at the time and place mentioned in the bond, and shall continue so to attend
until otherwise directed by the police officer or Court, as the case may be.
    (2) Where any condition is imposed for the release of any person on bail, the bond or bail bond shall
also contain that condition.
    (3) If the case so requires, the bond or bail bond shall also bind the person released on bail to appear
when called upon at the High Court, Court of Session or other Court to answer the charge.
    (4) For the purpose of determining whether the sureties are fit or sufficient, the Court may accept
affidavits in proof of the facts contained therein relating to the sufficiency or fitness of the sureties, or, if it
considers necessary, may either hold an enquiry itself or cause an inquiry to be made by a Magistrate
subordinate to the Court, as to such sufficiency or fitness.

breakdown.plain_summary: This sets out the mechanics of the bond/bail-bond instrument itself. Before release, the person must execute a bond in a sum the police officer or Court considers sufficient, and, where sureties are involved, one or more sufficient sureties must also execute it -- all conditioned on the person attending at the specified time and place, continuing to do so until otherwise directed. Any condition attached to the bail grant (e.g., under section 480(3) or 482(2)) must itself be written into the bond or bail bond, not left as a separate informal understanding. Where the case requires it, the bond can also bind the person to appear before the High Court, Court of Session, or other Court to answer the charge -- covering appearance obligations beyond the immediate releasing authority. Sub-section (4) addresses how surety fitness/sufficiency is verified: the Court may rely on affidavits, or, if it considers necessary, hold its own enquiry or have a subordinate Magistrate conduct one.
essential_elements: Before release, the person must execute a bond for a sum the police officer/Court considers sufficient.
Sufficient sureties (one or more) must also execute the bond where release is on bond/bail bond with sureties, conditioned on the person's continued attendance.
Any condition imposed for bail must be written into the bond or bail bond itself.
Where required, the bond can also bind the person to appear before the High Court, Court of Session, or other Court to answer the charge.
Surety fitness/sufficiency may be verified via affidavits, or by a Court enquiry (directly or through a subordinate Magistrate).
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the drafting-mechanics section for every bond executed in this Chapter -- counsel preparing a bail bond should ensure every condition actually granted by the Court is expressly recorded in the bond document itself, since sub-section (2) makes this a requirement, not a formality.

sections.title: Declaration by sureties
sections.raw_text:
486. Declaration by sureties.—Every person standing surety to an accused person for his release on
bail, shall make a declaration before the Court as to the number of persons to whom he has stood surety
including the accused, giving therein all the relevant particulars.

breakdown.plain_summary: A transparency safeguard against a single surety over-committing himself across multiple accused persons without the Court's knowledge: every person standing surety for an accused's bail release must declare before the Court how many persons (including this accused) he has stood surety for, along with all relevant particulars. This lets the Court properly assess whether the surety genuinely has the financial capacity to answer for everyone he has undertaken to guarantee.
essential_elements: Every surety standing bail for an accused must declare before the Court the total number of persons he has stood surety for, including the present accused.
The declaration must include all relevant particulars.
breakdown.how_to_read: This works with section 485(4)'s fitness/sufficiency enquiry -- a surety's declaration under this section gives the Court the raw information it needs to assess whether that surety is genuinely fit and sufficient once his other outstanding surety commitments are factored in.

sections.title: Discharge from custody
sections.raw_text:
487. Discharge from custody.—(1) As soon as the bond or bail bond has been executed, the person
for whose appearance it has been executed shall be released; and, when he is in jail, the court admitting him
to bail shall issue an order of release to the officer in charge of the jail, and such officer on receipt of the
orders shall release him.
    (2) Nothing in this section, section 478 or section 480, shall be deemed to require the release of any
person liable to be detained for some matter other than that in respect of which the bond or bail bond was
executed.

breakdown.plain_summary: This ensures bail execution translates promptly into actual release: as soon as the bond or bail bond is executed, the person for whose appearance it was given must be released, and if he's in jail, the Court admitting him to bail must issue a release order to the jail's officer in charge, who must release him on receiving it -- no further delay or additional formality is contemplated. Sub-section (2) is an important limiting clarification: this release duty, and the similar ones in sections 478 and 480, only cover the specific matter for which the bond was executed -- if the person is also liable to be detained for some other, separate matter (e.g., a different pending case or a different order of detention), this section does not require his release from that other detention.
essential_elements: Once a bond/bail bond is executed, the person must be released; if in jail, the admitting Court issues a release order to the officer in charge, who must release him on receipt.
This release duty does not extend to detention for any other matter beyond the one for which the bond was executed.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The multiple-matter carve-out in sub-section (2) prevents a bail order in one case from being read as securing release from an entirely separate, unrelated detention.
breakdown.how_to_read: Practitioners should always check whether their client has any other outstanding detention basis before assuming a bail order in one case will result in actual physical release -- sub-section (2) makes clear it will not, if a separate liability to detention exists.

sections.title: Power to order sufficient bail when that first taken is insufficient
sections.raw_text:
488. Power to order sufficient bail when that first taken is insufficient.—If, through mistake,
fraud or otherwise, insufficient sureties have been accepted, or if they afterwards become insufficient, the
Court may issue a warrant of arrest directing that the person released on bail be brought before it and may
order him to find sufficient sureties, and, on his failing so to do, may commit him to jail.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives the Court a corrective mechanism where the sureties backing someone's bail turn out to be, or later become, insufficient -- whether due to mistake, fraud, or any other reason. The Court may issue a warrant of arrest to bring the released person back before it, and then order him to find sufficient sureties. If he fails to do so, the Court may commit him to jail -- effectively reversing the earlier bail release because the security underpinning it has failed.
essential_elements: Applies where sureties accepted for bail are, or later become, insufficient -- whether through mistake, fraud, or otherwise.
The Court may issue a warrant of arrest to bring the person back before it.
The Court may order him to find sufficient sureties.
Failure to find sufficient sureties allows the Court to commit him to jail.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the mechanism to invoke when a surety's fraud or later-discovered insufficiency comes to light after bail has already been granted -- it is not a general power to revisit a bail decision on the merits, only to fix a defect in the security backing it.

sections.title: Discharge of sureties
sections.raw_text:
489. Discharge of sureties.—(1) All or any sureties for the attendance and appearance of a person
released on bail may at any time apply to a Magistrate to discharge the bond, either wholly or so far as
relates to the applicants.
    (2) On such application being made, the Magistrate shall issue his warrant of arrest directing that the
person so released be brought before him.
    (3) On the appearance of such person pursuant to the warrant, or on his voluntary surrender, the
Magistrate shall direct the bond to be discharged either wholly or so far as relates to the applicants, and
shall call upon such person to find other sufficient sureties, and, if he fails to do so, may commit him to jail.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives sureties themselves an exit route from an ongoing bail obligation: all or any of the sureties for a released person's attendance may apply to a Magistrate at any time to be discharged from the bond, wholly or just as it relates to the applicant sureties. Once such an application is made, the Magistrate must issue a warrant of arrest to bring the released person before him -- the surety's application to be let go triggers the accused's compelled re-appearance, since the surety was the mechanism ensuring he'd show up. On the person's appearance (whether pursuant to that warrant or by voluntarily surrendering himself), the Magistrate discharges the bond as requested and then calls on the person to find other sufficient sureties; if he fails to do so, the Magistrate may commit him to jail.
essential_elements: Any or all sureties for a released person's bail may apply to a Magistrate at any time to be discharged from the bond, wholly or partially.
Such an application triggers a warrant of arrest to bring the released person before the Magistrate.
On appearance (via warrant or voluntary surrender), the Magistrate discharges the bond as applied for and calls on the person to find fresh sufficient sureties.
Failure to find fresh sureties allows the Magistrate to commit the person to jail.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the counterpart to section 488 -- there the Court acts on its own initiative when sureties prove insufficient; here the sureties themselves initiate their own release from the ongoing obligation, but the practical consequence for the accused (re-appearance, need for fresh sureties, possible jail on failure) is functionally similar.

sections.title: Deposit instead of recognizance
sections.raw_text:
490. Deposit instead of recognizance.—When any person is required by any Court or officer to
execute a bond or bail bond, such Court or officer may, except in the case of a bond for good behaviour,
permit him to deposit a sum of money or Government promissory notes to such amount as the Court or
officer may fix in lieu of executing such bond.

breakdown.plain_summary: This offers an alternative to the surety-based bond mechanism: instead of executing a bond (which typically requires finding sureties), a person required to execute a bond or bail bond may, at the Court's or officer's discretion, simply deposit a sum of money or Government promissory notes of an amount the Court/officer fixes. This can be a simpler, faster route for someone who can afford the cash deposit but struggles to arrange acceptable sureties. The one express exclusion is a bond for good behaviour -- that specific category of bond cannot be satisfied by a cash/promissory-note deposit in lieu of the bond itself, presumably because good-behaviour bonds are about ongoing conduct assurance rather than a purely financial guarantee.
essential_elements: A person required to execute a bond or bail bond may be permitted to deposit money or Government promissory notes instead, in an amount the Court/officer fixes.
Exception: this deposit-in-lieu option does not apply to a bond for good behaviour.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The good-behaviour-bond exclusion is an express carve-out from an otherwise general deposit-in-lieu option.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a practical relief provision -- counsel for a client who can access liquid funds but not sureties should specifically request this deposit option, while noting it is unavailable if the underlying bond is specifically one for good behaviour.

sections.title: Procedure when bond has been forfeited
sections.raw_text:
491. Procedure when bond has been forfeited.—(1) Where, —
        (a) a bond under this Sanhita is for appearance, or for production of property, before a Court and it
    is proved to the satisfaction of that Court, or of any Court to which the case has subsequently been
    transferred, that the bond has been forfeited; or
        (b) in respect of any other bond under this Sanhita, it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court by
    which the bond was taken, or of any Court to which the case has subsequently been transferred, or of
    the Court of any Magistrate of the first class, that the bond has been forfeited,
the Court shall record the grounds of such proof, and may call upon any person bound by such bond to pay
the penalty thereof or to show cause why it should not be paid.
    Explanation.—A condition in a bond for appearance, or for production of property, before a Court shall
be construed as including a condition for appearance, or as the case may be, for production of property,
before any Court to which the case may subsequently be transferred.
   (2) If sufficient cause is not shown and the penalty is not paid, the Court may proceed to recover the
same as if such penalty were a fine imposed by it under this Sanhita:
    Provided that where such penalty is not paid and cannot be recovered in the manner aforesaid, the
person so bound as surety shall be liable, by order of the Court ordering the recovery of the penalty, to
imprisonment in civil jail for a term which may extend to six months.
    (3) The Court may, after recording its reasons for doing so, remit any portion of the penalty mentioned
and enforce payment in part only.
    (4) Where a surety to a bond dies before the bond is forfeited, his estate shall be discharged from all
liability in respect of the bond.
    (5) Where any person who has furnished security under section 125 or section 136 or section 401 is
convicted of an offence the commission of which constitutes a breach of the conditions of his bond, or of a
bond executed in lieu of his bond under section 494, a certified copy of the judgment of the Court by which
he was convicted of such offence may be used as evidence in proceedings under this section against his
surety or sureties, and, if such certified copy is so used, the Court shall presume that such offence was
committed by him unless the contrary is proved.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the master procedure for enforcing a broken bond, whether it was for appearance/production of property before a Court or any other kind of bond under the Sanhita. Once forfeiture is proved to the satisfaction of the competent Court (including a transferee Court, or, for non-appearance bonds, a Magistrate of the first class), the Court records its grounds and calls on the person bound to pay the penalty or show cause against paying it. If no sufficient cause is shown and payment isn't made, the Court recovers the penalty as if it were a fine -- and where recovery isn't possible that way, a defaulting surety faces imprisonment in civil jail for up to six months (sub-section (2)). The Court retains discretion to remit part of the penalty for recorded reasons (sub-section (3)). A surety's death before forfeiture discharges his estate entirely (sub-section (4)) -- liability doesn't survive him. Sub-section (5) creates an evidentiary shortcut for certain security-bond scenarios (sections 125, 136, 401, or a bond in lieu under section 494): a certified copy of the principal's conviction judgment can itself be used as evidence in the forfeiture proceeding against his surety, triggering a presumption (rebuttable) that he in fact committed the breach-constituting offence.
essential_elements: Applies once forfeiture of an appearance/property-production bond, or any other Sanhita bond, is proved to the satisfaction of the competent Court.
The Court records the grounds of proof and calls on the bound person to pay the penalty or show cause against payment.
If no sufficient cause is shown and payment fails, the Court recovers the penalty as if it were a fine.
If such recovery isn't possible, a defaulting surety may be imprisoned in civil jail for up to six months.
The Court may, for recorded reasons, remit part of the penalty and enforce only partial payment.
A surety's death before forfeiture discharges his estate from all liability on the bond.

For bonds under sections 125, 136, 401, or 494, a certified conviction judgment is admissible evidence against the surety and triggers a rebuttable presumption that the principal committed the breaching offence.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Explanation extends an appearance/production condition to cover appearance/production before any Court to which the case is later transferred -- forfeiture isn't defeated by a mid-case transfer.
Civil-jail imprisonment for a defaulting surety is a last resort, available only when the penalty cannot otherwise be recovered as a fine, and is capped at six months.
The section 491(5) evidentiary presumption is rebuttable -- the surety may still prove the contrary.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the anchor provision for the whole forfeiture regime -- sections 492 (cancellation), 493 (insolvency/death of surety), and 495 (appeal) all cross-reference and build on the procedure fixed here, so read them as a connected cluster rather than in isolation.

sections.title: Cancellation of bond and bail bond
sections.raw_text:
492. Cancellation of bond and bail bond.—Without prejudice to the provisions of section 491, where
a bond or bail bond under this Sanhita is for appearance of a person in a case and it is forfeited for breach
of a condition,—
        (a) the bond executed by such person as well as the bond, if any, executed by one or more of his
    sureties in that case shall stand cancelled; and
         (b) thereafter no such person shall be released only on his own bond in that case, if the police officer
    or the Court, as the case may be, for appearance before whom the bond was executed, is satisfied that
    there was no sufficient cause for the failure of the person bound by the bond to comply with its
    condition:
    Provided that subject to any other provisions of this Sanhita he may be released in that case upon the
execution of a fresh personal bond for such sum of money and bond by one or more of such sureties as the
police officer or the Court, as the case may be, thinks sufficient.

breakdown.plain_summary: This runs alongside (not instead of) section 491's penalty-recovery machinery: where an appearance bond or bail bond is forfeited for breach of its condition, the bond itself -- and any surety bond executed alongside it in that case -- automatically stands cancelled (clause (a)). Going forward, the person cannot simply be released again on his own bond alone in that case if the police officer or Court is satisfied there was no sufficient cause for the earlier breach (clause (b)) -- his own unsecured word is no longer good enough. The proviso keeps a door open, though: subject to the Sanhita's other provisions, he may still be released in that case, but only upon executing a fresh personal bond plus a bond from one or more sureties the officer/Court considers sufficient -- i.e., the bar is raised, not permanently shut.
essential_elements: Applies where an appearance bond or bail bond is forfeited for breach of its condition.
The forfeited bond, and any accompanying surety bond in that case, stand automatically cancelled.
The person cannot be released again on his own bond alone in that case if the officer/Court is satisfied there was no sufficient cause for the earlier breach.
He may still be released upon executing a fresh personal bond plus sufficient surety bond(s).
exceptions_and_qualifications: This operates without prejudice to section 491 -- cancellation under this section is additional to, not a substitute for, the penalty-recovery procedure there.
The bar on own-bond-only release applies only where the officer/Court is satisfied there was no sufficient cause for the earlier failure -- a genuine sufficient cause avoids this consequence.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read this together with section 491: 491 handles the money/penalty consequence of forfeiture, while 492 handles the release-terms consequence -- both fire off the same underlying forfeiture-for-breach event, and both can apply simultaneously to the same episode.

sections.title: Procedure in case of insolvency or death of surety or when a bond is forfeited
sections.raw_text:
493. Procedure in case of insolvency or death of surety or when a bond is forfeited.—When any
surety to a bail bond under this Sanhita becomes insolvent or dies, or when any bond is forfeited under the
provisions of section 491, the Court by whose order such bond was taken, or a Magistrate of the first class
may order the person from whom such security was demanded to furnish fresh security in accordance with
the directions of the original order, and if such security is not furnished, such Court or Magistrate may
proceed as if there had been a default in complying with such original order.

breakdown.plain_summary: This covers three distinct events that can undermine a bail bond's security -- the surety becoming insolvent, the surety dying, or the bond simply being forfeited under section 491 -- and gives a single uniform response: the Court that ordered the bond (or a Magistrate of the first class) may direct the person from whom security was originally demanded to furnish fresh security, on the same terms as the original order. If fresh security isn't furnished, the Court/Magistrate may treat this exactly as if the person had defaulted on the original order in the first place -- triggering whatever consequences would follow from that original default (e.g., custody, forfeiture procedures).
essential_elements: Triggers on any of three events: a surety to a bail bond becomes insolvent, a surety dies, or a bond is forfeited under section 491.
The Court that ordered the bond, or a Magistrate of the first class, may order fresh security in accordance with the original order's directions.
If fresh security is not furnished, the Court/Magistrate may treat it as a default of the original order.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a security-continuity provision -- it ensures a bail arrangement doesn't silently become unsecured just because a surety's circumstances change (insolvency, death) or the bond fails (forfeiture); the accused must promptly replace the lost security or face the same consequences as an original default.

sections.title: Bond required from child
sections.raw_text:
494. Bond required from child.—When the person required by any Court, or officer to execute a bond
is a child, such Court or officer may accept, in lieu thereof, a bond executed by a surety or sureties only.

breakdown.plain_summary: A protective accommodation for minors: where the person a Court or officer requires to execute a bond is a child, the Court or officer may accept, instead, a bond executed only by a surety or sureties -- sparing the child himself from being bound as a principal obligor on a bond, since a child cannot meaningfully be held to the same contractual/legal accountability as an adult.
essential_elements: Applies where the person required to execute a bond is a child.
The Court or officer may accept a bond executed only by a surety or sureties, in lieu of the child's own bond.
breakdown.how_to_read: This dovetails with section 491(5)'s reference to 'a bond executed in lieu of his bond under section 494' -- confirming that a section 494 surety-only bond is treated as a full substitute for the child's own bond for purposes of the forfeiture and evidentiary-presumption machinery elsewhere in this cluster.

sections.title: Appeal from orders under section 491
sections.raw_text:
495. Appeal from orders under section 491.—All orders passed under section 491 shall be
appealable,—
        (i) in the case of an order made by a Magistrate, to the Sessions Judge;
        (ii) in the case of an order made by a Court of Session, to the Court to which an appeal lies from an
    order made by such Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: This confirms a right of appeal against every order passed under section 491 (the bond-forfeiture procedure), and routes it based on which Court made the original order: an order made by a Magistrate is appealable to the Sessions Judge, while an order made by a Court of Session is appealable to whichever Court an appeal ordinarily lies from that Court's orders. This ensures a person penalized under the forfeiture procedure -- whether facing a penalty payment or civil-jail imprisonment -- always has an appellate avenue.
essential_elements: All orders passed under section 491 are appealable.
A Magistrate's order under section 491 is appealable to the Sessions Judge.
A Court of Session's order under section 491 is appealable to the Court to which appeals ordinarily lie from that Court.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the dedicated appellate route for the whole section 491 forfeiture procedure -- distinguish it from section 500 below, which provides a separate appeal route specifically for property-disposal orders under sections 498/499.

sections.title: Power to direct levy of amount due on certain recognizances
sections.raw_text:
496. Power to direct levy of amount due on certain recognizances.—The High Court or Court of
Session may direct any Magistrate to levy the amount due on a bond for appearance or attendance at such
High Court or Court of Session.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closing provision of Chapter XXXV gives the High Court or Court of Session a practical enforcement tool: rather than having to itself carry out the mechanics of recovering money due on a bond for appearance or attendance before it, it may simply direct any Magistrate to levy (collect/recover) that amount -- delegating the ground-level recovery work while the superior Court retains the authority to order it.
essential_elements: Applies to bonds for appearance or attendance at the High Court or Court of Session.
The High Court or Court of Session may direct any Magistrate to levy the amount due on such a bond.
breakdown.how_to_read: This closes out Chapter XXXV's bail-and-bonds scheme with a practical delegation mechanism for superior-Court-level bonds; Chapter XXXVI (Disposal of Property) begins immediately after at section 497.

sections.title: Order for custody and disposal of property pending trial in certain cases
sections.raw_text:
497. Order for custody and disposal of property pending trial in certain cases.—(1) When any
property is produced before any Criminal Court or the Magistrate empowered to take cognizance or commit
the case for trial during any investigation, inquiry or trial, the Court or the Magistrate may make such order
as it thinks fit for the proper custody of such property pending the conclusion of the investigation, inquiry
or trial, and, if the property is subject to speedy and natural decay, or if it is otherwise expedient so to do,
the Court or the Magistrate may, after recording such evidence as it thinks necessary, order it to be sold or
otherwise disposed of.
    Explanation.—For the purposes of this section, "property" includes—
        (a) property of any kind or document which is produced before the Court or which is in its custody;
       (b) any property regarding which an offence appears to have been committed or which appears to
    have been used for the commission of any offence.
    (2) The Court or the Magistrate shall, within a period of fourteen days from the production of the
property referred to in sub-section (1) before it, prepare a statement of such property containing its
description in such form and manner as the State Government may, by rules, provide.
   (3) The Court or the Magistrate shall cause to be taken the photograph and if necessary, videograph on
mobile phone or any electronic media, of the property referred to in sub-section (1).
    (4) The statement prepared under sub-section (2) and the photograph or the videography taken under
sub-section (3) shall be used as evidence in any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under the Sanhita.
    (5) The Court or the Magistrate shall, within a period of thirty days after the statement has been prepared
under sub-section (2) and the photograph or the videography has been taken under sub-section (3), order
the disposal, destruction, confiscation or delivery of the property in the manner specified hereinafter.

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Chapter XXXVI's scheme for handling property connected to a criminal case. Whenever property is produced before a Criminal Court or a Magistrate empowered to take cognizance/commit the case, pending the conclusion of investigation, inquiry, or trial that Court/Magistrate may make whatever order it thinks fit for the property's proper custody -- and where the property is subject to speedy and natural decay, or it's otherwise expedient, it may, after recording necessary evidence, order the property sold or otherwise disposed of even before the case concludes. The Explanation gives 'property' a broad reach: anything produced before or in the Court's custody, plus anything regarding which an offence appears to have been committed or which appears to have been used to commit one. Sub-sections (2)-(5) add a documentation-and-timeline discipline introduced by the new Sanhita: within 14 days of production, the Court/Magistrate must prepare a descriptive statement of the property (per State Government rules); it must also cause a photograph, and if necessary a videograph (via mobile phone or other electronic media), to be taken; both the statement and photograph/videograph become usable evidence in any inquiry, trial, or proceeding under the Sanhita; and within 30 days of that statement/photograph/videograph being completed, the Court/Magistrate must order the property's disposal, destruction, confiscation, or delivery per the sections that follow.
essential_elements: Applies to property produced before a Criminal Court or a Magistrate empowered to take cognizance/commit the case, during investigation, inquiry, or trial.
The Court/Magistrate may order proper custody pending conclusion of the case, or, for decaying/otherwise-expedient property, order sale/disposal after recording necessary evidence.
'Property' includes anything produced before or in the Court's custody, and anything an offence appears to have been committed regarding or used to commit.
Within 14 days of production, a descriptive statement of the property must be prepared per State Government rules.
A photograph, and videograph if necessary, of the property must be taken.
The statement and photograph/videograph are usable as evidence in any inquiry, trial, or proceeding under the Sanhita.
Within 30 days of the statement/photograph/videograph being completed, an order for disposal, destruction, confiscation, or delivery must be made.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Sale/disposal before conclusion of the case is permitted only for property subject to speedy/natural decay, or where otherwise expedient, and only after recording necessary evidence.
breakdown.how_to_read: The 14-day statement deadline and 30-day disposal-order deadline are new procedural timelines not found in the predecessor Code -- they convert what was often an open-ended interim-custody power into a documented, time-bound process, and the resulting statement/photograph/videograph doubles as independently admissible evidence, reducing dependence on producing the physical property itself at trial.

sections.title: Order for disposal of property at conclusion of trial
sections.raw_text:
498. Order for disposal of property at conclusion of trial.—(1) When an investigation, inquiry or
trial in any criminal case is concluded, the Court or the Magistrate may make such order as it thinks fit for
the disposal, by destruction, confiscation or delivery to any person claiming to be entitled to possession
thereof or otherwise, of any property or document produced before it or in its custody, or regarding which
any offence appears to have been committed, or which has been used for the commission of any offence.
    (2) An order may be made under sub-section (1) for the delivery of any property to any person claiming
to be entitled to the possession thereof, without any condition or on condition that he executes a bond, with
or without securities, to the satisfaction of the Court or the Magistrate, engaging to restore such property to
the Court if the order made under sub-section (1) is modified or set aside on appeal or revision.
    (3) A Court of Session may, instead of itself making an order under sub-section (1), direct the property
to be delivered to the Chief Judicial Magistrate, who shall thereupon deal with it in the manner provided in
sections 503, 504 and 505.
    (4) Except where the property is livestock or is subject to speedy and natural decay, or where a bond
has been executed in pursuance of sub-section (2), an order made under sub-section (1) shall not be carried
out for two months, or when an appeal is presented, until such appeal has been disposed of.
    (5) In this section, the term "property" includes, in the case of property regarding which an offence
appears to have been committed, not only such property as has been originally in the possession or under
the control of any party, but also any property into or for which the same may have been converted or
exchanged, and anything acquired by such conversion or exchange, whether immediately or otherwise.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the final-disposal counterpart to section 497's pending-trial custody power: once the investigation, inquiry, or trial concludes, the Court/Magistrate may order the property's disposal -- by destruction, confiscation, or delivery to a person claiming entitlement to it or otherwise -- covering property produced before or in its custody, or connected to the alleged offence. Delivery to a claimant may be unconditional or made conditional on his executing a bond (with or without securities) undertaking to restore the property to the Court if the order is later modified or set aside on appeal or revision (sub-section (2)) -- protecting against a premature final handover. A Court of Session has the option to route the actual disposal work to the Chief Judicial Magistrate instead of handling it itself (sub-section (3)), who then follows the specific procedure in sections 503-505. As a general stay-pending-finality safeguard, sub-section (4) blocks execution of a disposal order for two months, or until any appeal is disposed of if one is filed -- except where the property is livestock, subject to speedy/natural decay, or already bonded under sub-section (2), all of which justify immediate execution. Sub-section (5) extends 'property' to cover not just what was originally held/controlled by a party but also anything it was later converted or exchanged into or for, and anything acquired through such conversion/exchange -- closing an obvious evasion route (converting stolen property into a different asset to escape the disposal order).
essential_elements: Applies once investigation, inquiry, or trial in a criminal case concludes.
The Court/Magistrate may order disposal by destruction, confiscation, or delivery to a claimant or otherwise, covering property produced/in custody or connected to the offence.
Delivery to a claimant may be conditioned on a restitution-undertaking bond (with or without securities) in case the order is later modified/set aside on appeal or revision.
A Court of Session may instead direct the Chief Judicial Magistrate to handle disposal per sections 503-505.
A disposal order generally cannot be carried out for two months, or pending disposal of any appeal filed.
Livestock, speedily/naturally decaying property, and property already bonded under sub-section (2) are exempt from that delay.
'Property' includes anything originally held/controlled by a party plus anything it was converted or exchanged into, and anything acquired through that conversion/exchange.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The two-month/pending-appeal delay does not apply to livestock, decaying property, or already-bonded property.
breakdown.how_to_read: Read sub-section (5)'s expanded definition of 'property' as an anti-evasion provision -- it prevents a party from defeating a disposal order simply by converting the original property into a different form or asset before the order is executed.

sections.title: Payment to innocent purchaser of money found on accused
sections.raw_text:
499. Payment to innocent purchaser of money found on accused.—When any person is convicted
of any offence which includes, or amounts to, theft or receiving stolen property, and it is proved that any
other person bought the stolen property from him without knowing or having reason to believe that the
same was stolen, and that any money has on his arrest been taken out of the possession of the convicted
person, the Court may, on the application of such purchaser and on the restitution of the stolen property to
the person entitled to the possession thereof, order that out of such money a sum not exceeding the price
paid by such purchaser be delivered to him within six months from the date of such order.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is a targeted equitable relief for an innocent purchaser caught in the crossfire of a theft/stolen-property conviction. Where the convicted person's offence includes or amounts to theft or receiving stolen property, and it's proved that someone else bought that stolen property from him genuinely without knowing or having reason to believe it was stolen, and money was seized from the convicted person's possession at his arrest, the Court -- on the innocent purchaser's application, and only once the stolen property itself has been restored to its rightful owner -- may order that a sum up to what the purchaser actually paid be delivered to him out of the seized money, within six months of the order.
essential_elements: Applies where a person is convicted of an offence including or amounting to theft or receiving stolen property.
It must be proved another person bought the stolen property from him without knowing/having reason to believe it was stolen.
Money must have been taken from the convicted person's possession on his arrest.
On the innocent purchaser's application, and on restitution of the stolen property to its rightful owner, the Court may order payment to the purchaser out of the seized money.
The amount payable is capped at the price the purchaser actually paid, and must be delivered within six months of the order.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Relief is conditional on restitution of the stolen property to the person entitled to possession first -- the purchaser cannot keep both the goods and recover the money.
The purchaser must have bought genuinely without knowledge or reason to believe the property was stolen -- a purchaser with actual or constructive knowledge gets no relief.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a narrow, fact-specific relief valve within the broader disposal-of-property scheme -- it only operates where all its conditions align (theft/receiving conviction, an innocent purchaser, seized money, and restitution of the goods), and the payout is capped at the purchaser's actual outlay, not the property's value or any other measure.

sections.title: Appeal against orders under section 498 or section 499
sections.raw_text:
500. Appeal against orders under section 498 or section 499.—(1) Any person aggrieved by an order
made by a Court or Magistrate under section 498 or section 499, may appeal against it to the Court to which
appeals ordinarily lie from convictions by the former Court.
   (2) On such appeal, the Appellate Court may direct the order to be stayed pending disposal of the
appeal, or may modify, alter or annul the order and make any further orders that may be just.
    (3) The powers referred to in sub-section (2) may also be exercised by a Court of appeal, confirmation
or revision while dealing with the case in which the order referred to in sub-section (1) was made.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes Chapter XXXVI's property-disposal scheme with an appeal right against orders made under section 498 (disposal at conclusion of trial) or section 499 (innocent-purchaser payment): any aggrieved person may appeal to the Court to which appeals ordinarily lie from convictions by the Court/Magistrate that made the order. On appeal, the Appellate Court may stay the order pending the appeal's disposal, or modify, alter, or annul it and make whatever further orders are just (sub-section (2)). Sub-section (3) extends this same stay/modify/alter/annul power to any Court exercising appeal, confirmation, or revision jurisdiction over the underlying case in which the order was made -- so the property-disposal order can be corrected through whichever appellate, confirmation, or revisional channel the main case itself is passing through, not just through a freestanding appeal filed solely against the disposal order.
essential_elements: Any person aggrieved by an order under section 498 or 499 may appeal to the Court to which appeals ordinarily lie from convictions by the order-making Court.
The Appellate Court may stay the order pending appeal, or modify, alter, or annul it and make further just orders.
The same powers are exercisable by any Court dealing with the underlying case in its appeal, confirmation, or revision jurisdiction.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the dedicated appellate safeguard specific to property-disposal orders under sections 498-499, distinct from section 495's appeal route for bond-forfeiture orders under section 491 -- keep the two appellate tracks separate since they attach to different underlying orders.

sections.title: Destruction of libellous and other matter
sections.raw_text:
501. Destruction of libellous and other matter.—(1) On a conviction under section 294, section 295,
or sub-sections (3) and (4) of section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, the Court may order the
destruction of all the copies of the thing in respect of which the conviction was had, and which are in the
custody of the Court or remain in the possession or power of the person convicted.
    (2) The Court may, in like manner, on a conviction under section 274, section 275, section 276
or section 277 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, order the food, drink, drug or medical preparation in
respect of which the conviction was had, to be destroyed.

breakdown.plain_summary: This lets the Court order physical elimination of the harmful material itself once a conviction is secured for specific offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Sub-section (1) covers defamatory/obscene-type offences (BNS sections 294, 295, or 356(3)/(4)) -- the Court may order destroyed all copies of the offending thing, whether held in the Court's own custody or still in the possession/power of the convicted person, so the harm doesn't continue circulating after conviction. Sub-section (2) applies the same destruction power to adulterated food, drink, drugs, or medical preparations following a conviction under BNS sections 274-277 (adulteration-type offences) -- removing dangerous or unlawful substances from further use once guilt is established.
essential_elements: On conviction under BNS section 294, 295, or 356(3)/(4), the Court may order destruction of all copies of the offending thing in Court custody or still with the convicted person.
On conviction under BNS section 274, 275, 276, or 277, the Court may similarly order destruction of the food, drink, drug, or medical preparation involved.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a remedial/preventive power tied to specific BNS offence categories -- treat it as a natural adjunct to sentencing on those particular convictions, not a general-purpose destruction power available for any offence.

sections.title: Power to restore possession of immovable property
sections.raw_text:
502. Power to restore possession of immovable property.—(1) When a person is convicted of an
offence by use of criminal force or show of force or by criminal intimidation, and it appears to the Court
that, by such use of force or show of force or intimidation, any person has been dispossessed of any
immovable property, the Court may, if it thinks fit, order that possession of the same be restored to that
person after evicting by force, if necessary, any other person who may be in possession of the property:
   Provided that no such order shall be made by the Court more than one month after the date of the
conviction.
    (2) Where the Court trying the offence has not made an order under sub-section (1), the Court of appeal,
confirmation or revision may, if it thinks fit, make such order while disposing of the appeal, reference or
revision, as the case may be.
    (3) Where an order has been made under sub-section (1), the provisions of section 500 shall apply in
relation thereto as they apply in relation to an order under section 499.
    (4) No order made under this section shall prejudice any right or interest to or in such immovable
property which any person may be able to establish in a civil suit.

breakdown.plain_summary: This gives the criminal Court a quick restitution tool for forcible dispossession of land/buildings: where a person is convicted of an offence involving use of force, show of force, or criminal intimidation, and it appears the victim was thereby dispossessed of immovable property, the Court may order possession restored to him, evicting by force if necessary whoever is currently occupying it -- but only within one month of the conviction (sub-section (1)'s proviso). If the trial Court doesn't make such an order, an appellate, confirmation, or revisional Court may still make it while disposing of the appeal/reference/revision (sub-section (2)). An order under this section carries the same appeal rights as a section 499 order, via section 500's machinery (sub-section (3)). Crucially, sub-section (4) makes clear this is only a provisional, criminal-process remedy -- it does not prejudice or finally determine anyone's underlying civil right or interest in the property, which remains open to be established in a civil suit.
essential_elements: Applies on conviction for an offence involving criminal force, show of force, or criminal intimidation that dispossessed someone of immovable property.
The Court may order possession restored, evicting the current occupant by force if necessary.
The order must be made within one month of the conviction.
If the trial Court doesn't make the order, an appellate, confirmation, or revisional Court may make it while disposing of the appeal/reference/revision.
Section 500's appeal machinery applies to an order under this section as it applies to a section 499 order.
The order does not prejudice any right or interest in the property that may be established in a civil suit.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The one-month time limit in sub-section (1) is a strict outer bound on the trial Court's own power to make this order.
Sub-section (4) is an express reminder that this is a summary criminal-process remedy, not a final adjudication of civil title/possession rights.
breakdown.how_to_read: Always flag sub-section (4) to a client relying on this section -- restoration of possession here is fast and force-backed, but it settles nothing about underlying ownership or civil possessory rights, which must still be litigated separately if disputed.

sections.title: Procedure by police upon seizure of property
sections.raw_text:
503. Procedure by police upon seizure of property.—(1) Whenever the seizure of property by any
police officer is reported to a Magistrate under the provisions of this Sanhita, and such property is not
produced before a Criminal Court during an inquiry or trial, the Magistrate may make such order as he
thinks fit respecting the disposal of such property or the delivery of such property to the person entitled to
the possession thereof, or if such person cannot be ascertained, respecting the custody and production of
such property.
    (2) If the person so entitled is known, the Magistrate may order the property to be delivered to him on
such conditions (if any) as the Magistrate thinks fit and if such person is unknown, the Magistrate may
detain it and shall, in such case, issue a proclamation specifying the articles of which such property consists,
and requiring any person who may have a claim thereto, to appear before him and establish his claim within
six months from the date of such proclamation.

breakdown.plain_summary: This handles seized property that never actually reaches a Criminal Court during an inquiry or trial -- i.e., property a police officer seizes and reports to a Magistrate, but which stays outside the courtroom process. The Magistrate may order whatever disposition he thinks fit: delivery to the person entitled to possession, or, if that person can't be ascertained, custody and production arrangements pending identification. Sub-section (2) fleshes out the mechanics: if the entitled person is known, the Magistrate may order delivery to him on whatever conditions he thinks fit; if unknown, the Magistrate detains the property and must issue a proclamation describing the articles and calling on anyone with a claim to appear and establish it within six months.
essential_elements: Applies to property seized by police and reported to a Magistrate, where the property is not produced before a Criminal Court during inquiry or trial.
The Magistrate may order disposal or delivery to the person entitled, or, if unascertainable, custody/production arrangements.
If the entitled person is known, delivery may be ordered on conditions the Magistrate thinks fit.
If unknown, the Magistrate detains the property and issues a proclamation, giving claimants six months to appear and establish their claim.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the entry point of a three-section unclaimed/unascertained-property sequence -- section 503 (initial procedure and proclamation), section 504 (what happens if no claimant appears within six months), and section 505 (power to sell perishable property faster) -- read all three together as a single continuous process.

sections.title: Procedure where no claimant appears within six months
sections.raw_text:
504. Procedure where no claimant appears within six months.—(1) If no person within such period
establishes his claim to such property, and if the person in whose possession such property was found is
unable to show that it was legally acquired by him, the Magistrate may by order direct that such property
shall be at the disposal of the State Government and may be sold by that Government and the proceeds of
such sale shall be dealt with in such manner as the State Government may, by rules, provide.
   (2) An appeal shall lie against any such order to the Court to which appeals ordinarily lie from
convictions by the Magistrate.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the fallback outcome when section 503's six-month proclamation window closes without any successful claimant: if no one establishes a claim, and the person found in possession of the property can't show it was legally acquired by him, the Magistrate may direct that the property go to the disposal of the State Government, which may sell it, with proceeds handled per State Government rules. Sub-section (2) guarantees an appeal against such an order, to the Court to which appeals ordinarily lie from that Magistrate's convictions -- ensuring the person in possession (even if unable to prove legal acquisition) isn't left without any recourse against a disposal order.
essential_elements: Applies where no claimant establishes a claim within the section 503 six-month period.
The Magistrate must also find that the person in possession cannot show the property was legally acquired.
The Magistrate may direct the property to the State Government's disposal, which may sell it, proceeds handled per State Government rules.
An appeal lies against such an order to the Court to which appeals ordinarily lie from that Magistrate's convictions.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Both conditions -- no successful claimant AND inability to show legal acquisition -- must be satisfied before the property goes to State disposal.
breakdown.how_to_read: The double condition here matters for defense strategy: a possessor who cannot identify a specific rightful owner may still resist a section 504 order by simply establishing legal acquisition (e.g., a purchase receipt), even without naming who he acquired it from.

sections.title: Power to sell perishable property
sections.raw_text:
505. Power to sell perishable property.—If the person entitled to the possession of such property is
unknown or absent and the property is subject to speedy and natural decay, or if the Magistrate to whom its
seizure is reported is of opinion that its sale would be for the benefit of the owner, or that the value of such
property is less than ten thousand rupees, the Magistrate may at any time direct it to be sold; and the
provisions of sections 503 and 504 shall, as nearly as may be practicable, apply to the net proceeds of such
sale.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes out the unclaimed/unascertained-property sequence by giving the Magistrate a fast-track sale power that bypasses the six-month waiting period of sections 503-504, in three alternative situations: the entitled person is unknown/absent and the property is perishable; the Magistrate believes sale would benefit the owner; or the property's value is under ten thousand rupees. In any of these, the Magistrate may direct sale at any time -- and once sold, sections 503 and 504's procedures (proclamation, six-month claim window, disposal-to-State-if-unclaimed) apply, as nearly as practicable, to the net sale proceeds instead of to the physical property itself.
essential_elements: Applies where the entitled person is unknown/absent and the property is perishable, OR sale would benefit the owner in the Magistrate's opinion, OR the property's value is below ten thousand rupees.
The Magistrate may direct sale at any time under any of these three grounds.
Sections 503 and 504's procedures then apply, as nearly as practicable, to the net sale proceeds rather than the property itself.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a practical acceleration mechanism -- it substitutes money (sale proceeds) for the physical property as the thing subject to the claim/disposal procedure, recognizing that waiting six months would often destroy the property's value entirely.
breakdown.how_to_read: This closes Chapter XXXVI (Disposal of Property) in its entirety -- Chapter XXXVII (Irregular Proceedings) begins immediately after at section 506.

sections.title: Irregularities which do not vitiate proceedings

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Chapter XXXVII's curative scheme by listing nine specific categories of Magistrate action (issuing a search warrant, ordering police investigation, holding an inquest, issuing process for extra-jurisdictional apprehension, taking cognizance under specific clauses, making over a case, tendering a pardon, recalling a case to try himself, or selling property under sections 504/505) where, if a Magistrate not actually empowered by law to do that thing nonetheless does it erroneously and in good faith, the resulting proceedings are NOT to be set aside merely because he lacked the power. This protects the validity of proceedings against a purely technical want-of-authority defect, so long as the error was made honestly rather than in bad faith.
essential_elements: Lists nine specific categories of Magistrate action where lack of legal empowerment, if acted on erroneously and in good faith, does not vitiate the proceedings.
The categories span search warrants, investigation orders, inquests, extra-jurisdictional process, cognizance-taking, case transfers, pardons, case recall, and property sales.
The proceedings survive despite the want of power, provided the Magistrate acted erroneously and in good faith.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The protection is conditional on good faith -- a Magistrate knowingly acting outside his power does not get this shelter.
This list is exhaustive of the specific categories covered -- contrast with section 507's separately listed categories that DO vitiate proceedings.
breakdown.how_to_read: Always read this section directly against section 507 -- together they form a deliberate, itemized allocation of which want-of-power defects are curable (here) versus fatal (507); nothing outside these two lists is directly governed by either, so classify any defect precisely into the right list before arguing its consequence.

sections.title: Irregularities which vitiate proceedings

breakdown.plain_summary: This is section 506's mirror-image counterpart: for a different, separately enumerated list of seventeen categories of Magistrate action (attaching/selling property, issuing postal search warrants, demanding security to keep the peace or for good behaviour, discharging a good-behaviour bond, cancelling a peace bond, making maintenance orders, acting on local/public nuisances, acting under Chapter XI Parts C/D, taking cognizance under a specific clause, trying an offender (regularly or summarily), passing sentence on another Magistrate's recorded proceedings, deciding an appeal, calling for proceedings, or revising a section 491 order), if a Magistrate not empowered by law does any of these things, his proceedings are simply void -- no good-faith saving grace applies here as it does in section 506. These are treated as more fundamental jurisdictional defects going to the heart of judicial authority (trying offenders, deciding appeals, coercive security/property measures) rather than administrative missteps.
essential_elements: Lists seventeen specific categories of Magistrate action where lack of legal empowerment renders the proceedings void, with no good-faith exception.

The categories include property attachment/sale, postal search warrants, peace/good-behaviour security demands, maintenance orders, nuisance orders, trying offenders (regular or summary), passing sentence on another Magistrate's proceedings, deciding appeals, and revising section 491 orders.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Unlike section 506, there is no good-faith savings clause here -- voidness follows automatically from the want of power for these categories.
breakdown.how_to_read: Practitioners challenging a Magistrate's order for want of jurisdiction should first check whether the specific act falls within this section's list (fatal, void) or section 506's list (curable if done in good faith) -- the categorization, not the Magistrate's intent, is generally what determines the outcome here.

sections.title: Proceedings in wrong place
sections.raw_text:
508. Proceedings in wrong place.—No finding, sentence or order of any Criminal Court shall be set
aside merely on the ground that the inquiry, trial or other proceedings in the course of which it was arrived
at or passed, took place in a wrong sessions division, district, sub-division or other local area, unless it
appears that such error has in fact occasioned a failure of justice.

breakdown.plain_summary: This protects proceedings from being invalidated on a purely territorial/venue technicality: a Criminal Court's finding, sentence, or order is not to be set aside merely because the underlying inquiry, trial, or proceedings happened in the wrong sessions division, district, sub-division, or other local area -- unless that venue error actually caused a failure of justice. The focus shifts from the formal correctness of venue to whether the mistake had any real prejudicial effect.
essential_elements: A finding, sentence, or order is not to be set aside merely for having proceeded in the wrong sessions division, district, sub-division, or local area.
Setting aside is warranted only if the venue error has in fact occasioned a failure of justice.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is part of the same curative philosophy running through sections 506-511 -- technical/procedural defects (here, wrong venue) don't automatically doom a proceeding; the challenging party must show actual prejudice (failure of justice), not just the bare fact of the irregularity.

sections.title: Non-compliance with provisions of section 183 or section 316
sections.raw_text:
509. Non-compliance with provisions of section 183 or section 316.—(1) If any Court before which
a confession or other statement of an accused person recorded, or purporting to be recorded under section
183 or section 316, is tendered, or has been received, in evidence finds that any of the provisions of either
of such sections have not been complied with by the Magistrate recording the statement, it may,
notwithstanding anything contained in section 94 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, take evidence
in regard to such non-compliance, and may, if satisfied that such non-compliance has not injured the
accused in his defence on the merits and that he duly made the statement recorded, admit such statement.
    (2) The provisions of this section apply to Courts of appeal, reference and revision.

breakdown.plain_summary: This provides a specific curative route for procedural defects in recording confessions/statements under sections 183 or 316. Where a confession or statement, recorded or purporting to be recorded under either section, is tendered or received in evidence, and the Court finds the recording Magistrate failed to comply with those sections' requirements, the Court may -- overriding the ordinary evidentiary bar in section 94 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 -- take evidence specifically about that non-compliance. If satisfied both that the non-compliance did not injure the accused's defence on the merits, and that he genuinely did make the statement as recorded, the Court may admit the statement despite the procedural defect. Sub-section (2) extends this same curative power to appellate, reference, and revisional Courts, not just the trial Court.
essential_elements: Applies where a confession/statement recorded or purporting to be recorded under section 183 or 316 is tendered/received in evidence, and the recording Magistrate did not comply with those sections' requirements.
The Court may take evidence about the non-compliance, notwithstanding section 94 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.
The Court may admit the statement if satisfied the non-compliance did not injure the accused's defence on the merits and that he duly made the statement.
This power extends to Courts of appeal, reference, and revision.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Admission is conditional on BOTH findings: no injury to the defence on the merits, AND genuine authorship of the statement as recorded.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a narrow, fact-intensive curative gateway specific to confession/statement recording defects -- unlike sections 506-508's blanket rules, here the Court must affirmatively take evidence and make two specific findings before the defect is cured.

sections.title: Effect of omission to frame, or absence of, or error in, charge
sections.raw_text:
510. Effect of omission to frame, or absence of, or error in, charge.—(1) No finding, sentence or
order by a Court of competent jurisdiction shall be deemed invalid merely on the ground that no charge was
framed or on the ground of any error, omission or irregularity in the charge including any misjoinder of
charges, unless, in the opinion of the Court of appeal, confirmation or revision, a failure of justice has in
fact been occasioned thereby.
    (2) If the Court of appeal, confirmation or revision, is of opinion that a failure of justice has in fact been
occasioned, it may,—
        (a) in the case of an omission to frame a charge, order that a charge be framed, and that the trial be
    recommenced from the point immediately after the framing of the charge;
        (b) in the case of an error, omission or irregularity in the charge, direct a new trial to be had upon
    a charge framed in whatever manner it thinks fit:
        Provided that if the Court is of opinion that the facts of the case are such that no valid charge could
    be preferred against the accused in respect of the facts proved, it shall quash the conviction.
