breakdown.plain_summary: This extends the same failure-of-justice principle specifically to charge-framing defects: no finding, sentence, or order of a competent Court is invalid merely because no charge was framed at all, or because of any error, omission, or irregularity in the charge (including misjoinder of charges), unless the appellate, confirmation, or revisional Court considers that a failure of justice actually resulted. Where such a failure of justice IS found, sub-section (2) prescribes the specific remedies: for an omission to frame a charge, order that a charge be framed and the trial recommence from immediately after framing; for an error/omission/irregularity in the charge, direct an entirely new trial on a freshly framed charge. But the proviso caps this: if the Court concludes that no valid charge could ever be preferred against the accused on the facts actually proved, it must quash the conviction outright rather than order a re-trial that could never succeed.
essential_elements: A charge-framing omission, error, or irregularity (including misjoinder) does not invalidate a finding/sentence/order unless it occasioned a failure of justice.
For an omission to frame a charge causing a failure of justice: the appellate/confirmation/revision Court orders a charge framed and the trial recommenced from that point.
For an error/omission/irregularity in the charge causing a failure of justice: the Court directs a new trial on a freshly framed charge.
If no valid charge could ever be framed on the facts proved, the conviction must be quashed rather than retried.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The quash-instead-of-retry outcome under the proviso applies only where the underlying facts proved could never support any valid charge -- not merely where the original charge itself was defective.
breakdown.how_to_read: This section works as a direct, specialized application of the general failure-of-justice principle in sections 508 and 511 to the particular problem of charge defects -- always check whether the facts proved could support a valid charge at all before assuming a retry (rather than an outright quash) is the available remedy.

sections.title: Finding or sentence when reversible by reason of error, omission or irregularity
sections.raw_text:
511. Finding or sentence when reversible by reason of error, omission or irregularity.—(1) Subject
to the provisions hereinbefore contained, no finding, sentence or order passed by a Court of competent
jurisdiction shall be reversed or altered by a Court of appeal, confirmation of revision on account of any
error, omission or irregularity in the complaint, summons, warrant, proclamation, order, judgment or other
proceedings before or during trial or in any inquiry or other proceedings under this Sanhita, or any error, or
irregularity in any sanction for the prosecution, unless in the opinion of that Court, a failure of justice has
in fact been occasioned thereby.
    (2) In determining whether any error, omission or irregularity in any proceeding under this Sanhita, or
any error, or irregularity in any sanction for the prosecution has occasioned a failure of justice, the Court
shall have regard to the fact whether the objection could and should have been raised at an earlier stage in
the proceedings.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the broadest, catch-all statement of the failure-of-justice principle running through the whole of Chapter XXXVII: subject to the earlier, more specific provisions of the Chapter, no finding, sentence, or order of a competent Court can be reversed or altered on appeal, confirmation, or revision merely because of an error, omission, or irregularity in the complaint, summons, warrant, proclamation, order, judgment, or other proceedings before or during trial (or in any inquiry/other proceeding), or any error/irregularity in a prosecution sanction -- unless the reviewing Court considers a failure of justice actually resulted. Sub-section (2) gives the Court a specific consideration when deciding that question: whether the objection could and should have been raised earlier in the proceedings -- a party who sat on a known defect and only raises it late faces an uphill battle showing real prejudice.
essential_elements: No finding/sentence/order is reversed or altered on appeal, confirmation, or revision merely for an error, omission, or irregularity in listed documents/proceedings or in a prosecution sanction.
Reversal/alteration requires the reviewing Court's opinion that a failure of justice has in fact been occasioned.
In assessing failure of justice, the Court must consider whether the objection could and should have been raised earlier in the proceedings.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This section operates subject to the more specific provisions earlier in the Chapter (sections 506-510) -- it is the residual/general rule, not an override of those specific rules.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the master failure-of-justice principle for the whole Chapter -- sections 508, 509, and 510 are specific applications of it to particular defect types (venue, confession recording, charge framing), while section 511 mops up every other kind of procedural error/irregularity not separately addressed, always subject to the same late-objection consideration in sub-section (2).

sections.title: Defect or error not to make attachment unlawful
sections.raw_text:
512. Defect or error not to make attachment unlawful.—No attachment made under this Sanhita
shall be deemed unlawful, nor shall any person making the same be deemed a trespasser, on account of any
defect or want of form in the summons, conviction, writ of attachment or other proceedings relating thereto.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes Chapter XXXVII with a targeted protection for attachments carried out under the Sanhita: an attachment is not to be deemed unlawful, nor the person carrying it out treated as a trespasser, merely because of a defect or want of form in the summons, conviction, writ of attachment, or other related proceedings. Like the rest of the Chapter, this shields the substantive act (here, attachment) from being unwound purely on formal/technical grounds.
essential_elements: An attachment under the Sanhita is not unlawful merely for a defect or want of form in the summons, conviction, writ of attachment, or related proceedings.
The person carrying out the attachment is not deemed a trespasser on that ground.
breakdown.how_to_read: This closes Chapter XXXVII (Irregular Proceedings) in its entirety, sections 506-512, all built around the same theme: purely formal/technical defects don't unwind an otherwise valid proceeding or action unless real prejudice (failure of justice) resulted. Chapter XXXVIII (Limitation for Taking Cognizance of Certain Offences) begins immediately after at section 513.

sections.title: Definitions
sections.raw_text:
513. Definitions.—For the purposes of this Chapter, unless the context otherwise requires, "period of
limitation" means the period specified in section 514 for taking cognizance of an offence.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is a short definitional anchor opening Chapter XXXVIII: for purposes of this Chapter, 'period of limitation' simply means whatever period section 514 specifies for taking cognizance of an offence -- pointing the reader directly to the operative time limits fixed there.
essential_elements: 'Period of limitation', for this Chapter, means the period specified in section 514 for taking cognizance of an offence.
breakdown.how_to_read: This definition is purely a cross-reference to section 514 -- read them together rather than treating section 513 as containing any independent substantive content.

sections.title: Bar to taking cognizance after lapse of period of limitation
sections.raw_text:
514. Bar to taking cognizance after lapse of period of limitation.—(1) Except as otherwise provided
in this Sanhita, no Court shall take cognizance of an offence of the category specified in sub-section (2),
after the expiry of the period of limitation.
    (2) The period of limitation shall be—
        (a) six months, if the offence is punishable with fine only;
        (b) one year, if the offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year;
        (c) three years, if the offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding one year but
    not exceeding three years.
    (3) For the purposes of this section, the period of limitation, in relation to offences which may be tried
together, shall be determined with reference to the offence which is punishable with the more severe
punishment or, as the case may be, the most severe punishment.
     Explanation.—For the purpose of computing the period of limitation, the relevant date shall be the date
of filing complaint under section 223 or the date of recording of information under section 173.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the core operative bar of Chapter XXXVIII: except where the Sanhita provides otherwise, a Court cannot take cognizance of an offence falling within the categories in sub-section (2) once the applicable limitation period has expired. That period scales with the offence's punishment severity: six months for fine-only offences, one year for offences punishable with imprisonment up to one year, and three years for offences punishable with imprisonment exceeding one year but not exceeding three years -- note that this limitation scheme only covers relatively minor offences (up to three years' imprisonment); more serious offences fall outside it entirely and face no limitation bar. Where multiple offences are tried together, sub-section (3) resolves the limitation period by reference to whichever offence carries the more/most severe punishment among them -- so a minor offence tried alongside a more serious one gets the benefit (or burden) of the more serious offence's longer period. The Explanation fixes the relevant date for computing the period: the date of filing a complaint under section 223, or the date information was recorded under section 173, whichever applies.
essential_elements: A Court cannot take cognizance of an offence within the specified categories after the limitation period expires, except as otherwise provided in the Sanhita.

Six months for fine-only offences; one year for offences punishable with imprisonment up to one year; three years for offences punishable with imprisonment exceeding one year but not exceeding three years.
For offences triable together, the limitation period is determined by the offence with the more/most severe punishment.
The relevant date for computing the period is the date of filing a complaint under section 223 or of recording information under section 173.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This bar applies only to the three specified categories of relatively minor offences -- offences punishable with imprisonment exceeding three years fall outside this limitation scheme altogether.
The bar operates 'except as otherwise provided in this Sanhita' -- other provisions (e.g., section 519's extension power) can displace the default bar.
breakdown.how_to_read: Always check the maximum punishment for the offence in question first -- if it exceeds three years' imprisonment, this whole Chapter's limitation bar is simply inapplicable, and cognizance can be taken at any time subject to other provisions of the Sanhita.

sections.title: Commencement of period of limitation
sections.raw_text:
515. Commencement of period of limitation.—(1) The period of limitation, in relation to an offender,
shall commence,—
        (a) on the date of the offence; or
        (b) where the commission of the offence was not known to the person aggrieved by the offence or
    to any police officer, the first day on which such offence comes to the knowledge of such person or to
    any police officer, whichever is earlier; or
        (c) where it is not known by whom the offence was committed, the first day on which the identity
    of the offender is known to the person aggrieved by the offence or to the police officer making
    investigation into the offence, whichever is earlier.
    (2) In computing the said period, the day from which such period is to be computed shall be excluded.

breakdown.plain_summary: This fixes the starting point (the clock's zero date) for the limitation period fixed by section 514, offering three alternative triggers depending on the facts: ordinarily, the clock starts on the date of the offence itself (clause (a)); but if the offence's commission wasn't known to the aggrieved person or any police officer, the clock instead starts on the first day either of them actually learns of it, whichever is earlier (clause (b)) -- so a concealed or undiscovered offence doesn't silently run out its limitation period; and if the offender's identity is unknown, the clock starts on the first day either the aggrieved person or the investigating police officer learns who committed it, whichever is earlier (clause (c)) -- addressing offences where the act is known but the culprit isn't. Sub-section (2) applies the standard exclusionary computation rule: the day from which the period is computed is itself excluded from the count.
essential_elements: Ordinarily, the limitation period commences on the date of the offence.
If the offence's commission was unknown to the aggrieved person or police, the period commences on the first day either learns of it, whichever is earlier.
If the offender's identity is unknown, the period commences on the first day either the aggrieved person or the investigating police officer learns his identity, whichever is earlier.
The starting day itself is excluded when computing the period.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clauses (b) and (c) are alternative triggers to the default in clause (a), applicable specifically where knowledge of the offence, or of the offender's identity, was delayed.
breakdown.how_to_read: This section's knowledge-based triggers (clauses (b) and (c)) are essential for concealed-offence or unknown-offender scenarios -- always check which of the three triggers actually applies on the facts before calculating whether a complaint is time-barred, rather than defaulting to the date of the offence.

sections.title: Exclusion of time in certain cases
sections.raw_text:
516. Exclusion of time in certain cases.—(1) In computing the period of limitation, the time during
which any person has been prosecuting with due diligence another prosecution, whether in a Court of first
instance or in a Court of appeal or revision, against the offender, shall be excluded:
    Provided that no such exclusion shall be made unless the prosecution relates to the same facts and is
prosecuted in good faith in a Court which from defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature, is
unable to entertain it.
    (2) Where the institution of the prosecution in respect of an offence has been stayed by an injunction
or order, then, in computing the period of limitation, the period of the continuance of the injunction or order,
the day on which it was issued or made, and the day on which it was withdrawn, shall be excluded.
     (3) Where notice of prosecution for an offence has been given, or where, under any law for the time
being in force, the previous consent or sanction of the Government or any other authority is required for
the institution of any prosecution for an offence, then, in computing the period of limitation, the period of
such notice or, as the case may be, the time required for obtaining such consent or sanction shall be
excluded.
    Explanation.—In computing the time required for obtaining the consent or sanction of the Government
or any other authority, the date on which the application was made for obtaining the consent or sanction
and the date of receipt of the order of the Government or other authority shall both be excluded.
    (4) In computing the period of limitation, the time during which the offender—
         (a) has been absent from India or from any territory outside India which is under the administration
    of the Central Government; or
        (b) has avoided arrest by absconding or concealing himself,
shall be excluded.

breakdown.plain_summary: This provision excludes several categories of time from counting against the limitation clock, effectively extending the practical window for taking cognizance in fairness-driven circumstances. Sub-section (1): time spent diligently prosecuting another proceeding on the same facts, in a Court unable to entertain it for jurisdictional or similar defects, is excluded -- so a complainant who genuinely (and diligently, good-faith) pursued the wrong forum first isn't penalized for that detour. Sub-section (2): where a prosecution's institution was stayed by an injunction/order, the entire period of the stay (including its start and end days) is excluded. Sub-section (3): where prosecution requires prior notice or Government/authority consent/sanction, the time spent on that notice period or awaiting consent/sanction is excluded, with the Explanation clarifying that both the application date and the date the order is received are excluded from the count. Sub-section (4): time during which the offender was absent from India (or Central-Government-administered territory outside India), or was evading arrest by absconding/concealing himself, is excluded -- so a fugitive cannot simply outlast the limitation period by fleeing or hiding.
essential_elements: Time diligently spent prosecuting another same-facts proceeding, in good faith, in a Court unable to entertain it for jurisdictional/similar defects, is excluded.
The full period a prosecution's institution was stayed by injunction/order (including the issuance and withdrawal days) is excluded.
Time spent on a required prosecution notice, or awaiting Government/authority consent/sanction (including application and receipt dates), is excluded.
Time the offender was absent from India/Central-Government territory, or evading arrest by absconding/concealing himself, is excluded.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The sub-section (1) exclusion for a prior prosecution requires both good faith and that the earlier Court's inability to entertain it stemmed from jurisdictional or similar defects -- not any and all earlier prosecutions qualify.
breakdown.how_to_read: When calculating whether a complaint is time-barred under section 514, always check each of these four exclusion categories against the case facts before concluding the period has actually expired -- genuine delay caused by these specific circumstances doesn't count against the complainant.

sections.title: Exclusion of date on which Court is closed
sections.raw_text:
517. Exclusion of date on which Court is closed.—Where the period of limitation expires on a day
when the Court is closed, the Court may take cognizance on the day on which the Court reopens.
    Explanation.—A Court shall be deemed to be closed on any day within the meaning of this section, if,
during its normal working hours, it remains closed on that day.

breakdown.plain_summary: A practical accommodation for court-closure timing: if the limitation period happens to expire on a day the Court is closed, the Court may still take cognizance on the day it reopens -- the closure doesn't extinguish the right merely because the deadline fell on a non-working day. The Explanation clarifies 'closed' means the Court remains closed throughout its normal working hours on that day.
essential_elements: If the limitation period expires on a day the Court is closed, cognizance may be taken on the day the Court reopens.
A Court is 'closed' for this purpose if it remains closed throughout its normal working hours on that day.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a straightforward calendar-accommodation rule, analogous to general limitation-law principles that a deadline falling on a holiday/closed day rolls over to the next working day.

sections.title: Continuing offence
sections.raw_text:
518. Continuing offence.—In the case of a continuing offence, a fresh period of limitation shall begin
to run at every moment of the time during which the offence continues.

breakdown.plain_summary: This addresses offences that are not a single, completed act but an ongoing state of affairs (a 'continuing offence'): for such offences, a fresh limitation period starts running at every single moment the offence continues -- meaning the limitation clock effectively never fully expires as long as the offending conduct persists, since each moment generates its own new starting point.
essential_elements: For a continuing offence, a fresh period of limitation begins at every moment during which the offence continues.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a significant practical safeguard against limitation defeating prosecution of ongoing wrongs -- when assessing time-bar arguments, first determine whether the offence charged is a single completed act (ordinary limitation rules under sections 514-515 apply) or a continuing offence (limitation effectively resets continuously under this section).

sections.title: Extension of period of limitation in certain cases
sections.raw_text:
519. Extension of period of limitation in certain cases.—Notwithstanding anything contained in the
foregoing provisions of this Chapter, any Court may take cognizance of an offence after the expiry of the
period of limitation, if it is satisfied on the facts and in the circumstances of the case that the delay has been
properly explained or that it is necessary so to do in the interests of justice.

breakdown.plain_summary: This closes Chapter XXXVIII with an overriding judicial discretion: notwithstanding everything else in the Chapter, a Court may still take cognizance of an offence even after the limitation period has expired, if satisfied -- on the facts and circumstances of the case -- either that the delay has been properly explained, or that taking cognizance despite the delay is necessary in the interests of justice. This functions as a safety valve preventing the limitation bar from becoming an absolute, mechanical rule that defeats genuine, explicable, or justice-demanding cases.
essential_elements: A Court may take cognizance of an offence after the limitation period has expired, notwithstanding the Chapter's other provisions.
This requires the Court's satisfaction, on the case's facts and circumstances, either that the delay is properly explained or that cognizance is necessary in the interests of justice.
exceptions_and_qualifications: This is a discretionary override, not an automatic extension -- the Court must be affirmatively satisfied on one of the two specified grounds before proceeding despite the expired limitation period.
breakdown.how_to_read: This closes Chapter XXXVIII (Limitation for Taking Cognizance of Certain Offences), sections 513-519, as a complete, self-contained scheme: the bar itself (514), its commencement (515), exclusions (516-517), the continuing-offence exception (518), and this final discretionary extension safety valve (519). Chapter XXXIX (Miscellaneous) begins immediately after at section 520.

sections.title: Trials before High Courts
sections.raw_text: 520. Trials before High Courts.—When an offence is tried by the High Court otherwise than under section 447, it shall, in the trial of the offence, observe the same procedure as a Court of Sessions would observe if it were trying the case.

breakdown.plain_summary: This opens Chapter XXXIX, the Sanhita's final miscellaneous chapter. When the High Court itself tries an offence as a trial court (not on appeal, and not under section 447's separate procedure for contempt of subordinate courts), it must follow the same trial procedure that a Court of Sessions would use for that case -- the High Court does not get a different, simplified procedure merely because of its higher status.
essential_elements: The High Court is trying an offence directly (as a trial court), not hearing an appeal or revision.
The trial is not being conducted under section 447 (which has its own dedicated procedure).
The High Court must observe the same procedure a Court of Sessions would use for that case.
breakdown.how_to_read: High Courts trying criminal cases as a court of first instance are rare in practice, but where it happens, this section ensures procedural uniformity -- the same safeguards (charge, evidence, arguments) that would apply in a Sessions trial apply here too, just before a higher forum.

sections.title: Delivery to commanding officers of persons liable to be tried by Court-martial
sections.raw_text:
521. Delivery to commanding officers of persons liable to be tried by Court-martial.—(1) The Central Government may make rules consistent with this Sanhita and the Air Force Act, 1950 (45 of 1950), the Army Act, 1950 (46 of 1950), the Navy Act, 1957 (62 of 1957), and any other law, relating to the Armed Forces of the Union, for the time being in force, as to cases in which persons subject to army, naval or air-force law, or such other law, shall be tried by a Court to which this Sanhita applies, or by a Court-martial; and when any person is brought before a Magistrate and charged with an offence for which he is liable to be tried either by a Court to which this Sanhita applies or by a Court-martial, such Magistrate shall have regard to such rules, and shall in proper cases deliver him, together with a statement of the offence of which he is accused, to the commanding officer of the unit to which he belongs, or to the commanding officer of the nearest army, naval or air-force station, as the case may be, for the purpose of being tried by a Court-martial.
    Explanation.—In this section—
        (a) “unit” includes a regiment, corps, ship, detachment, group, battalion or company;
       (b) “Court-martial” includes any Tribunal with the powers similar to those of a Court-martial constituted under the relevant law applicable to the Armed Forces of the Union.
    (2) Every Magistrate shall, on receiving a written application for that purpose by the commanding officer of any unit or body of soldiers, sailors or airmen stationed or employed at any such place, use his utmost endeavours to apprehend and secure any person accused of such offence.
    (3) A High Court may, if it thinks fit, direct that a prisoner detained in any jail situate within the State be brought before a Court-martial for trial or to be examined touching any matter pending before the Court-martial.

breakdown.plain_summary: This section resolves the overlap between ordinary criminal courts and military justice. The Central Government can make rules deciding, for persons subject to military law, whether they are tried by an ordinary criminal court under this Sanhita or by a Court-martial. When such a person is charged before a Magistrate, the Magistrate must follow those rules and, where appropriate, hand the accused over to their commanding officer for a Court-martial instead of proceeding under this Sanhita. Magistrates must also actively help commanding officers apprehend such accused persons on request, and a High Court can order a prisoner already in civil custody produced before a Court-martial.
essential_elements: The Central Government may frame rules, consistent with this Sanhita and the Armed Forces Acts, governing whether a person subject to military law is tried by an ordinary Court or by Court-martial.
A Magistrate before whom such a person is charged must have regard to those rules and, in proper cases, deliver the accused (with a statement of the offence) to the appropriate commanding officer.
On written application from a commanding officer, every Magistrate must use utmost endeavours to apprehend and secure the accused person.
A High Court may direct that a prisoner in a State jail be produced before a Court-martial for trial or examination.
exceptions_and_qualifications: “Unit” is defined broadly to include a regiment, corps, ship, detachment, group, battalion or company.
“Court-martial” is defined to include any Tribunal with powers similar to a Court-martial under the law applicable to the Armed Forces of the Union.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is one of the coordination points between civilian criminal procedure and military law -- it does not itself decide which forum tries a case, but sets up the mechanism (Central Government rules, Magistrate cooperation, High Court directions) by which that choice is implemented in practice.

sections.title: Forms
sections.raw_text: 522. Forms.—Subject to the power conferred by article 227 of the Constitution, the forms set forth in the Second Schedule, with such variations as the circumstances of each case require, may be used for the respective purposes therein mentioned, and if used shall be sufficient.

breakdown.plain_summary: The Sanhita's Second Schedule contains model forms (for summonses, warrants, charges, and similar documents). Using these forms, adapted as each case requires, is legally sufficient -- courts and officials do not need to draft such documents from scratch or worry about minor variations, so long as the High Court's own rule-making power under article 227 of the Constitution is respected.
essential_elements: The forms in the Second Schedule may be used, with variations suited to each case's circumstances.
Using a prescribed form for its stated purpose is legally sufficient.
This is subject to the High Court's power under article 227 of the Constitution (superintendence over subordinate courts, which includes prescribing forms and practice).
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a practical drafting-and-compliance provision: if a summons, warrant, or similar document follows the Second Schedule's model form (adapted as needed), it cannot be challenged merely for not using different wording.

sections.title: Power of High Court to make rules

breakdown.plain_summary: Each High Court, with the State Government's prior approval, can make rules governing 'petition-writers' -- non-advocate persons permitted to draft petitions for litigants in the criminal courts under it -- including who may act as one, how licences are issued, what fees they may charge, and penalties for breaking these rules. All such rules must be published in the Official Gazette to take effect.
essential_elements: The High Court makes the rules, but only with the State Government's previous approval.
The rules may govern: who may act as a petition-writer, licensing and conduct, fee scales, and penalties (with the authority to investigate and impose them) for contravention.
The High Court may also make rules on any other matter the State Government is required or permitted to provide for by rules.
Every rule made under this section must be published in the Official Gazette.
breakdown.how_to_read: Petition-writers are a recognised, regulated category assisting unrepresented litigants in lower criminal courts (distinct from enrolled advocates); this section is the source of the licensing regime that governs them in each State.

sections.title: Power to alter functions allocated to Executive Magistrate in certain cases
sections.raw_text: 524. Power to alter functions allocated to Executive Magistrate in certain cases.—If the Legislative Assembly of a State by a resolution so permits, the State Government may, after consultation with the High Court, by notification, direct that references in sections 127, 128, 129, 164 and 166 to an Executive Magistrate shall be construed as references to a Judicial Magistrate of the first class.
key_terms: Judicial Magistrate of the first class

breakdown.plain_summary: Certain functions under sections 127, 128, 129, 164, and 166 (all dealing with unlawful assemblies and use of force to disperse them) are ordinarily assigned to Executive Magistrates. This section lets a State, if its Legislative Assembly passes a resolution permitting it, shift those functions to Judicial Magistrates of the first class instead, by State Government notification issued after consulting the High Court.
essential_elements: The State's Legislative Assembly must first pass a resolution permitting the change.
The State Government then consults the High Court.
The State Government issues a notification redirecting references to 'Executive Magistrate' in sections 127, 128, 129, 164, and 166 to mean 'Judicial Magistrate of the first class' instead.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a State-specific opt-in mechanism: it does not itself change who exercises these dispersal-of-assembly powers nationally, but gives individual States a constitutionally sanctioned route to move that function from the executive to the judicial magistracy if their legislature and High Court agree.

sections.title: Cases in which Judge or Magistrate is personally interested
sections.raw_text:
525. Cases in which Judge or Magistrate is personally interested.—No Judge or Magistrate shall, except with the permission of the Court to which an appeal lies from his Court, try or commit for trial any case to or in which he is a party, or personally interested, and no Judge or Magistrate shall hear an appeal from any judgment or order passed or made by himself.
    Explanation.—A Judge or Magistrate shall not be deemed to be a party to, or personally interested in, any case by reason only that he is concerned therein in a public capacity, or by reason only that he has viewed the place in which an offence is alleged to have been committed, or any other place in which any other transaction material to the case is alleged to have occurred, and made an inquiry in connection with the case.

breakdown.plain_summary: This codifies the rule against bias: a Judge or Magistrate cannot try or commit for trial a case in which they are personally a party or personally interested, unless the appellate court above them permits it. They also can never hear an appeal from their own earlier judgment or order. The Explanation clarifies that merely acting in an official/public capacity, or having visited the crime scene or another relevant site to make an inquiry, does not by itself make a Judge or Magistrate 'interested' in the case.
essential_elements: A Judge or Magistrate must not try or commit for trial any case in which they are a party or personally interested.
The only exception is with the express permission of the Court to which an appeal from their Court lies.
A Judge or Magistrate can never hear an appeal from a judgment or order they themselves passed.
Acting in a public/official capacity, or having viewed the offence scene or a related site for the purpose of inquiry, does not count as being a party or personally interested.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The Explanation is itself an exception-defining clause: it narrows what 'personally interested' means so that ordinary judicial functions (site inspections, acting in one's official capacity) don't trigger disqualification.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a natural-justice safeguard (nemo judex in causa sua -- no one should judge their own cause) with a narrow, permission-based escape valve; a challenge to a Judge's or Magistrate's participation on bias grounds should be tested against both the general rule and the Explanation's carve-outs.

sections.title: Practising advocate not to sit as Magistrate in certain Courts
sections.raw_text: 526. Practising advocate not to sit as Magistrate in certain Courts.—No advocate who practices in the Court of any Magistrate shall sit as a Magistrate in that Court or in any Court within the local jurisdiction of that Court.

breakdown.plain_summary: An advocate who practises before a particular Magistrate's Court is barred from ever sitting as a Magistrate in that same Court, or in any other Court within that Court's local jurisdiction -- preventing an obvious conflict of interest between a lawyer's practice and judicial office in the same local forum.
essential_elements: The bar applies to an advocate who practises in the Court of a particular Magistrate.
That advocate cannot sit as Magistrate in that same Court.
The bar extends to any other Court within the local jurisdiction of that Court as well.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is another conflict-of-interest safeguard, complementing section 525's bias rule -- it prevents the structural problem of a practising lawyer adjudicating in the very local judicial ecosystem where they appear as counsel.

sections.title: Public servant concerned in sale not to purchase or bid for property
sections.raw_text: 527. Public servant concerned in sale not to purchase or bid for property.—A public servant having any duty to perform in connection with the sale of any property under this Sanhita shall not purchase or bid for the property.

breakdown.plain_summary: A public servant who has an official duty relating to a sale of property conducted under this Sanhita (for example, a sale of confiscated or unclaimed property under Chapter XXXVI) is barred from purchasing that property or bidding for it themselves.
essential_elements: The public servant must have some duty to perform in connection with the particular sale.
That public servant is prohibited from purchasing the property being sold.
The public servant is equally prohibited from bidding for it.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is a straightforward anti-self-dealing rule for property sales conducted under the Sanhita's own procedures (e.g., disposal of case property) -- it prevents the official running or supervising the sale from also being its buyer.

sections.title: Saving of inherent powers of High Court
sections.raw_text: 528. Saving of inherent powers of High Court.—Nothing in this Sanhita shall be deemed to limit or affect the inherent powers of the High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under this Sanhita, or to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the Sanhita's counterpart to the old Code's section 482 -- it preserves the High Court's broad, residual inherent powers untouched by anything else in the Sanhita. The High Court can still make whatever orders are necessary to give effect to its own or a subordinate court's orders, to stop abuse of any Court's process, or more generally to secure the ends of justice, regardless of whether a specific provision elsewhere in the Sanhita covers the situation.
essential_elements: The High Court's inherent powers are not limited or affected by anything in this Sanhita.
Those powers extend to making orders necessary to give effect to any order under this Sanhita.
They also extend to preventing abuse of the process of any Court.
They also extend, more broadly, to securing the ends of justice.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is one of the most powerful and frequently invoked provisions in criminal practice (quashing of FIRs and proceedings, staying trials, and other extraordinary relief typically rest on this section) -- a petition invoking it should tie the relief sought to one of the three named purposes: giving effect to an order, preventing abuse of process, or securing the ends of justice.

sections.title: Duty of High Court to exercise continuous superintendence over Courts
sections.raw_text: 529. Duty of High Court to exercise continuous superintendence over Courts.—Every High Court shall so exercise its superintendence over the Courts of Session and Courts of Judicial Magistrates subordinate to it as to ensure that there is an expeditious and proper disposal of cases by the Judges and Magistrates.

breakdown.plain_summary: Every High Court has an affirmative duty -- not merely a power -- to continuously superintend the Courts of Session and Judicial Magistrates below it, specifically so as to ensure cases are disposed of both expeditiously and properly.
essential_elements: Every High Court must exercise superintendence over subordinate Courts of Session and Courts of Judicial Magistrates.
That superintendence must be exercised so as to ensure expeditious disposal of cases.
It must also ensure proper disposal of cases -- speed alone is not the goal.
breakdown.how_to_read: This duty-framing (as opposed to a mere discretionary power) underlies High Courts' administrative oversight of trial-court pendency and delay, and is often cited alongside section 528's inherent powers when seeking directions for expeditious disposal of a stalled case.

sections.title: Trial and proceedings to be held in electronic mode

breakdown.plain_summary: This is a sweeping, general enabling provision (new to the BNSS, without a direct predecessor in the old Code) that authorises essentially the entire criminal process -- trials, inquiries, and other proceedings, including issuing and serving summonses and warrants, examining complainants and witnesses, recording evidence, and appeals -- to be conducted electronically, using electronic communication or audio-video means, instead of requiring physical presence.
essential_elements: The provision covers all trials, inquiries and proceedings under the Sanhita.
It expressly lists issuance, service and execution of summons and warrant as coverable.
It expressly lists examination of complainant and witnesses as coverable.
It expressly lists recording of evidence in inquiries and trials as coverable.
It expressly lists all appellate proceedings or any other proceeding as coverable.
Such proceedings 'may' -- not must -- be held electronically, by electronic communication or audio-video electronic means.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is the Sanhita's technology-modernisation cornerstone, working together with the electronic-FIR, electronic-summons, and electronic-evidence provisions found earlier in the Sanhita -- it is permissive ('may'), so a party cannot demand a purely electronic proceeding as of right, but it removes any doubt that courts and police may lawfully conduct these steps online.

sections.title: Repeal and savings

breakdown.plain_summary: This is the Sanhita's final section, and its transition bridge from the old law to the new. Subsection (1) repeals the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, outright. But subsections (2) and (3) are 'savings' clauses softening that repeal's impact: pending appeals, applications, trials, inquiries, and investigations continue under the old Code as if the Sanhita never came into force; things already done under the old Code (notifications, forms, jurisdictions, sentences, orders, rules, and most appointments) are deemed to have been done under the new Sanhita's equivalent provisions; and sanctions or consents already given but not yet acted upon carry over to support proceedings under the new Sanhita. Subsection (3), however, is a limit on that generosity: if a limitation period under the old Code had already expired before the Sanhita commenced, the Sanhita's own (possibly longer) limitation periods cannot be used to revive it.
essential_elements: Subsection (1): the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is repealed.
Subsection (2)(a): matters pending immediately before commencement continue to be governed by the old Code as if the Sanhita had not come into force.

Subsection (2)(b): notifications, proclamations, conferred powers, prescribed forms, defined jurisdictions, passed sentences, and orders/rules/appointments (other than Special Magistrate appointments) made under the old Code and still in force are deemed made under the Sanhita's corresponding provisions.

Subsection (2)(c): sanctions or consents given under the old Code, where no proceeding had yet begun, are deemed given under the Sanhita, and proceedings may now be commenced under the Sanhita on that basis.

Subsection (3): where a limitation period under the old Code had already expired before the Sanhita commenced, the Sanhita's provisions (including any longer periods or extension mechanisms) cannot be used to enable an application or proceeding that was already time-barred.
exceptions_and_qualifications: Appointments as Special Magistrates are expressly carved out of subsection (2)(b)'s savings -- they are not automatically deemed to continue under the Sanhita.
Subsection (3) is itself an exception to the generally generous savings scheme -- it prevents the Sanhita's provisions from reviving claims already dead under the old Code's limitation rules.
breakdown.how_to_read: This closing section is essential in any transitional dispute over whether the old Code or the new Sanhita governs a given case: the default rule is 'pending matters continue under the old Code, everything else deemed carried over,' but always check subsection (3) where limitation has already run out under the old Code before concluding the new Sanhita revives it.
